array.tldr: Lay the array out as a line of prefix sums or a sorted axis, and every "sum equals/at-most/closest target" question collapses into a complement lookup, a two-pointer sweep, or a knapsack over indices.
insight: The unifying move is to stop thinking about the *values* and start thinking about a derived 1-D structure over the array: either the **prefix-sum array** `P[i]=A[0..i-1]` (for *contiguous subarray* sums) or a **sorted copy** (for *unordered pair/triple* sums). Once you have that structure, a target query `sum(i..j)=K` becomes `P[j]-P[i]=K`, i.e. "have I seen the complement `P[j]-K`?" — answered in `O(1)` by a **hash map**, or by **two pointers** converging on a sorted line, or by **binary search**. The interviewer is probing whether you recognize that *contiguity* maps to prefix-sum differences while *combination/subset* maps to choosing elements, and that **sortedness** is the lever that turns `O(n^2)`/`O(n^3)` brute force into `O(n log n)` or linear sweeps.

The split is structural. When order is fixed and you want a *window/subarray*, prefix sums plus a hash map (exact `K`, divisible-by-`K`, range counts) or a **monotonic deque** (shortest subarray ≥ `K` with negatives) is the tool. When order is free and you want a *fixed-size tuple* summing to a target, **sort then two-pointer** (`2Sum`/`3Sum`/`4Sum` family, fixing `k-2` outer indices). When you may pick *any subset/multiset* to hit a target, the array becomes the item list of a **subset-sum / knapsack DP** or backtracking with pruning. Recognizing which of these three regimes a problem lives in is the whole game.
tricks: **Prefix-sum + hashmap** for *contiguous* exact-target: count/find `j` with `P[j]-K` seen. Seed the map with `{0:1}` (or index `-1`) so prefixes that themselves equal `K` are counted.

**Sort + two pointers** for *unordered* fixed-arity sums: fix the outer index/indices, then shrink `lo<hi` inward — move `lo` up when sum is too small, `hi` down when too big. Skip duplicate values at every level to dedupe results without a set.

For **closest / at-most-K** variants, don't require exact equality: track best `|sum-target|` (3Sum Closest) or add `hi-lo` to the count when `sum<target` (3Sum Smaller), still in one two-pointer pass.
For **divisible-by-K / range** counting, key the hashmap on `P[j] mod K` (normalize negatives with `((r%K)+K)%K`), or use a **BIT/merge-sort** over prefix sums for `lower<=P[j]-P[i]<=upper` ranges.

**Negatives break the sliding window**: a plain shrinking window only works when all elements are non-negative (209). With negatives and a lower bound (862), switch to a **monotonic-increasing deque** over prefix sums. For circular max-sum (918) use total minus the min-subarray.

**Subset/knapsack** targets: 1-D boolean/int DP indexed by achievable sum, iterating the array as items; reverse the inner loop for 0/1 (each element once, 416/494) vs. forward for unbounded order-counting (377). Backtracking variants prune by sorting and breaking when the sorted candidate exceeds the remaining target (39/40/216).

problems.title: Two Sum
problems.note: Walk the array once keeping a hashmap value->index; for each `x` check if `target-x` was already seen. Unsorted array, so the complement lookup replaces sorting.

problems.title: 3Sum
problems.note: Sort, fix index `i`, then two-pointer `lo/hi` on the suffix to hit `-A[i]`; skip equal values at all three levels to dedupe triples in `O(n^2)`.

problems.title: 3Sum Closest
problems.note: Same sort + fix-one + two-pointer sweep, but instead of equality track the running minimum `|A[i]+A[lo]+A[hi]-target|` and return that closest sum.

problems.title: 4Sum
problems.note: Sort, fix two outer indices `i<j`, two-pointer the remaining suffix for `target-A[i]-A[j]`; dedupe at each of the four levels, `O(n^3)`.

problems.title: Combination Sum
problems.note: Backtrack over the (sorted) array picking elements with reuse allowed; subtract from remaining target and prune when a candidate exceeds the remainder. Unbounded subset-sum enumeration.

problems.title: Combination Sum II
problems.note: Same backtracking but each array element used once; sort and skip duplicate candidates at the same recursion depth to avoid repeated combinations.

problems.title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
problems.note: Array is already sorted, so two pointers from both ends move inward by comparing `A[lo]+A[hi]` to target — `O(n)`, no hashmap needed.

problems.title: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
problems.note: All-positive array lets a sliding window grow the right edge and shrink the left while the window sum `>= target`, tracking the minimum length in one pass.

problems.title: Combination Sum III
problems.note: Backtrack choosing `k` distinct numbers from `1..9` whose sum is `n`; prune on count and on remaining sum bounds. Fixed-size subset-sum over a tiny implicit array.

problems.title: 3Sum Smaller
problems.note: Sort, fix `i`, two-pointer: when `A[i]+A[lo]+A[hi] < target`, all `hi-lo` pairs qualify, so add `hi-lo` and advance `lo`; else decrement `hi`.

problems.title: Count of Range Sum
problems.note: Build prefix sums, then count pairs `i<j` with `lower <= P[j]-P[i] <= upper` using merge sort (or a BIT) over the prefix array for `O(n log n)`.

problems.title: Max Sum of Rectangle No Larger Than K
problems.note: Fix a column pair, compress rows into a 1-D array, then for that array find the max subarray sum `<= K` via prefix sums in an ordered set (best `P[j]-P[i]<=K` lookup).

problems.title: Combination Sum IV
problems.note: Order counts, so it is an unbounded-knapsack count DP: `dp[t] = sum over a in A of dp[t-a]`, iterating target outer and the array inner.

problems.title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
problems.note: Reduce to subset-sum for `total/2`: 1-D boolean DP over achievable sums, iterating each array element with the inner loop reversed (0/1 knapsack).

problems.title: Target Sum
problems.note: Assigning +/- signs reduces to counting subsets summing to `(total+target)/2`; a 1-D count DP over the array elements (0/1, reversed inner loop) gives the answer.

problems.title: Continuous Subarray Sum
problems.note: Hashmap of first-seen `prefix mod k` index; a later index with the same remainder means the subarray between them is divisible by `k` (length `>= 2` check).

problems.title: Subarray Sum Equals K
problems.note: The canonical prefix-sum + hashmap: count occurrences of `prefix-K` seen so far, seeding `{0:1}`, for `O(n)` exact-sum subarray counting.

problems.title: Two Sum IV - Input is a BST
problems.note: Flatten/traverse the BST into a (sorted) value stream and apply Two Sum — hashset of seen values, or two pointers on the in-order array.

problems.title: Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets
problems.note: Target each bucket at `total/k`; backtrack assigning array elements to `k` buckets with pruning (sort descending, skip full buckets, bitmask memo) — multi-way subset-sum.

problems.title: Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K
problems.note: Negatives break the simple window, so use a monotonic-increasing deque over prefix sums: pop front while `P[j]-P[front] >= K` (record length), pop back to keep prefixes increasing.

problems.title: Maximum Sum Circular Subarray
problems.note: Max circular sum is `max(non-wrapping Kadane, total - min-subarray)`; both are prefix/running-sum sweeps over the array, with the all-negative edge case guarded.

problems.title: 3Sum With Multiplicity
problems.note: Count value frequencies, then two-pointer/iterate over distinct values summing to target, multiplying counts (handling the equal-value `C(n,2)`/`C(n,3)` cases) modulo `1e9+7`.

problems.title: Binary Subarrays With Sum
problems.note: Prefix-sum + hashmap counting subarrays summing to `goal` (works because entries are 0/1); equivalently `atMost(goal)-atMost(goal-1)` with a sliding window.

problems.title: Subarray Sums Divisible by K
problems.note: Hashmap of counts of `prefix mod K` (normalize negatives to `[0,K)`); each prior same-remainder prefix forms a divisible subarray, summed via `C(count,2)`-style accumulation.

problems.title: Two Sum Less Than K
problems.note: Sort, then two pointers: when `A[lo]+A[hi] < K` update the best sum and advance `lo`, else decrement `hi` — maximize the largest pair-sum under `K`.

problems.title: Max Number of K-Sum Pairs
problems.note: Either sort + two pointers removing matched ends, or a hashmap of counts pairing `x` with `k-x`; each successful pair increments the operation count.

problems.title: Maximum Sum of Distinct Subarrays With Length K
problems.note: Fixed-size sliding window of length `k` maintaining a running sum and a frequency map; the window is valid (all distinct) when its size equals its distinct count, then track the max sum.

problems.title: Prime Pairs With Target Sum
problems.note: Sieve primes up to `n`, then a Two-Sum-style scan: for each prime `x <= n/2`, check if `n-x` is also prime, collecting the pairs.

problems.title: 3Sum With Multiplicity
problems.note: See above: frequency-count the array values and combine distinct value-triples summing to target via combinatorial counts, modulo `1e9+7`.

problems.title: Solve and optimize 3Sum and variants at scale
problems.note: Generalize the sort + fix-`(k-2)`-indices + two-pointer template across the kSum family, layering dedup, early-termination pruning (smallest/largest bounds), and hashing to push from brute force to optimal complexity at scale.

tree.tldr: Sum/Target on trees is just DFS where every node returns or accumulates a sum — root-to-leaf path sums, max-gain branch sums, or whole-subtree sums — and the answer is read off at leaves, at the root, or via a running prefix.
insight: A binary tree turns a **sum problem** into a **recursion problem**: the recursive call boundary *is* the structural decomposition. Every node's answer is a pure function of its `val` plus the results returned by its two children, so you pick exactly one of three accumulation contracts — (1) **downward running sum** passed as a parameter and tested at leaves (`#112/#113/#129`), (2) **upward subtree aggregate** returned from the call so a parent can combine left+right (`#124/#10014`), or (3) a **prefix-sum over the current root-to-node path** stored in a hash map for O(n) counting (`#437`). The interviewer is probing whether you can identify *which direction the sum flows* and *where the target is checked*.

The decisive subtlety is the difference between a **path that must terminate at a leaf** versus a **path/branch usable mid-tree**. Root-to-leaf problems only commit an answer when `left == right == null`; max-path-sum and prefix-sum problems must consider partial paths that bend through an internal node, which forces the split between what a node *returns* to its parent (a single downward branch, never both children) and what it *records globally* (the full bent path). Conflating these two quantities is the canonical bug.
tricks: Decide the sum's direction first: **downward** (pass `acc` as a parameter, decide at leaves) vs **upward** (return subtree/branch sum, combine in parent). Mixing them silently breaks the recurrence.
For root-to-leaf targets, the base case is `node && !node.left && !node.right` — checking `node == null` alone double-counts or wrongly accepts single-child internal nodes as leaves.

In `#124` the value **returned** to the parent is `val + max(0, leftGain, only one side)` — a single branch — while the value used to **update the global max** is `val + max(0,L) + max(0,R)` (both sides, the path's apex). Clamp negative gains to `0`.

`#437` is prefix-sum-on-a-path: maintain a `map[runningSum] -> count`, add `map[running - target]`, and **decrement the map on the way back up** (backtrack) so counts don't leak across sibling subtrees.
Build the root-to-leaf number in `#129` as `acc = acc*10 + val`, accumulating digits positionally, not by string concatenation.
When a problem returns an aggregate (`#10014`, `#124`), do post-order: children must resolve before the parent can compute its sum.
tree.pseudo:
// Pattern A — downward running sum, decide at leaf (#112/#113/#129)
dfs(node, acc):
    if node == null: return
    acc += node.val            // or acc = acc*10 + node.val for #129
    if isLeaf(node): handle(acc)     // compare to target / collect / sum
    dfs(node.left, acc); dfs(node.right, acc)

// Pattern B — upward subtree/branch aggregate (#124/#10014)
gain(node):
    if node == null: return 0
    L = max(0, gain(node.left)); R = max(0, gain(node.right))
    best = max(best, node.val + L + R)   // path bending at node (#124)
    return node.val + max(L, R)          // single branch to parent

// Pattern C — prefix-sum over current path (#437)
count(node, run, map):
    if node == null: return
    run += node.val; total += map[run - target]
    map[run]++; count(left); count(right); map[run]--   // backtrack

problems.title: Path Sum
problems.note: Downward running-sum DFS: carry `acc` down, and at a true leaf (`!left && !right`) return whether `acc == targetSum`; OR-combine the two child calls.

problems.title: Path Sum II
problems.note: Same downward accumulation as #112 but collect the full path: push `node.val`, on a leaf with `acc == target` snapshot the path, then pop on backtrack so siblings reuse a clean prefix.

problems.title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
problems.note: Post-order `gain` returns the best single downward branch `val + max(0,L,R)`, while a global max is updated with the bent path `val + max(0,L) + max(0,R)`; negative branches are clamped to 0 so they're dropped.

problems.title: Sum Root to Leaf Numbers
problems.note: Downward accumulation with positional digits: `acc = acc*10 + node.val`; at each leaf add `acc` to the running total — the leaf value is the decoded root-to-leaf number.

problems.title: Path Sum III
problems.note: Prefix-sum-on-path: maintain `map[runningSum]->count`, add `map[running - target]` to count downward paths ending at the current node, and decrement the map on backtrack so counts don't bleed into sibling subtrees — O(n).

problems.title: Set second tree values by subtree sums (T2 ← sum of T1 subtree)
problems.note: Upward aggregate over two shape-identical trees: a post-order DFS returns each T1 node's subtree sum (`val + leftSum + rightSum`) and writes it into the corresponding T2 node during the same traversal, in O(n).

matrices.tldr: Collapse one matrix dimension into 1-D column-prefix sums, then on each row-band run a "best subarray sum closest to K" scan using an ordered set of prefix sums.
insight: A 2-D **sum/target** problem on a **matrix** reduces to a 1-D problem by fixing a pair of row boundaries (`top`, `bottom`) and compressing every column in that band into a single value via **column prefix sums**. Once a band is fixed, the question "max submatrix sum ≤ K" becomes "max subarray sum ≤ K" over the compressed row — the matrix has been flattened along one axis while the other axis is brute-forced. This row-pair enumeration is the structural key: it turns an intractable O(n^4) rectangle search into a tractable per-band 1-D scan.

The 1-D subproblem (max subarray sum ≤ K) is itself the real probe: a plain sliding window fails because entries can be **negative**, so you cannot grow/shrink monotonically. The fix is to scan prefix sums `S[j]` and, for each `j`, find the smallest earlier prefix `S[i] ≥ S[j] − K`, giving `S[j] − S[i] ≤ K` maximized — done with an **ordered set / balanced BST** and a `lowerBound` query. The interviewer is probing whether you recognize that dimensionality reduction plus an ordered-set bound query, not a naive window, is what handles the ≤K constraint with negatives.
tricks: Iterate over the **smaller dimension** as the fixed pair: if `rows > cols`, transpose so column-compression runs O(min(m,n)^2 · max · log max) instead of the other way — a real constant-factor (and complexity) win.
Use **column-cumulative arrays**: for fixed `top`, extend a running `colSum[c] += matrix[bottom][c]` as `bottom` descends, so each band is built incrementally in O(cols) rather than recomputing.

The inner 1-D step needs `lowerBound(S[j] − K)` over an ordered set of prior prefix sums; pre-seed the set with `0` to allow subarrays starting at index 0. Track the global best and short-circuit / return if it ever equals `K` exactly.
Pitfall: **negatives forbid sliding window** — Kadane gives max sum but not max sum *bounded by K*; you must use the prefix-set bound query. Don't reach for a monotonic-window trick.
Pitfall: query for `S[j] − K` (the *minimum* qualifying prefix), not `S[j] + K`; you want the largest sum that stays ≤ K, i.e. the smallest `S[i]` with `S[i] ≥ S[j] − K`.
If K is +∞ or no constraint, this degenerates to plain max-submatrix (Kadane per band) in O(min^2 · max) — know both forms.
matrices.pseudo:
best = -INF
for top in 0..rows-1:
    colSum = array of 0s, length cols
    for bottom in top..rows-1:
        for c in 0..cols-1: colSum[c] += matrix[bottom][c]   # compress band to 1-D row
        # 1-D: max subarray sum of colSum that is <= K
        seen = ordered_set({0}); prefix = 0
        for v in colSum:
            prefix += v
            it = seen.lowerBound(prefix - K)        # smallest S[i] >= prefix-K
            if it exists: best = max(best, prefix - it)
            seen.insert(prefix)
        if best == K: return K
return best

problems.title: Max Sum of Rectangle No Larger Than K
problems.note: Fix every pair of rows (top, bottom), compress the band into a 1-D column-sum array, then find the max subarray sum ≤ K via an ordered set of prefix sums using `lowerBound(prefix − K)`; transpose first to fix the smaller dimension. Negatives in the matrix are why a sliding window is replaced by the prefix-set bound query.

bst.tldr: Flatten a BST's sorted order via in-order traversal, then attack the sum/target with two-pointer or hash-set — the BST gives you sorted data for free.
insight: The unifying realization is that a **BST's in-order traversal yields a sorted array**, which converts a tree problem into a classic **Two Sum on a sorted sequence**. Once you see the sorted structure, the `target` constraint splits into two complementary halves: for any value `x`, you need `target - x`. The interviewer is probing whether you recognize that BST ordering is the bridge between an unstructured-looking tree and the well-known two-pointer / hash-set sum templates.

The structural condition that makes BST fit Sum/Target is the **monotonic ordering**: it lets a `two-pointer` walk converge (move left pointer up to increase the running sum, right pointer down to decrease it), giving `O(n)` time after flattening. Alternatively a `HashSet` lookup during a single traversal trades the sorted-array space for `O(n)` set space but needs no flattening. The deeper trick — true BST search — only pays off when you can prune: search for the complement `target - node.val` starting from the root, exploiting the BST property to get `O(n log n)` time and `O(h)` space without materializing the array.
tricks: **In-order = sorted**: flatten the BST in-order to an ascending array, then run the standard two-pointer `lo/hi` converging on `target` in `O(n)` time, `O(n)` space.

**Single-tree pitfall (#653)**: when searching for the complement with a `HashSet` during traversal, check `set.contains(target - node.val)` BEFORE inserting `node.val`, so a single node can't pair with itself (e.g. `target = 2*node.val`).

**Two-tree variant (#1214)**: you do NOT need both pointers in the same tree — flatten one tree ascending and the other descending, then two-pointer across the two arrays; or hash one tree's values and probe `target - x` for each value of the other.

**True BST pruning**: to avoid `O(n)` extra space, for each node search the *whole tree* (or the other tree) for `target - node.val` using BST navigation in `O(h)`, giving `O(n log n)` overall and `O(h)` recursion space.
**Reverse in-order**: a right→node→left traversal yields descending order — useful to get a high-side pointer or a descending stream for the two-tree case without reversing an array.
**Overflow / duplicates**: guard the self-pair case and beware that BSTs in these problems may not contain duplicates, so an exact complement match is a genuine distinct pair.

problems.title: Two Sum IV - Input is a BST
problems.note: In-order traverse the single BST into a sorted array and run a converging two-pointer for `target`; or do one DFS with a `HashSet`, checking `set.contains(k - node.val)` before inserting `node.val` to avoid pairing a node with itself.

problems.title: Two Sum BSTs
problems.note: Flatten `root1` ascending and `root2` descending (reverse in-order), then two-pointer across the two arrays toward `target`; equivalently hash all of `root1`'s values and, for each value `v` in `root2`, test whether `target - v` is in the set.

hash.tldr: Store what you've already seen so the matching value of `target - x` (or a prefix-sum residue) becomes an O(1) lookup instead of a nested scan.
insight: The unifying idea is **complement lookup**: any "two things must sum to T" or "contiguous run must sum to K" question can be rewritten as *"have I already seen the partner I need?"* A hash table answers that in O(1), collapsing an O(n^2) pair search or O(n^2) subarray scan into O(n). For pair problems the partner is `target - x`; for subarray problems the partner is a **prefix sum** `prefix - K` (or, under modular constraints, a matching **remainder** `prefix mod K`).

The structural condition that makes it apply: the answer depends only on *membership/count of previously observed values*, not their order or position — so you trade a sorted-structure / two-pointer pass for unordered O(1) membership. The interviewer is probing whether you recognize the **prefix-sum + hashmap** identity `sum(i..j) = P[j] - P[i-1]`, that you seed the map with `{0: 1}` (or `{0: -1}`) to count subarrays starting at index 0, and that for counting you must read the map for the complement *before* inserting the current value to avoid matching an element with itself.
tricks: **Pair problems**: iterate once; for each `x` check if `target - x` is already in the map *before* inserting `x` — this guarantees distinct indices and avoids reusing one element twice.

**Subarray = prefix-sum diff**: `count of subarrays summing to K` ⇒ run `prefix`, ask how many earlier prefixes equal `prefix - K`. Seed `map = {0: 1}` so prefixes equal to `K` themselves are counted.
Use **count maps, not seen-sets**, for #560/#974 — you need *how many* prior prefixes matched, not just whether one existed.
**Modular trick (#974)**: key on `((prefix % K) + K) % K`; equal remainders mean the gap is divisible by K. The `+K` normalizes negatives that `%` leaves signed.
Don't sort if it destroys index/order semantics — Two Sum returns indices, so the hashmap beats sort+two-pointer; but on an **already-sorted** input (#167) two pointers win on O(1) space.
Pitfall: duplicate values (e.g. `[3,3]`, target 6) — store the latest index or a list, but with the check-before-insert pattern a single stored index per value suffices.
hash.pseudo:
// PAIR: target sum -> return indices
seen = {}                       // value -> index
for i, x in enumerate(A):
    need = target - x
    if need in seen: return [seen[need], i]
    seen[x] = i

// SUBARRAY: count runs summing to K (mod variant: use prefix % K)
count = 0; prefix = 0
freq = {0: 1}                   // empty-prefix seed
for x in A:
    prefix += x
    count += freq.get(prefix - K, 0)     // complement prefix
    freq[prefix] += 1
return count

problems.title: Two Sum
problems.note: Canonical complement lookup: one pass storing value->index, and for each `x` return the pair as soon as `target - x` is in the map. Hashmap gives O(n) vs the O(n^2) brute force and preserves the original indices the problem demands.

problems.title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
problems.note: Solvable by the same complement-hashmap, but because the array is sorted the intended O(1)-space answer is two pointers converging from both ends; the hashmap framing is the contrast that shows when sortedness lets you drop the table.

problems.title: Subarray Sum Equals K
problems.note: Prefix-sum + count map: maintain running `prefix` and a frequency map of prior prefixes, adding `freq[prefix - K]` at each step (seeded with `{0:1}`). Each earlier matching prefix marks a subarray ending here that sums to K.

problems.title: Two Sum IV - Input is a BST
problems.note: Two Sum over tree values: traverse the BST and use a hash set of visited values, returning true when `k - node.val` was already seen. The hashmap turns tree-pair-search into the same O(n) complement check, ignoring BST order.

problems.title: Subarray Sums Divisible by K
problems.note: Prefix-sum on remainders: two prefixes with the same `prefix % K` bound a subarray divisible by K, so count pairs by hashing normalized remainders `((prefix%K)+K)%K`, seeded with `{0:1}`. Each repeated remainder contributes `C(freq,2)` divisible subarrays.

sorting.tldr: Sorting turns a Sum/Target search into a **monotone scan**: order the array once, then let **two pointers** (or fixed-prefix + two pointers) collapse the quadratic/cubic search by exploiting that moving inward predictably increases or decreases the running sum.
insight: The unifying idea is **monotonicity by ordering**. Once an array is sorted, the sum of a pair `a[lo] + a[hi]` becomes a monotone function of the window: incrementing `lo` only raises the sum, decrementing `hi` only lowers it. That single structural fact converts the naive O(n^2) pair search into an O(n) **opposing two-pointer** sweep, and by extension k-Sum into O(n^(k-1)) by fixing the outer `k-2` indices and running the two-pointer inside. Sorting is the enabling preprocessing step; the two-pointer (or binary search) is the payoff.

WHY it fits: Sum/Target problems ask whether/which elements combine to a value, and the absolute values don't matter for the search structure — only their *relative order* does. The interviewer is probing whether you realize sorting is *free leverage* (O(n log n), dominated by the O(n^2) work anyway) that both enables the pointer movement AND gives a clean, contiguous way to **skip duplicates** for distinct-tuple problems. The structural condition is that the operation (sum) is monotone in each operand and you need value-based matching rather than index-based, so reordering is permissible.
tricks: **Opposing pointers invariant**: with sorted input, if `sum < target` advance `lo`, if `sum > target` retreat `hi`; equality is a hit. Each step strictly shrinks the window, guaranteeing O(n) per inner pass.

**Dedup by skipping equal neighbors**, not a hash set: after recording a tuple, do `while lo<hi and a[lo]==a[lo-1]: lo++` (and symmetrically for `hi`, and for fixed outer indices) — this is the canonical way 3Sum/4Sum emit *distinct* triples/quadruples.

**Prune with sorted bounds** in k-Sum: if `a[i] + (smallest remaining) > target` break the whole loop; if `a[i] + (largest remaining) < target` skip this `i`. These early exits cut huge swaths and rely entirely on sortedness.

**Closest, not exact** (3Sum Closest): track `min|sum-target|` globally while still using the *exact* comparison `sum<target / >target` to decide pointer movement — proximity is what you record, ordering is what you steer by.
**Watch overflow** in 4Sum: a sum of four ints can exceed 32-bit; widen to 64-bit before comparing to target.
Two Sum II is **1-indexed** and demands O(1) extra space — that's precisely why it forbids a hash map and forces the sorted two-pointer; don't regress to the hash solution of the original Two Sum.
sorting.pseudo:
sort(a)
for i in 0..n-1:                      # fix outer (skip for plain 2Sum)
    if i>0 and a[i]==a[i-1]: continue  # dedup outer
    lo, hi = i+1, n-1
    while lo < hi:
        s = a[i] + a[lo] + a[hi]
        if s == target:
            record(i, lo, hi)
            lo++; hi--
            while lo<hi and a[lo]==a[lo-1]: lo++   # dedup
            while lo<hi and a[hi]==a[hi+1]: hi--
        elif s < target: lo++          # need bigger -> raise low end
        else:            hi--          # need smaller -> lower high end

problems.title: 3Sum
problems.note: Sort, fix one index `i`, then run an opposing two-pointer on the suffix to find pairs summing to `-a[i]`; skip equal neighbors at all three positions to emit only distinct triples in O(n^2).

problems.title: 3Sum Closest
problems.note: Same sorted fix-one + two-pointer structure, but instead of testing equality you track the minimum `|a[i]+a[lo]+a[hi] - target|` seen, still steering pointers by whether the current sum is below or above target.

problems.title: 4Sum
problems.note: Generalize k-Sum: sort, fix two outer indices in nested loops, two-pointer the rest; add sorted-bound pruning and neighbor-dedup at every level, using 64-bit sums to avoid overflow, for O(n^3).

problems.title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
problems.note: The pure canonical case — input is already sorted, so a single opposing two-pointer from both ends finds the unique pair in O(n) and O(1) space, returning 1-based indices.

problems.title: Count of Range Sum
problems.note: The odd one out: sorting is applied to *prefix sums*, not the array, inside a merge sort; during merge you count pairs whose prefix-sum difference (a range sum) lands in `[lower,upper]` via two moving boundaries over the sorted half — a divide-and-conquer cousin of the two-pointer scan in O(n log n).

two-pointers.tldr: Sort the array, then collapse a search over pairs/triples into linear sweeps by moving two pointers inward whose current sum monotonically responds to which end you advance.
insight: Every problem here asks: do indices exist whose values hit (or approach) a target sum? The enabling structural fact is **monotonicity on a sorted array**: with a left pointer `lo` and right pointer `hi`, the pair sum `a[lo]+a[hi]` *increases* when you move `lo` right and *decreases* when you move `hi` left. That single monotone relationship lets you discard a whole row/column of the implicit pair matrix per step, turning an O(n^2) scan into an O(n) sweep — exactly the saddleback-search idea. Sorting (O(n log n)) is the price of admission; once sorted, comparison of `sum` vs `target` deterministically dictates the move, so no candidate is ever missed.

For k-Sum (3Sum, 4Sum), the realization an interviewer probes is **reduction**: fix the outer index(es) with loops and reduce to the two-pointer Two-Sum core on the remaining suffix, giving O(n^(k-1)). The hard part is not the pointer motion but *deduplication* — skipping equal neighbors after sorting — and choosing the right comparison for the variant: exact equality (collect/count), closeness (track min |diff|), or threshold (`< target`, where one pointer position certifies a *batch* of valid pairs at once).
tricks: **Always sort first.** The entire technique rests on monotonicity; an unsorted input either needs sorting or a hash-set instead. Exception: #167 is given sorted.

**Move decision is mechanical:** if `sum < target` advance `lo` (need larger), if `sum > target` retreat `hi` (need smaller), if equal you've found it. Never move both unless you just recorded an exact hit.

**Dedup by skipping equal neighbors** at every level: skip duplicate fixed elements (`if i>0 and a[i]==a[i-1]: continue`) AND, after recording a triple, advance `lo`/`hi` past repeats. This is the #1 source of bugs in 3Sum/4Sum.

**Counting/threshold variants batch:** for `sum < target` (#259, #1099), when `a[lo]+a[hi] < target` ALL pairs `(lo, lo+1..hi)` qualify, so add `hi-lo` and `lo++` instead of stepping one at a time — O(n) not O(n^2).
**Closest tracks a running best:** for #16, update `best` by `|sum-target|` on every pointer position before deciding the move; early-exit if `sum==target`.

**Prune for k-Sum:** with sorted input, break when the smallest possible sum from the current prefix already exceeds target, or skip when the largest possible sum is below it — turns worst cases near-linear.
two-pointers.pseudo:
sort(a)
function twoSum(a, start, target):      # two-pointer core
    lo, hi = start, len(a)-1
    while lo < hi:
        s = a[lo] + a[hi]
        if s == target: record(lo,hi); lo++; hi--; skip_dups()
        elif s < target: lo++          # need bigger
        else: hi--                     # need smaller

# k-Sum: fix outer index, recurse/loop into twoSum
for i in 0..n-1:
    if i>0 and a[i]==a[i-1]: continue   # dedup fixed elem
    twoSum(a, i+1, target - a[i])

problems.title: 3Sum
problems.note: Sort, fix each `a[i]` as the smallest element, then run the two-pointer core on the suffix to find pairs summing to `-a[i]`; skip duplicate `i`, `lo`, and `hi` values to avoid repeated triples.

problems.title: 3Sum Closest
problems.note: Same fix-one + two-pointer scan, but instead of matching exactly you track the triple whose sum minimizes `|sum - target|`, moving `lo`/`hi` by the sign of `sum - target` and returning early on an exact hit.

problems.title: 4Sum
problems.note: Add a second outer loop (fix two indices `i<j`) reducing to the two-pointer Two-Sum core on the remaining suffix for O(n^3); dedup at both fixed levels and at the pointers, and prune with min/max-sum bounds.

problems.title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
problems.note: The canonical bare two-pointer: input is already sorted, so start `lo`/`hi` at the ends and move inward by comparing `a[lo]+a[hi]` to target until they meet — O(n), O(1) space.

problems.title: 3Sum Smaller
problems.note: Fix `a[i]`, then for the suffix count pairs with `a[lo]+a[hi] < target`: whenever the condition holds, all `hi-lo` pairs between `lo` and `hi` qualify so add `hi-lo` and `lo++`, else `hi--`.

problems.title: 3Sum With Multiplicity
problems.note: Because values are bounded, count occurrences and fix `a[i]`, then two-pointer over distinct values; combinatorially multiply counts (handling the cases `lo<hi`, `lo==hi` choose-2/choose-3) modulo 1e9+7 rather than enumerating triples.

problems.title: Two Sum Less Than K
problems.note: Sort, then two pointers from both ends: when `a[lo]+a[hi] < k` it's a candidate — update the max sum and `lo++` to try a larger pair; otherwise `hi--`.

problems.title: Max Number of K-Sum Pairs
problems.note: Sort, then greedily two-pointer for pairs summing to `k`: on a match increment the count and move both pointers inward; if sum `< k` advance `lo`, if `> k` retreat `hi` (a hashmap of counts is the alternative).

problems.title: Solve and optimize 3Sum and variants at scale
problems.note: Generalizes the family: the kSum recursion bottoms out in the two-pointer Two-Sum core (O(n^(k-1))), with sorting once up front, neighbor-skip dedup at every level, and min/max prefix-sum pruning to keep large inputs fast.

backtrack.tldr: Backtracking enumerates candidate subsets via a DFS over a sorted array, pruning branches the instant the running sum overshoots `target`, while skipping duplicate choices to emit each summing combination exactly once.
insight: Sum/Target combination problems ask for **all** subsets (or fixed-size subsets) of a candidate set that add up to a `target` — an enumeration task over an exponential space where a greedy or single-pass DP value isn't enough because you must reconstruct the actual tuples. Backtracking fits because the answer is a *path* through a decision tree: at each node you either include the current candidate or move past it, the running `sum` (or equivalently the shrinking `remaining = target - sum`) is the **monotone state** you carry down, and `target` gives you a clean two-sided bound for pruning. The structural condition that unlocks all of this is **sorting the candidates ascending**: it lets you (a) `break` out of the loop the moment `candidate > remaining` since every later candidate is even larger, and (b) skip duplicates with a single `i > start && nums[i]==nums[i-1]` test.

The key realization an interviewer probes is the difference between **reuse-allowed vs. use-once**, encoded purely by the recursion's start index: pass `i` (not `i+1`) to recurse when an element may be reused unbounded times (#39), and pass `i+1` when each element is consumed once (#40, #216). Layered on top is **duplicate suppression at the sibling level** — you only skip equal values that appear *later in the same loop iteration*, never the first occurrence — which is what prevents emitting the same multiset twice in #40. Everything else (a count cap in #216) is just an extra coordinate of the same monotone descent.
tricks: **Sort first**, then carry `remaining = target - sum` down; this enables the `if candidate > remaining: break` prune that turns a full subset scan into an early-terminating one.
Encode reuse policy via the recursion index: `dfs(i, ...)` allows reusing `nums[i]` (#39); `dfs(i+1, ...)` consumes it (#40, #216).

Sibling-level dedup: inside the loop use `if i > start and nums[i] == nums[i-1]: continue` to skip duplicate *branches* — guard with `i > start` so the first occurrence at this depth still fires (critical for #40).

Prune low side too: if `remaining < nums[i]` (smallest remaining candidate) you can `break`; for #216 also prune when remaining slots can't possibly reach `target` given min/max achievable digit sums.
Append to `path` before recursing and pop after (`path.pop()`) — the shared mutable `path` is the backtracking invariant; push a *copy* into results, never the live list.

Subtract into the parameter rather than tracking a cumulative sum; `remaining == 0` is the success leaf and `remaining < 0` is impossible if you pruned correctly, so the base case is a clean equality test.
backtrack.pseudo:
sort(nums)                      # ascending → enables prune + dedup
result = []
def dfs(start, remaining, path):
    if remaining == 0:
        result.add(copy(path)); return
    for i in range(start, len(nums)):
        if nums[i] > remaining: break            # prune: rest are larger
        if i > start and nums[i] == nums[i-1]:    # skip duplicate siblings
            continue                              # (#40 / multiset inputs)
        path.push(nums[i])
        # reuse-allowed → dfs(i, ...) ; use-once → dfs(i+1, ...)
        dfs(i + 1, remaining - nums[i], path)
        path.pop()                                # undo choice
dfs(0, target, [])
return result

problems.title: Combination Sum
problems.note: Candidates are distinct and reusable, so recurse with `dfs(i, remaining - nums[i])` (pass `i`, not `i+1`) to allow repeating the same element; no duplicate-skip needed, just the sorted `nums[i] > remaining` prune to bound depth.

problems.title: Combination Sum II
problems.note: Each candidate is used once and the input may contain duplicates, so recurse with `dfs(i+1, ...)` and add the sibling-dedup guard `if i > start and nums[i]==nums[i-1]: continue` so equal values produce one branch per depth and no repeated multiset appears in the output.

problems.title: Combination Sum III
problems.note: Fixed candidate pool `1..9` (each usable once) with a hard cardinality cap `k`, so carry both `remaining` and slots-left: succeed only when `remaining == 0 and len(path) == k`, recurse with `dfs(i+1, ...)`, and prune when slots remaining can't bridge the gap to `target`.

dfs.tldr: DFS turns "reach a target sum" into a recursion where each node either commits a value to a running total and recurses, or returns the best sum its subtree can contribute.
insight: Sum/Target problems ask whether a *combination of choices* hits or maximizes a numeric total, and DFS is the natural engine because the choice space is a tree: at each node you decide what to include and recurse with the total updated. The unifying realization is that the **running sum is carried as a parameter (top-down)** or **returned as a value (bottom-up)** — the two faces of DFS on a sum problem. In `#39` you grow a partial sum downward toward an exact `target`; in `#124` each call returns the maximum *downward* path sum upward to its parent.

The structural condition that makes DFS apply is that the answer **decomposes recursively**: a valid combination is one element plus a valid combination of the rest, and a best path is one node plus the best of its children. The interviewer is probing whether you can separate the **value that propagates up the recursion** (what a call returns to its caller) from the **global answer that you update as a side effect**. `#124` is the canonical test of this: a node can only hand its parent a *single straight branch*, yet the global maximum may *bend through* the node using both children.
tricks: Decide **carry-down vs. return-up**: `#39` carries `remaining = target - pick` down and succeeds at `remaining == 0`; `#124` returns the best single-branch gain up while updating a global max separately.
In `#124` clamp negative subtrees with `max(child, 0)` — a branch that hurts the sum should be dropped, not added.

The **split between contribution and answer** in `#124`: the value *returned* to the parent is `node.val + max(left,0,right)` (one branch only), but the value used to *update the global max* is `node.val + max(left,0) + max(right,0)` (both branches, the bend point).
`#39` allows reuse of an element: recurse with the **same start index `i`**, not `i+1`, to permit unlimited repeats while sorting + a `start` pointer avoids duplicate combinations.
Prune in `#39`: sort candidates and `break` once `candidate > remaining`, since all later candidates also overshoot.

Pitfall: forgetting to **copy the path** when recording a combination in `#39` (push a snapshot), and forgetting that `#124`'s global max must be initialized to negative infinity since all values may be negative.
dfs.pseudo:
// #39 carry-down: reach exact target
dfs(start, remaining, path):
  if remaining == 0: record(copy(path)); return
  for i in start..n:
    if cand[i] > remaining: break        // pruned (sorted)
    path.push(cand[i])
    dfs(i, remaining - cand[i], path)     // i, not i+1 -> reuse
    path.pop()

// #124 return-up: best path, bend at node
dfs(node):
  if node is null: return 0
  L = max(dfs(node.left), 0)              // drop negative branch
  R = max(dfs(node.right), 0)
  best = max(best, node.val + L + R)      // bend: both branches
  return node.val + max(L, R)             // hand parent one branch

problems.title: Combination Sum
problems.note: DFS over choices carrying `remaining = target - sum` downward; at each level pick a candidate from index `start` (recursing with the same index `i` to allow reuse), succeeding when `remaining` hits 0 and pruning when a sorted candidate exceeds `remaining`.

problems.title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
problems.note: Post-order DFS where each call returns the best single-branch downward gain `node.val + max(L,0,R,0-clamped)`, while a global max is updated with the bend value `node.val + max(L,0) + max(R,0)` that fuses both children through the node.

dp.tldr: For Sum/Target problems, DP turns "can we hit a value / how many ways / best value" into a table indexed by *achievable subtotal*, where each element either contributes or not.
insight: The unifying idea is that a **target sum** is a perfect DP *state*: it is a single bounded integer that fully summarizes the past. Whatever subset of items you have already chosen, all that matters going forward is the **remaining/accumulated sum**, not *which* items produced it — this is **optimal substructure** plus **overlapping subproblems**, the two preconditions for DP. So the canonical reformulation is `dp[s] = ` (reachable? / #ways / best value) for subtotal `s`, and each item drives the transition `dp[s] += dp[s - num]` (count), `dp[s] |= dp[s - num]` (feasibility), or `dp[s] = best(dp[s], dp[s-num] + v)` (optimization).

The interviewer is probing whether you recognize that **subset-sum is a 0/1 knapsack** in disguise: items used at most once force an **outer loop over items, inner loop over sums iterated in reverse** so each item is counted once; whereas **unbounded / order-matters** variants flip the loop nesting. Two further realizations separate strong answers: (1) a *target* can be derived even when it is not given — e.g. partition needs `total/2`, and `+/-` assignments map to a subset summing to `(total+target)/2`; (2) on trees the 'sum' state is computed **bottom-up via post-order recursion**, the tree analog of a DP table where each node's answer is built from its children's returned sums.
tricks: **0/1 vs unbounded loop order is the whole game.** Each item used once → iterate sums *descending* (`for s = target down to num`) so the same item isn't reused. Reuse allowed → iterate *ascending*. For Combination Sum IV (order matters) put the **sum loop outer, items inner** to count ordered sequences, not combinations.

**Reduce target before building the table.** Sum of subset = `S` is feasible only if `(total - S)` and `S` share parity and `S <= total`; for `+/-` sign problems convert to subset-sum `P = (total + target)/2`, rejecting if `total+target` is odd or `target > total`.
**Prune impossible early.** Odd `total` ⇒ no equal partition; any single element `> target` (or `> total/k`) ⇒ impossible. These O(1) checks kill exponential search.
**Counting needs `+=`, feasibility needs `|=`/`or`, optimization needs `max/min`** — but the table shape and transition `dp[s] op f(dp[s-num])` is identical; only the semiring operator changes.

**When k>2 subsets, plain knapsack breaks** — you need bitmask DP over *which elements are used* (`dp[mask] = ` current bucket fill) or backtracking with sorting + pruning, because a single target axis can't track multiple simultaneous buckets.

**Tree 'sum' problems are DP via post-order:** return the subtree aggregate to the parent, and at each node combine children's returns; never recompute a subtree sum top-down (that's the overlapping-subproblem blowup DP avoids).

problems.title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
problems.note: Tree DP via post-order: each node returns the best *downward* single-branch sum `node.val + max(0, max(L,R))` to its parent, while updating a global max with the through-node path `node.val + max(0,L) + max(0,R)`. The 'sum' state is computed bottom-up, exactly a DP table indexed by subtree.

problems.title: Combination Sum IV
problems.note: Counting DP where **order matters**, so the sum is the outer loop and nums the inner: `dp[s] += dp[s-num]` for every `num`, with `dp[0]=1`. This counts ordered sequences (permutations) reaching the target — the loop nesting is what distinguishes it from a combination count.

problems.title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
problems.note: Derive the hidden target `total/2` (impossible if `total` is odd), then 0/1 subset-sum feasibility: `dp[s] |= dp[s-num]` iterating `s` descending so each element is used at most once. Answer is `dp[total/2]`.

problems.title: Target Sum
problems.note: Map `+/-` assignments to a subset-sum: positives form set `P` with `sum(P) = (total+target)/2`, then **count** ways with `dp[s] += dp[s-num]` (0/1, descending). Reject if `total+target` is odd or `target>total`; this is the counting semiring of the same table.

problems.title: Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets
problems.note: Single-axis knapsack fails for k>2 buckets, so use **bitmask DP** `dp[mask]` = leftover fill of the current bucket given used-element set `mask`, or backtracking with sorting + pruning; target per bucket is `total/k` (impossible unless divisible and no element exceeds it).

problems.title: Set second tree values by subtree sums (T2 ← sum of T1 subtree)
problems.note: Pure post-order tree DP: recursively compute each T1 node's subtree sum (`node.val + leftSum + rightSum`), assign it into the mirror T2 node, and return the sum upward — the tree analog of filling a DP table where every node's value is built from its children's aggregates.

sliding-window.tldr: When a subarray's sum is the target, slide a window and exploit monotonicity (or atMost subtraction) to find min length, count, or max sum in linear time.
insight: Sliding window turns a quadratic "check every subarray sum" search into linear time by maintaining a **running window sum** and **two pointers** that never move backward. The structural precondition is **monotonicity of the sum as the window grows**: with all-nonnegative values, extending `right` only increases the sum and shrinking `left` only decreases it, so once the sum overshoots the target you can confidently advance `left` without missing any answer. This is exactly the condition an interviewer probes — the technique breaks if negatives are present (then you need prefix-sum + hashmap instead).

The three flavors share one engine but differ in the window's invariant. For a **minimum-length** problem the window is *variable* and you shrink greedily while the constraint stays satisfied (`sum >= target`). For **counting subarrays with an exact sum** of nonnegatives, equality is not monotone, so you reduce it via `atMost(S) - atMost(S-1)`, where each `atMost` is a clean variable window. For a **fixed-length** maximum-sum window you slide a window of *constant* size `k`, adjusting the sum in O(1) per step and layering a side constraint (distinctness) on top. The unifying realization: identify whether you want *shortest*, *count*, or *fixed-k*, then pick shrink-on-violate vs. atMost-subtraction vs. fixed-slide.
tricks: **Nonnegativity is the license.** Sliding window for sum targets is only valid when elements are `>= 0` (so the window sum is monotone). If negatives appear, switch to prefix-sum + hashmap — interviewers plant this trap.

**Exact-sum counting needs the atMost trick.** `count(sum == S) = atMost(S) - atMost(S - 1)`. Equality has no monotone shrink condition, but `<= S` does, so run two `atMost` windows. Guard `S - 1 < 0`.

**Min-length: shrink while still valid, record before shrinking.** Inner loop is `while sum >= target: ans = min(ans, right-left+1); sum -= a[left]; left++`. Initialize `ans = INF` and return `0` if it stays infinite.
**Fixed-k window: O(1) slide.** Add `a[right]`, and once `right - left + 1 > k` subtract `a[left]` and advance `left`; the window auto-stays at width `k`. Only score when width `== k`.

**Distinctness as a secondary invariant (#2461).** Maintain a frequency map; the window is valid only when no count exceeds 1. On a duplicate, advance `left` (evicting elements) until the duplicate is resolved BEFORE checking the size-`k` answer.
**Each pointer moves at most n times** -> amortized O(n). Don't re-scan the window; update `sum` incrementally, never recompute it from scratch inside the loop.

problems.title: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
problems.note: Grow a variable window adding `a[right]`; whenever `sum >= target`, record `right-left+1` as a candidate minimum and shrink from the left (`sum -= a[left]`) to seek a shorter valid window, since nonnegativity makes the sum monotone.

problems.title: Binary Subarrays With Sum
problems.note: Exact-sum counting on a 0/1 array isn't monotone under equality, so compute `atMost(goal) - atMost(goal-1)`, where each `atMost(S)` slides a window shrinking while `sum > S` and adds `right-left+1` valid subarrays ending at each `right`.

problems.title: Maximum Sum of Distinct Subarrays With Length K
problems.note: Slide a fixed-width-`k` window tracking its running sum and a frequency map; when a duplicate appears or width exceeds `k`, evict from the left, and whenever the window has exactly `k` all-distinct elements, update the answer with its sum.

prefix-sum.tldr: Prefix sums turn "find a subarray whose sum hits a target" into "find two prefix endpoints whose difference (or residue) hits the target" — a hash-map lookup over running sums.
insight: The unifying realization is that any contiguous subarray sum `sum(i..j)` equals `P[j+1] - P[i]`, where `P` is the prefix-sum array. So every Sum/Target question — "does a subarray sum to `k`?", "is it divisible by `k`?", "is it the largest sum `<= k`?" — becomes a question about a **pair of prefix values**. This converts an O(n^2) scan over all (start,end) pairs into an O(n) (or O(n log n)) pass, because as you sweep the right endpoint you only need to know which *left* prefix values you've already seen, not re-scan them.

The structural condition that makes Prefix Sum apply is **contiguity plus an additive/group target**: you need `target = f(P[j]) - f(P[i])` form where `f` is the running aggregate. When the target is an exact value, you hash raw prefixes (`P[i] = P[j] - k`); when it's divisibility, you hash the **modular residue** (equal residues cancel); when it's an extremum bound, you keep prefixes in a **sorted/ordered structure** so you can binary-search the best feasible `P[i]`. The interviewer is probing whether you see that 'subarray over an array' reduces to 'difference of two points', and whether you pick the right keying of prefixes (value vs. residue vs. order) for the specific target predicate.
tricks: **Seed the map with `{0: ...}` / a base prefix `0`** before the loop, so subarrays starting at index 0 (where the left prefix is the empty prefix) are counted; forgetting this is the #1 bug.
**Exact-sum target** (`#560`): for each running prefix `s`, look up `s - k` in a count map; for **counting** store frequencies and add, for **existence/length** store the earliest index.
**Divisibility target** (`#974`, `#523`): key the map by the *normalized residue* `((s % k) + k) % k` to handle negatives; two prefixes with equal residue bound a subarray sum divisible by `k`.
**Length/index constraints** (`#523` needs length `>= 2`): store the *first* index a residue appeared and only count when the gap is large enough — don't overwrite an existing key.

**2D / bounded target** (`#363`): fix a pair of columns, collapse rows to a 1D running sum, then to find the max subarray sum `<= K` use an ordered set of prefixes and `lower_bound(prefix - K)` instead of a plain hash (no clean cancellation for `<=`).
Pitfall: a hash map gives O(n) only for *equality/residue* targets; **inequality targets** (`<= K`, closest) force an ordered structure and an extra log factor — don't reach for a plain dict there.

problems.title: Subarray Sum Equals K
problems.note: The archetype: keep running prefix `s` and a hash map of prefix-value frequencies; for each `s` add `count[s - k]` to the answer, then increment `count[s]`. Seed `count[0]=1` so prefixes equal to `k` are counted.

problems.title: Continuous Subarray Sum
problems.note: Reduce to divisibility: two prefixes with the same residue `s % k` enclose a subarray sum that is a multiple of `k`. Store the *earliest index* per residue (seed residue 0 at index -1) and report true only when the index gap is `>= 2` to satisfy the length-at-least-2 constraint.

problems.title: Subarray Sums Divisible by K
problems.note: Like #560 but key by normalized residue `((s % k) + k) % k`; each previously seen prefix with the same residue forms a divisible subarray, so add `count[residue]` then increment it. Seed `count[0]=1` for prefixes that are themselves divisible by `k`.

problems.title: Max Sum of Rectangle No Larger Than K
problems.note: 2D extension with an inequality target: fix left/right column pair, compress each row-range into a 1D running sum, then find the max subarray sum `<= K` by keeping seen prefixes in an ordered set and querying `lower_bound(prefix - K)` — the `<=` bound rules out a plain hash and needs the sorted-prefix / binary-search variant.

deque-topic.tldr: When prefix sums turn a sum-target query into "find the closest earlier index with a small enough prefix," a monotonic-increasing deque of prefix-sum indices delivers each answer in amortized O(1).
insight: Both problems reduce a subarray-**sum** condition to a relation between two **prefix sums** `P[j] - P[i]`, and the deque stores candidate left endpoints `i` as indices into `P`. The unifying realization: once you fix the right endpoint `j`, an earlier index `i` is **useless forever** if a later index `k > i` has `P[k] <= P[i]` — `k` is both more recent (shorter subarray, closer in a window) and gives a larger sum `P[j]-P[k]`. That domination test is exactly what justifies keeping `P` values **monotonically increasing** along the deque, which is the structural condition that makes the technique apply.

The interviewer is probing whether you see that a plain sliding window fails here because **negative numbers** break monotonicity of the window sum — you cannot simply shrink from the left. The deque restores the two operations a sliding window gives you for free: pop from the **front** to harvest answers (any `i` with `P[j]-P[i] >= K` is satisfiable and never beats `j` again, so discard it), and pop from the **back** to maintain the increasing invariant before pushing `j`. Each index enters and leaves the deque once, giving O(n).
tricks: Build prefix sums with `P[0]=0` and iterate `j` over `P`; the deque holds **indices into `P`**, never raw array positions, so an empty-prefix start is naturally a candidate.

**Front pop (answer harvest):** while `P[j] - P[front] >= K`, record `j - front` and `popFront()` — that `front` can never give a shorter qualifying subarray for any future `j`, so remove it permanently.

**Back pop (invariant maintenance):** before pushing `j`, while `P[back] >= P[j]`, `popBack()`; `j` dominates those tails (smaller-or-equal prefix and more recent), keeping the deque strictly increasing.
Order matters: do **front harvesting first, then back cleanup, then push** — harvesting must see the old front, and pushing `j` is the only `enqueue`.
Pitfall: a naive shrinking sliding window is wrong with negatives because the running sum is **not monotonic** in window length — this is the whole reason a deque is needed over two pointers.

For circular max-sum, the deque/window operates over the **doubled prefix array** of length `2n`, with the left endpoint constrained to a window of width `n` (front-pop indices that fall outside `j - n`).
deque-topic.pseudo:
P[0] = 0
for i in 1..n: P[i] = P[i-1] + a[i-1]
deque = []          # holds indices into P, P-values increasing
ans = +inf          # shortest length (#862)
for j in 0..n:
    # harvest: front gives a valid, never-reusable left end
    while deque not empty and P[j] - P[deque.front] >= K:
        ans = min(ans, j - deque.popFront())
    # maintain increasing invariant: j dominates larger tails
    while deque not empty and P[deque.back] >= P[j]:
        deque.popBack()
    deque.pushBack(j)
return ans if ans < inf else -1

problems.title: Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K
problems.note: Over prefix sums `P`, for each right end `j` find the largest left index `i` with `P[j]-P[i] >= K`; a deque kept increasing in `P` lets you front-pop satisfied/dominated `i`s to track the minimum length `j-i`. The deque (not a sliding window) is mandatory because negative values destroy window-sum monotonicity.

problems.title: Maximum Sum Circular Subarray
problems.note: Duplicate the array to length `2n`, build prefix sums, and for each `j` maximize `P[j]-P[i]` with `i` in the width-`n` window `[j-n, j)`; a deque increasing in `P` keeps the minimal `P[i]` at the front while front-popping indices that exit the window. Equivalent to the classic max(non-wrap, total - min-subarray) trick, but the monotonic deque expresses it directly as a sliding-window minimum of prefix sums.

math.tldr: Split a target sum into a pair of primes by sieving once and testing each `x ≤ n/2` for both `x` and `n - x` being prime.
insight: The **Sum / Target** subject here is the classic *additive decomposition*: find pairs `(x, y)` with `x + y = n`. The **Math** lens reframes the constraint that both components be **prime** into a precomputation problem — instead of primality-testing each candidate on the fly, you run a **Sieve of Eratosthenes** once over `[2, n]`, then the pair search becomes a linear scan. This is essentially a constructive, computational nod to **Goldbach's conjecture** (every even integer > 2 is a sum of two primes), but you must handle odd `n` and small `n` rigorously rather than assuming.

The key realization an interviewer probes is the **monotone-pair pruning**: by enforcing `x ≤ y`, i.e. `x ≤ n/2`, you iterate `x` from `2` to `n/2`, set `y = n - x`, and emit the pair only if `isPrime[x] && isPrime[y]`. The natural ordering of `x` already yields pairs sorted by `x` ascending, so no extra sort is needed. The structural condition that makes Math fit: the search space of one coordinate fully determines the other, turning a 2D search into a 1D scan gated by an `O(n log log n)` sieve.
tricks: **Sieve once, query O(1)**: build `isPrime[0..n]` via Sieve of Eratosthenes in `O(n log log n)`; never call a per-number primality test inside the loop.
**Iterate only to `n/2`**: loop `x` from `2` to `n/2` and let `y = n - x`. This guarantees `x ≤ y`, avoids duplicate `(y, x)` pairs, and produces output already sorted by `x` ascending.

**Parity / Goldbach pitfall**: if `n` is odd, the *only* possible prime pair is `2 + (n-2)` since one addend must be even and `2` is the sole even prime — most odd `n` yield zero or one pair, not many.
**Edge cases**: for `n < 4` there are no valid pairs (smallest prime pair is `2 + 2 = 4`); return empty. Also `n = 4` gives the lone pair `[2, 2]`.
**Don't forget `n - x` bound**: `y = n - x` stays in `[2, n]` for `x` in `[2, n/2]`, so the sieve sized to `n` always covers it — sizing the sieve to `n/2` is a bug.
**0 and 1 are not prime**: initialize `isPrime[0] = isPrime[1] = false` explicitly before sieving.

problems.title: Prime Pairs With Target Sum
problems.note: Sieve all primes up to `n` once, then scan `x` from `2` to `n/2`, emitting `[x, n-x]` whenever both are prime; the `x ≤ n/2` bound enforces `x ≤ y` and yields the answer pre-sorted, while parity (odd `n` forces the even addend to be `2`) prunes most candidates.

string.tldr: Palindrome problems on strings reduce to **two-pointer symmetry checks** and **center/interval expansion**, where the string's random-access indexing is what makes mirroring `s[i] == s[j]` and interval DP `[i..j]` cheap.
insight: A palindrome is defined by an **index symmetry**: `s[i] == s[n-1-i]` for all `i`. Because a **String** gives O(1) positional access, that definition translates directly into two complementary engines — **two pointers** converging from both ends to verify/repair symmetry, and **expand-around-center** / **interval DP `dp[i][j]`** to discover or count palindromic spans. The whole family is just choosing which engine fits: substring (contiguous, indices) vs. subsequence (order-preserving, DP), and verification vs. construction.

The structural condition an interviewer probes is recognizing that the answer space is **O(n^2) intervals**, and that each interval's palindrome-ness is a one-character-comparison extension of a smaller interval: `s[i..j]` is a palindrome iff `s[i]==s[j]` AND `s[i+1..j-1]` is. This recurrence — plus **character-frequency parity** for permutation/rearrangement variants (at most one odd count) — covers nearly every problem. Hashing/prefix tricks (KMP, palindrome hashing) appear when you must glue strings or find palindromic prefixes in linear time.
tricks: **Expand-around-center**: 2n-1 centers (n single + n-1 gaps) handle odd/even lengths uniformly; gives O(n^2) longest/count without DP table.
**Interval DP order**: fill `dp[i][j]` by increasing length (or decreasing `i`, increasing `j`) so `dp[i+1][j-1]` is ready; base cases length 1 (true) and length 2 (`s[i]==s[j]`).
**Frequency parity** is the rearrangement signature: a permutation can form a palindrome iff at most one char has odd count; longest palindrome length = sum of even parts + (1 if any odd).
**Two-pointer with k-skips**: for Valid Palindrome II/III, on mismatch branch to delete left or right (II: one skip) or use LPS/edit-style DP (III: `n - LPS(s) <= k`).
**Subsequence palindromes via LPS**: longest palindromic subsequence of `s` = `LCS(s, reverse(s))`; min insertions/deletions to make palindrome = `n - LPS`.
**Pitfall**: skip-non-alphanumeric and case-fold lazily inside the two-pointer loop (#125), don't pre-clean — and never confuse substring (contiguous) with subsequence (DP) recurrences.

problems.title: Longest Palindromic Substring
problems.note: **Expand-around-center** over all 2n-1 centers, tracking the widest span where `s[l]==s[r]`; O(n^2) time, O(1) space (or Manacher for O(n)).

problems.title: Valid Palindrome
problems.note: Single **two-pointer** pass from both ends, skipping non-alphanumeric chars and case-folding, asserting `s[i]==s[j]` until pointers cross.

problems.title: Palindrome Partitioning
problems.note: **Backtracking** over cut positions, extending only when the current prefix `s[start..i]` is a palindrome; precompute `dp[i][j]` palindrome table to make each check O(1).

problems.title: Shortest Palindrome
problems.note: Find the **longest palindromic prefix** of `s`, then prepend the reverse of the remaining suffix; computed in O(n) via **KMP failure function** on `s + '#' + reverse(s)`.

problems.title: Palindrome Linked List
problems.note: List analog of the string two-pointer: find midpoint via slow/fast, **reverse the second half**, then compare both halves node-by-node for symmetry.

problems.title: Palindrome Permutation
problems.note: Pure **frequency-parity** test on the string: count char occurrences; a palindromic permutation exists iff at most one character has an odd count.

problems.title: Palindrome Pairs
problems.note: For each word, split into prefix/suffix; using a **hash map of reversed words**, a pair `(i,j)` forms a palindrome when one part is itself a palindrome and the complement's reverse exists in the map.

problems.title: Longest Palindrome
problems.note: **Frequency counting**: sum the largest even count below each frequency (`c & ~1`), plus 1 if any character had an odd count to occupy the center.

problems.title: Palindromic Substrings
problems.note: Count total palindromic substrings by **expand-around-center**, incrementing the counter for every successful `s[l]==s[r]` expansion across all 2n-1 centers.

problems.title: Valid Palindrome II
problems.note: **Two pointers**; on first mismatch, branch to skip either the left or right character and verify the remaining interval is a palindrome — at most one deletion allowed.

problems.title: Valid Palindrome III
problems.note: Reduce to deletions = `n - LPS(s)`; compute **longest palindromic subsequence** via interval DP and return whether `n - dp[0][n-1] <= k`.

problems.title: Minimum Insertion Steps to Make a String Palindrome
problems.note: Answer is `n - LPS(s)` (= `LCS(s, reverse(s))`); each char not in the longest palindromic subsequence needs one mirrored insertion, solved by interval DP.

problems.title: Maximum Product of the Length of Two Palindromic Subsequences
problems.note: Enumerate **subset partitions via bitmask** of the (short) string, compute the longest palindromic subsequence length of each disjoint half, and maximize the product.

linked-list.tldr: A palindrome check on a linked list becomes an `O(1)`-space exercise in finding the middle with fast/slow pointers, reversing the second half in place, and walking the two halves toward each other.
insight: A linked list has no random access, so the array-style two-pointer palindrome test (`i` from front, `j` from back) is impossible directly — you cannot walk backward through a singly linked list. The unifying trick is to **physically transform the structure** so that backward traversal becomes forward traversal: split the list at its midpoint and **reverse the second half**, after which two forward walks (one from `head`, one from the reversed tail) effectively compare the list against its mirror image.

The structural condition that makes Linked List 'fit' Palindrome is exactly this absence of backward links: the problem is really probing whether you know the **slow/fast midpoint** idiom and **in-place reversal** well enough to compose them, and whether you handle the even/odd length split correctly. The naive `O(n)` *space* answer (copy values to an array, then two-pointer) always works and is fine to state first — but the interviewer's real target is the `O(1)`-space version, ideally with the bonus of **restoring the list** to its original order before returning.
tricks: Find the middle with **slow/fast pointers**: advance `slow` by 1 and `fast` by 2; when `fast` reaches the end, `slow` sits at the start of the second half. With the `while fast and fast.next` condition, for **odd** length `slow` lands on the exact center node — let the center belong to either half, the comparison still works.

Reverse the **second half only** (everything from `slow` onward), then compare the first half against the reversed second half node-by-node; stop when the second-half pointer hits `null` — this naturally ignores the lone middle element on odd-length lists.
Compare until the **shorter (second) half** is exhausted, not until both are: the first half may be one node longer on odd length, and that extra middle node must not be compared.

Be careful **not to create a cycle**: when reversing, the original first-half tail still points into the second half. Either cut the link (`first_tail.next = null`) before reversing, or reverse purely by pointer-rewiring so no node links forward into a node that now points back.
For a clean follow-up, **restore the list** by reversing the second half again after the check — interviewers love the non-destructive variant.

Edge cases: empty list and single node are trivially palindromes; a recursion-based approach exists (outer pointer advances via the call stack unwinding) but uses `O(n)` stack space, so prefer the iterative reverse for true `O(1)` extra space.
linked-list.pseudo:
function isPalindrome(head):
    if head is null or head.next is null: return true
    slow = head; fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:          # find midpoint
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
    second = reverse(slow)             # reverse 2nd half (slow = start of 2nd half)
    first = head
    ok = true
    while second is not null:          # compare; 2nd half is the shorter side
        if first.val != second.val: ok = false; break
        first = first.next
        second = second.next
    # optional: reverse(reversedSecond) to restore original list
    return ok

problems.title: Palindrome Linked List
problems.note: Use slow/fast pointers to locate the midpoint, reverse the second half in place, then walk `first` from `head` and `second` from the reversed tail comparing values until the second half is exhausted; this yields `O(n)` time and `O(1)` extra space (optionally re-reverse to restore the list).

tree.tldr: A pseudo-palindrome means at most one odd digit count, so DFS each root-to-leaf path while tracking digit-count parity as a 9-bit mask and check `popcount(mask) <= 1` at every leaf.
insight: The bridge between Palindrome and Binary Tree is that a sequence can be *permuted* into a palindrome iff at most one element appears an odd number of times. On a binary tree, each **root-to-leaf path** is such a sequence (of node values 1..9), so the palindrome question reduces to a parity-counting question over path elements — no actual reversal or two-pointer check is needed. The tree contributes the branching structure: every distinct path is an independent candidate, and DFS naturally enumerates all paths while sharing prefixes.

The key realization an interviewer probes is the *odd-count* characterization plus the trick of encoding it compactly. Since values are bounded to digits 1..9, the multiset's parity collapses to a 9-bit integer where bit `v` toggles each time you see value `v`. XOR-toggling on the way down and checking `mask & (mask - 1) == 0` (zero or one bit set) at a leaf turns an O(9) frequency scan into O(1), and the state is trivially shared and restored across the recursion.
tricks: **Odd-count rule, not reversal**: a path is pseudo-palindromic iff every digit's count is even except at most one — you never compare characters, you count parities.
Encode parity as a **bitmask**: `mask ^= (1 << val)` on entry. At a leaf, valid iff `mask & (mask - 1) == 0` (popcount 0 or 1). This handles the 'at most one odd' in O(1).
Toggling on the way down is **self-undoing** with XOR — pass `mask` by value (or XOR back when returning) so siblings don't see each other's state; no explicit backtrack array needed.
**Only count at leaves** (`left == null && right == null`), not at internal nodes — a path is defined root-to-leaf, so internal nodes are not endpoints.
Values are constrained to **1..9**, which is exactly why 9 bits (or a length-10 freq array) suffices; don't assume general integers.
Pitfall: a single-node tree is always pseudo-palindromic (one odd count is allowed); make sure the base/leaf logic returns 1 there.

problems.title: Pseudo-Palindromic Paths in a Binary Tree
problems.note: DFS every root-to-leaf path while XOR-toggling a 9-bit mask of digit-count parities; at each leaf a path is pseudo-palindromic iff at most one digit has odd count, tested via `mask & (mask - 1) == 0`. The tree only supplies the path enumeration — the palindrome logic is pure parity counting on the path's multiset.

math.tldr: Reverse half the digits with pure arithmetic — no string conversion — and check the palindrome by comparing the two halves directly.
insight: A number is a palindrome iff its **digit sequence** reads the same forwards and backwards, and the elegant insight is that you never need a string or even the full reversal: you can **peel digits off the back** using `x % 10` / `x /= 10` while **building the reverse** as `rev = rev*10 + digit`, stopping once `rev >= x`. At that moment you have consumed exactly the back half, so the front half (`x`) and reversed back half (`rev`) can be compared arithmetically. This is the Math lens on palindromes: positional decimal arithmetic *is* the digit array, so modular extraction replaces indexing.

Why Math fits: palindrome-ness is a property of base-`b` representation, and `%`/`/` are the canonical operators that read that representation without materializing it. The structural condition the interviewer probes is the **early termination at the midpoint** (`rev >= x`) plus correct handling of the **odd-length middle digit** (`x == rev / 10`) and the **negative / trailing-zero** edge cases that fail trivially.
tricks: Reject immediately when `x < 0` (the `-` sign breaks symmetry) and when `x != 0 && x % 10 == 0` (a trailing zero would require a leading zero, impossible except for `0` itself).
Reverse only **half** the number: loop `while x > rev: rev = rev*10 + x%10; x /= 10`. This halves the work and sidesteps **integer overflow** that full reversal of a 32-bit value can cause.
Even length is palindrome iff `x == rev`; **odd length** iff `x == rev / 10` (the shared middle digit lives in `rev`'s last slot and is discarded by integer division).
The loop terminator `x > rev` is correct because after consuming the back half `rev` becomes `>= x`; using `>=` instead would over-consume on even-length numbers.
If you instead do full reversal, compare `rev == original` and guard the multiply against overflow (e.g., use a 64-bit accumulator) — but half-reversal avoids this entirely.
Single digits (including `0`) are palindromes and fall out naturally since the loop body runs zero or one time.
math.pseudo:
function isPalindrome(x):
    if x < 0: return false
    if x != 0 and x % 10 == 0: return false   # trailing zero
    rev = 0
    while x > rev:
        rev = rev * 10 + (x % 10)              # push back digit
        x   = x / 10                            # integer division
    # even length: x == rev ; odd length: middle digit in rev
    return x == rev or x == rev / 10

problems.title: Palindrome Number
problems.note: Avoid string conversion by extracting digits with `x % 10` and `x /= 10`, building the reverse of the **back half** via `rev = rev*10 + digit` until `rev >= x`; the integer is a palindrome iff `x == rev` (even digit count) or `x == rev/10` (odd count, discarding the shared middle digit), after fast-rejecting negatives and nonzero trailing zeros.

two-pointers.tldr: Palindromes are symmetric, so converge two pointers from both ends and assert mirror-equality at every step — `O(n)` time, `O(1)` extra space.
insight: A palindrome is defined by **central symmetry**: position `i` from the left must equal position `i` from the right. This is *exactly* the structural condition two pointers exploits — a `left` pointer starting at index 0 and a `right` pointer at index `n-1` walk toward the center, and the string is a palindrome iff `s[left] == s[right]` holds for every step until they cross. No auxiliary data structure is needed because the comparison is purely positional and bidirectional.

The interviewer is probing whether you recognize that **verification can happen in-place by mirroring** rather than building a reversed copy and comparing (`O(n)` space). The twist across these problems is what you do at the boundary: filtering non-relevant characters (skip on each side), tolerating one mismatch (branch into two candidate substrings), or first reaching the back of a one-directional structure (a linked list, where you must reverse the second half to simulate a backward pointer).
tricks: **Convergence invariant**: loop `while left < right` and compare `s[left]` vs `s[right]`; on mismatch the answer is false immediately, on match do `left++, right--`. Equality of all checked pairs proves palindrome.

**In-place skipping** (#125): on each side advance past characters that fail the predicate (`while left < right and not isalnum(s[left]): left++`) BEFORE comparing, and normalize case with `.lower()` on the fly — never pre-build a cleaned string if asked for `O(1)` space.

**One-deletion branch** (#680): at the first mismatch you have exactly two repair options — delete `left` or delete `right`. Recurse/check `isPalindrome(left+1, right)` OR `isPalindrome(left, right-1)`; if either is a clean palindrome, return true.

**Linked-list lacks backward traversal** (#234): you can't decrement a `next`-only pointer, so the two-pointer phase is preceded by **slow/fast to find the midpoint** then **reverse the second half**, after which two pointers walk the two halves inward (or one from head, one from reversed-mid).
**Pitfall — re-scanning after a skip**: in #125 keep the inner skip loops bounded by `left < right` to avoid the pointers crossing while skipping, which would otherwise read out of range.
**Odd vs even length is free**: convergence naturally handles both — for odd length the pointers meet on the center element (never compared against itself), for even they cross past it.

problems.title: Valid Palindrome
problems.note: Run `left`/`right` pointers inward, on each side skipping any non-alphanumeric character and lowercasing in place, then assert `s[left] == s[right]`; mismatch means not a palindrome. Achieves `O(n)` time and `O(1)` space without building a filtered string.

problems.title: Palindrome Linked List
problems.note: A singly linked list has no backward pointer, so use slow/fast pointers to locate the midpoint, reverse the second half, then walk one pointer from the head and one from the reversed tail inward comparing values. `O(n)` time, `O(1)` space (optionally restore the list).

problems.title: Valid Palindrome II
