problems.note: Converge the two pointers until the first mismatch; at that point you may delete one character, so check whether either `s[left+1..right]` or `s[left..right-1]` is a palindrome via the same two-pointer scan. Returning true if either branch succeeds.

backtrack.tldr: Backtracking enumerates every way to cut a string into substrings, pruning any branch where the next prefix isn't a palindrome — turning "all palindrome partitions" into a DFS over cut positions.
insight: Palindrome partitioning is a **subset-of-cuts** problem: between the `n-1` gaps of a string you either cut or don't, giving `2^(n-1)` candidate partitions. The palindrome constraint is what makes **backtracking** (rather than brute-force enumeration) the right fit — instead of generating all partitions and filtering, you grow a partition one piece at a time and only recurse when the *current* prefix `s[start..i]` is itself a palindrome. That feasibility-of-the-prefix check is the **prune**: an invalid first piece kills an entire exponential subtree before it's ever explored.

The structural realization an interviewer probes is that a valid partition is built **left-to-right by fixing the next palindromic prefix**: pick `i` such that `s[start..i]` is a palindrome, append it, recurse on `start = i+1`, then **pop and try a longer prefix**. The base case `start == n` means the whole string was consumed by palindromes — emit a copy of the path. Because output size itself is exponential, you can't beat `O(2^n)` in the worst case (e.g. `"aaaa"`), so the only lever is cheap palindrome checks via memo/DP.
tricks: **Prune on the prefix, not the whole partition**: test `isPalindrome(s, start, i)` before recursing; never generate a full partition then validate it.
Iterate the cut endpoint `i` from `start` to `n-1`; the substring is `s[start..i]` inclusive, and recursion continues at `start = i+1` — off-by-one here is the classic bug.
**Base case** is `start == n` (entire string consumed) → push a *copy* of the current path (`list(path)`), since `path` is mutated on backtrack.
Always **append then pop** (`path.add(piece)` / recurse / `path.removeLast()`) to restore state for the next sibling branch.
Precompute palindromes with a `dp[i][j]` table or expand-around-center in `O(n^2)` so each check is `O(1)`; this removes a redundant `O(n)` factor inside the DFS.
Worst case is still exponential output (`"aaaa"` → `2^3` partitions), so don't expect to prune to polynomial — the goal is to avoid wasted recursion, not to change the complexity class.

problems.title: Palindrome Partitioning
problems.note: DFS over cut positions: at index `start`, try every prefix `s[start..i]`, recurse only when that prefix is a palindrome, append it to the running path, and on reaching `start == n` record a copy of the path; backtrack by popping. Optionally precompute an `O(n^2)` palindrome DP table so each prefix test is `O(1)`.

hash.tldr: A string can be permuted into a palindrome iff a frequency map has at most one odd-count character — so you count chars in a hash table and inspect the parity of the counts.
insight: The defining structural fact of a palindrome is **symmetry around the center**: every character must appear in matching pairs, with **at most one** character allowed to occupy the unpaired center. A **hash table** (or fixed-size frequency array) is the natural fit because the question is never *where* characters sit but *how many times each appears* — order is irrelevant once you reduce to counts. This is the key realization an interviewer probes: collapse the string to a `char -> count` multiset, then reason purely about the **parity** of those counts.

Both problems hinge on one invariant: characters with **even** counts contribute fully (they pair off), and characters with **odd** counts can contribute all-but-one to the paired body, with a single leftover eligible to sit in the center. So a permutation is palindromic iff the number of odd counts is `<= 1`, and the longest palindrome you can *build* is the sum of all counts rounded down to even, plus `+1` if any odd count existed (to claim the center). The hash table reduces both to a single parity scan.
tricks: You never need the actual counts after building the map — only their **parity**. A `Set` toggle (add on first sight, remove on second) collapses #266 to: palindrome-permutation iff the set's final size is `<= 1`.
For #409, accumulate `length += count - (count & 1)` (drop one when odd), then add `1` once at the end if **any** odd count was seen — this single bonus is the center slot.
Use a fixed-size array (`int[128]` ASCII or `int[58]` for mixed-case A-Za-z) instead of a HashMap for O(1) constant-factor speed when the alphabet is bounded.
Common pitfall in #409: adding `+1` for *every* odd character instead of exactly once — only one odd character can occupy the unique center.
Parity beats summation: you can answer #266 in a single pass with bit-toggling without ever storing integer counts, and #409 with `count & 1` masks.
Edge cases: empty string is a valid palindrome permutation; a single odd character yields length 1, not 0.

problems.title: Palindrome Permutation
problems.note: Build a `char -> count` map (or a toggling `Set`) and return true iff at most one character has an odd count, since a palindromic arrangement permits exactly one unpaired center character.

problems.title: Longest Palindrome
problems.note: Count each character with a hash table, sum the largest even portion of every count (`count - count&1`), then add `1` if any count was odd to claim the single center slot — giving the longest palindrome buildable from the multiset.

trie-topic.tldr: Insert every word's reverse into a Trie, then walk each word forward through it so palindromic remainders let you discover all complementary pairs in roughly linear time per word.
insight: A pair `(i, j)` forms a palindrome when `words[i] + words[j]` reads the same forwards and backwards. The structural realization is that this only happens in three regimes: the two words are exact reverses of each other, or one word is **longer** and its non-matching prefix/suffix is itself a palindrome that 'hangs off' the shorter word's reversal. A **Trie** is the perfect tool because it indexes words by shared prefixes, and the matching condition for concatenation is precisely a prefix/suffix relationship between a word and the *reverse* of another word.

The trick an interviewer probes for is the **reverse-storage inversion**: store each word's *reverse* in the Trie, then feed each query word *forward* character by character. At any node where the query word ends, if the remaining (still-unconsumed) reversed-word suffix below that node is a palindrome, those words pair. Symmetrically, if the query word is fully consumed at an internal node, any word ending below it whose extra prefix is a palindrome also pairs. Augmenting each Trie node with a list of word-indices whose remaining suffix-from-here is a palindrome turns each lookup into O(word length) instead of O(word length squared).
tricks: Store **reversed** words in the Trie; traverse with the **forward** query word. The concatenation `a+b` is a palindrome iff matching `a` against `reverse(b)` leaves a palindromic leftover on exactly one side.
Augment each Trie node with two fields: `wordIndex` (a complete word ends here) and `palindromeBelow` (a list of indices of words whose remaining suffix *past this node* is itself a palindrome).

Case A — query word **fully consumed** at a node that is a word-end: that stored word is the exact reverse, so they pair (guard against pairing a word with itself, and handle the empty-string `""` which pairs with every palindrome).
Case B — query word fully consumed but Trie continues: every index in this node's `palindromeBelow` pairs, because the extra reversed-prefix forms a palindrome in the middle.
Case C — query word has leftover characters after reaching a word-end node: pair them only if that leftover query suffix is itself a palindrome.
Watch the empty string and self-pairing pitfalls: `""` is a palindrome and must be paired both as left and right partner; never emit `(i, i)`.
trie-topic.pseudo:
build Trie of reverse(word) for each word i:
  for each prefix position p of reverse(word):
    if suffix(word, from p) is palindrome: node.palindromeBelow.add(i)
  leaf.wordIndex = i

for each word w (index i):
  node = root
  for k, ch in enumerate(w):
    # query consumed, palindromic leftover hangs below -> case B
    if node.wordIndex != -1 and node.wordIndex != i
       and isPalindrome(w[k:]): emit (i, node.wordIndex)
    node = node.children[ch]; if none: break next word
  else:                       # w fully consumed
    if node.wordIndex != -1 and node.wordIndex != i: emit (i, node.wordIndex)   # case A
    for j in node.palindromeBelow: if j != i: emit (i, j)                       # case B

problems.title: Palindrome Pairs
problems.note: Insert each word reversed into a Trie, annotating nodes with which words have a palindromic remaining suffix; then run each word forward through the Trie so that a fully-matched word with a palindromic leftover (either in the query tail or in the Trie's `palindromeBelow` lists) yields a valid pair. This finds all ordered palindrome-concatenation pairs in O(n * k^2) total (k = average word length) instead of the brute-force O(n^2 * k).

dp.tldr: Palindrome DP = compute the longest palindromic subsequence (or min deletions) on the interval `[i..j]`, where matching endpoints shrink both ends and mismatches branch — and a string is a "k-palindrome" iff `n - LPS(s) <= k`.
insight: Palindromes have a recursive **two-pointer structure that is intrinsically interval DP**: the predicate "is `s[i..j]` a palindrome" depends on `s[i] == s[j]` AND the inner interval `s[i+1..j-1]`. That self-similarity over shrinking ranges is exactly the optimal-substructure + overlapping-subproblems signature DP exploits. So almost every palindrome optimization (longest subsequence, fewest deletions/insertions, partition counts) becomes a 2D table `dp[i][j]` over substrings, filled by increasing length.

The key realization an interviewer probes with #1216 is the **reduction**: "valid palindrome after deleting at most `k` chars" is NOT a greedy two-pointer problem — it is `minDeletionsToPalindrome(s) <= k`. And the minimum deletions to make a string a palindrome equals `n - LPS(s)`, where `LPS` (longest palindromic subsequence) is `LCS(s, reverse(s))`. Recognizing this chain (k-palindrome → min deletions → LPS → LCS-with-reverse) is the whole problem; once stated, it is a textbook interval DP.
tricks: **Reduce, don't simulate**: `isKPalindrome(s, k)` ⇔ `n - LPS(s) <= k` ⇔ `(n - LCS(s, reverse(s))) <= k`. Greedy two-pointer skipping fails because each mismatch offers two branches that interleave.

**Define LPS directly with interval DP**: `dp[i][j]` = longest palindromic subsequence of `s[i..j]`. Base `dp[i][i] = 1`. Transition: if `s[i]==s[j]` then `dp[i][j] = 2 + dp[i+1][j-1]`, else `dp[i][j] = max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j-1])`.

**Fill order matters**: iterate `i` from `n-1` down to `0` and `j` from `i+1` up, OR iterate by increasing substring length — both guarantee `dp[i+1][j-1]`, `dp[i+1][j]`, `dp[i][j-1]` are already computed.

**Equivalent dual formulation**: `dp[i][j]` = minimum deletions to make `s[i..j]` a palindrome; if `s[i]==s[j]` carry `dp[i+1][j-1]`, else `1 + min(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j-1])`. Answer is `dp[0][n-1] <= k`. This avoids the `n - LPS` arithmetic step.

**Pitfall — subsequence vs substring**: #1216 deletes characters (keeps order, gaps allowed), so it is *subsequence*-based. Do NOT use the contiguous palindromic-substring DP (`s[i]==s[j] && dp[i+1][j-1]`) used for counting/longest substring.
**Complexity**: `O(n^2)` time, `O(n^2)` space; reducible to `O(n)` space with two rolling rows since each cell needs only the previous diagonal/row.

problems.title: Valid Palindrome III
problems.note: Reduce "is `s` a palindrome after deleting at most `k` chars" to `minDeletionsToPalindrome(s) <= k`; compute that via interval DP `dp[i][j]` (carry inner interval when `s[i]==s[j]`, else `1 + min` of dropping either end), equivalently `n - LPS(s) <= k` where `LPS = LCS(s, reverse(s))`. Greedy two-pointer is wrong because each endpoint mismatch forks into two deletion choices that must be optimized jointly — the `O(n^2)` table does exactly that.

dfs.tldr: DFS walks root-to-leaf paths while a single parity bitmask tracks digit counts, so a path is "pseudo-palindromic" iff at most one bit is set at a leaf.
insight: The bridge between **Palindrome** and **DFS** here is the *order-independent* palindrome characterization: a multiset of digits can be rearranged into a palindrome **iff at most one digit has an odd count**. Tree-path problems hand you the digits along a root-to-leaf path one node at a time, which is exactly what DFS enumerates, so you never need to materialize or sort the path — you just maintain a running tally of parities as you descend and test it at each leaf.

The key realization an interviewer probes is that you should *not* count occurrences (a `map` of size up to 9) and you should *not* store the path; instead carry an integer **parity bitmask** where bit `d` is XOR-toggled on entering a node with value `d`. The palindrome test collapses to a single popcount-style check `mask & (mask-1) == 0` at a leaf. DFS makes the bitmask natural because XOR is self-inverse: you can toggle on the way down and untoggle on the way back up (or just pass the mask by value), giving O(1) state per frame and O(N) total.
tricks: Encode digit counts as a **parity bitmask**, not a frequency array: on visiting value `v`, do `mask ^= (1 << v)`. XOR's self-inverse property means duplicates cancel, leaving exactly the odd-count digits as set bits.
Test palindrome-feasibility ONLY at leaves (both children null), and use the bit trick `mask & (mask - 1) == 0` — true when zero or one bits are set (zero or one digit with odd count).
Pass the mask **by value** down the recursion so backtracking is automatic; if you mutate a shared mask, you must XOR-toggle again after the recursive calls to restore it.
Values in #1457 are digits `1..9`, so a 32-bit int suffices; don't over-engineer with a hash map — that's the anti-pattern the problem is testing against.
Pitfall: counting a node as a 'leaf' when only one child is null. A true leaf has BOTH children null; an internal node with one child must not contribute to the answer.
An empty mask (`mask == 0`) at a leaf is still pseudo-palindromic (all digits appear an even number of times) — `0 & -1 == 0` correctly returns true.
dfs.pseudo:
function dfs(node, mask):
    if node is null: return 0
    mask ^= (1 << node.val)          # toggle parity of this digit
    if node.left is null and node.right is null:   # leaf
        return 1 if (mask & (mask - 1)) == 0 else 0
    return dfs(node.left, mask) + dfs(node.right, mask)

answer = dfs(root, 0)

problems.title: Pseudo-Palindromic Paths in a Binary Tree
problems.note: DFS each root-to-leaf path while XOR-toggling a parity bitmask over node values `1..9`; at every leaf, count the path iff `mask & (mask-1) == 0`, i.e. at most one digit has an odd frequency, the exact condition for the path's digits to be rearrangeable into a palindrome.

bits.tldr: Encode each subsequence's character set as a bitmask and brute-force all `2^n` subsets, since with only lowercase letters a palindromic subsequence is fully described by which letters it uses.
insight: The bridge between Palindrome and Bit Manipulation is that the input string is short (`n <= 12`), so the dominant cost is choosing **which indices go to subsequence A vs B**, not checking palindromicity. A bitmask of `n` bits enumerates every subset of positions in `O(2^n)`; the **bit operators** then make the disjointness constraint trivial — two subsequences use disjoint character positions iff `maskA & maskB == 0`, and the leftover characters are `full ^ (maskA | maskB)`.

The key realization an interviewer probes: instead of separately splitting the string and searching for palindromes, you **precompute the longest palindromic subsequence length for every one of the `2^n` index-subsets once**, then iterate over disjoint mask pairs and maximize the product. Bit tricks reduce the disjoint-pair search to enumerating **submasks of the complement** (`sub = (sub-1) & comp`), giving a clean `O(3^n)` total — Bit Manipulation is the indexing machinery that turns an exponential combinatorial split into a tight, constant-overhead loop.
tricks: **Mask = chosen indices, not chosen letters.** With `n` bits each set bit picks one position of the string; build the candidate substring by iterating bits via `mask & (1<<i)`.
**Disjointness via AND:** two subsequences are non-overlapping exactly when `maskA & maskB == 0`. Never compare sets manually.

**Precompute palindrome length per mask** in a table `pal[mask]` once (`O(2^n * n)`), so the pair loop is pure arithmetic; checking a candidate is a two-pointer palindrome test on the bit-selected characters.

**Submask enumeration of the complement:** fix `maskA`, let `comp = ((1<<n)-1) ^ maskA`, then iterate `for sub = comp; sub; sub = (sub-1) & comp` to get every disjoint `maskB` — avoids the full `2^n x 2^n` double loop.
**Prune non-palindromes early:** store `pal[mask] = 0` (or skip) when the bit-selected string isn't a palindrome, so the product loop only multiplies valid lengths.
**Pitfall:** popcount of the mask is the candidate length only if it is a palindrome; don't use `popcount(mask)` directly as the palindrome length without verifying.
bits.pseudo:
n = len(s); FULL = (1<<n) - 1
pal = array[1<<n] of 0
for mask in 0 .. FULL:
    t = chars of s where bit set in mask        # via mask & (1<<i)
    if isPalindrome(t): pal[mask] = len(t)
ans = 0
for a in 1 .. FULL:
    if pal[a] == 0: continue
    comp = FULL ^ a                              # indices free for B
    sub = comp
    while sub > 0:                               # enumerate disjoint B
        if pal[sub] > 0:
            ans = max(ans, pal[a] * pal[sub])
        sub = (sub - 1) & comp
return ans

problems.title: Maximum Product of the Length of Two Palindromic Subsequences
problems.note: Because `n <= 12`, enumerate all `2^n` index bitmasks, precompute `pal[mask]` = palindromic-subsequence length for the characters those set bits select, then for each palindromic mask `a` iterate submasks of its complement `comp = FULL ^ a` to find disjoint palindromic mask `b` (guaranteed by `a & b == 0`) and maximize `pal[a] * pal[b]`. Bit manipulation provides both the subset enumeration and the `O(1)` disjointness/complement checks.

string.tldr: Every bracket problem is a variation on **one invariant**: the running **balance** `bal = (#open − #close)` scanned left→right.
insight: A string of one bracket type is valid **iff** two things hold: `bal` **never goes negative** (no `)` before a matching `(`) and `bal == 0` at the end (every `(` is closed). That is the whole theory — validation, repair, longest-run, and generation are all just *questions asked against this invariant*.

The key realization for an interview: with a **single** bracket type you do **not** need a stack — a single integer counter is enough, because a stack here only ever holds a run of identical `(`. You reach for a real stack only when (a) there are **multiple** bracket types `()[]{}` that must match by kind, or (b) you need the **index/position** of an opener (to measure a span or to mark it for deletion).
tricks: **Counter, not stack** for one type: maintain `bal`, fail fast if `bal < 0`, accept iff `bal == 0`.
**Two-pass for two-sided repair**: a left→right pass catches surplus `)`; a right→left pass catches surplus `(` (used by 921 / 1249).
Repair count = **unmatched opens + unmatched closes**, counted independently.
Need **lengths or positions** (32) or to **delete specific chars** (1249)? push **indices**; value-only validity (20/921)? push/track nothing but a counter.
string.pseudo:
isValid(s):            # single bracket type
  bal = 0
  for c in s:
    bal += (c == '(') ? +1 : -1
    if bal < 0: return false      # ')' with no open
  return bal == 0                 # all opens closed

problems.title: Valid Parentheses
problems.note: **Multiple types** ⇒ real **stack**: push each opener; on a closer the popped top must be its match. Valid iff the stack ends empty.

problems.title: Generate Parentheses
problems.note: The string is the canvas — **backtrack** placing `(`/`)`, pruned by the invariant `close < open`. See ×Backtracking.

problems.title: Longest Valid Parentheses
problems.note: Needs **positions** ⇒ stack of **indices** (with a `-1` sentinel); a valid run length is `i − stack.top`. (DP alternative: `dp[i]` from the matched `(`.)

problems.title: Different Ways to Add Parentheses
problems.note: Re-parenthesize an **expression**: split at every operator, recurse on the two substrings, combine all left×right results — divide & conquer over substrings.

problems.title: Remove Invalid Parentheses
problems.note: Compute the **minimum** surplus `(` and `)` to drop, then search removing exactly that many — minimal edit to restore `bal` validity.

problems.title: Minimum Add to Make Parentheses Valid
problems.note: Pure **counter**: track open surplus + closes that underflow; answer = leftover opens + leftover closes.

problems.title: Minimum Remove to Make Valid Parentheses
problems.note: Mark indices of unmatched `)` (underflow) and unmatched `(` (left on the stack), then rebuild the string skipping marked indices.

stack-topic.tldr: Reach for a **stack** the moment you must remember **which / where** an opener was — not just **how many**.
insight: The stack stores one of two things: the **opener character** (to enforce type matching in `()[]{}`, problem 20) or the **opener's index** (to measure spans or mark positions, problems 32 / 1249). If you never need either, the stack collapses into a plain counter — which is exactly why the single-type problems (921) can drop it.

The signature move for span problems is the **`-1` sentinel** pushed at the bottom: it lets you compute a valid run as `i − stack.top` uniformly, with no special case for a run that starts at index 0. Whatever remains on the stack at the end is precisely the set of **unmatched openers** — the things you must add to or remove from the string.
tricks: Push **indices**, not characters, when the answer is a length or a position.
**Sentinel `-1`** at the bottom makes `i − top` the current valid-run length without edge cases (32).
If the stack pops to empty on every match, it *is* a counter — that's the bridge to the O(1)-space single-type solutions.
**Leftovers on the stack** = the unmatched openers to fix (delete in 1249, count in 921).

problems.title: Valid Parentheses
problems.note: Push openers; each closer must equal the **matching** popped top — this is the case a bare counter can't handle (`([)]` is invalid).

problems.title: Longest Valid Parentheses
problems.note: Stack of **indices** + `-1` sentinel; after each pop the live valid length is `i − top`. Track the max.

problems.title: Minimum Add to Make Parentheses Valid
problems.note: A stack of opens popped by closes — but since there's one type it reduces to two counters; additions = unmatched on each side.

problems.title: Minimum Remove to Make Valid Parentheses
problems.note: Stack holds **indices** of unmatched `(`; a closer with an empty stack is an unmatched `)`. Remove every marked index.

backtrack.tldr: Backtracking appears when the task is to **enumerate** or **repair** rather than validate — explore a decision tree of placements/removals and **prune with the balance invariant**.
insight: Brute-forcing all `2^(2n)` bracket strings (or all subsets of chars to remove) is exponential; backtracking is only tractable because the **invariant prunes whole subtrees**. In generation, refusing to add `)` when `close == open` kills every prefix that can never recover. In removal, pre-computing the **exact** surplus means you never recurse deeper than necessary.

Problem 241 is the interesting outlier: it's backtracking *as divide & conquer*. Splitting at each operator yields independent left/right subproblems whose result **sets** are combined — and because substrings repeat, **memoization** turns it from exponential into polynomial.
tricks: **Prune with the invariant**: generate `(` only while `open < n`, `)` only while `close < open`.
For removal, compute the **minimum** removals first, then search exactly that depth (301).
**Dedup siblings** (skip equal consecutive removals) so identical results aren't produced twice.
Combine **result sets** (not single values) when recursing on subexpressions, and **memoize** by substring (241).
backtrack.pseudo:
generate(open, close, cur):       # 22
  if len(cur) == 2*n: emit(cur); return
  if open  < n:     generate(open+1, close,   cur + '(')
  if close < open:  generate(open,   close+1, cur + ')')   # prune: never close past open

problems.title: Generate Parentheses
problems.note: DFS adding `(` (while `open < n`) or `)` (while `close < open`); the second guard prunes every invalid prefix, so only well-formed strings are emitted.

problems.title: Different Ways to Add Parentheses
problems.note: Recurse at **every operator**: for each, combine each left result with each right result. **Memoize** by substring to avoid recomputing shared subexpressions.

problems.title: Remove Invalid Parentheses
problems.note: First count min `(`/`)` to remove; then DFS removing exactly that many, **deduping** sibling removals, and keep only strings that end fully valid.

string.tldr: Word/Dict problems become String problems the moment you treat each word as a hashable key — canonicalizing, slicing, and matching substrings against a dictionary set is the whole game.
insight: The unifying realization is that a **dictionary is a `set`/`map` of strings** and the question is always some flavor of *"does this slice/canonical form exist as a key?"* String operations supply the bridge: you **hash whole words** for O(1) membership, **slice the input** to probe candidates, or **transform a word into a canonical signature** (sorted letters, run-length encoding, abbreviation mask, pattern-of-first-occurrence) so that all words sharing a structural property collide into the same key. The structural condition that makes String fit is *finite, comparable units*: words are short, immutable, and cheaply hashed, so set-membership replaces explicit search edges (Word Ladder), and string equality replaces deep structural comparison (Word Pattern).

Interviewers are probing whether you can pick the **right canonical key**: a bijective `char↔word` map (Word Pattern), a sorted-or-RLE signature (Expressive Words), a bitmask over 26 letters (abbreviation/Max Score), or a normalized substring (Replace Words, Valid Word Abbreviation). The second probe is the **probe direction** — given a target string and a dict, do you generate neighbors and look them up, or scan the dict and test each candidate? Choosing the cheaper side (dict size vs. neighbor count vs. input length) is the performance crux.
tricks: **Canonicalize, then bucket**: map each word to a signature key — sorted chars (anagrams), `(char, count)` run-length groups (#809 Expressive Words), or a 26-bit letter mask (#1255, #843) — and group/compare on the key, never the raw string.
**Two-way bijection for patterns**: #290/#291 need *both* `pattern→word` and `word→pattern` maps to reject many-to-one collisions; a one-directional map silently passes `"ab"→"dog dog"`.
**Set the dict, slice the input**: #139/#140/#648 put words in a `HashSet` (or build a trie) and DP/probe over prefixes — `dp[i] |= dp[j] and s[j:i] in dict`. Cap inner work by the max word length.

**Pick the smaller frontier in BFS**: Word Ladder (#127/#126) generates `26*L` wildcard neighbors per word; if the dict is huge, precompute `*` -intermediate buckets or do bidirectional BFS from both ends.

**Abbreviation = bitmask diff**: #408/#411 model an abbreviation as a mask of which letters are revealed; a candidate matches iff `word XOR target` has no set bit *inside any kept-letter run*. Minimize over masks that distinguish target from all other equal-length words.
**Tie-break carefully on output order**: #692/#819 sort by frequency *then lexicographically*; a max-heap needs a custom comparator that flips the string order relative to the count order.
string.pseudo:
canonical_key(word):                # the core abstraction
    return signature(word)          # sorted / RLE / 26-bit mask / first-seen pattern

# membership / break-style probe (Word Break, Replace Words)
dict = set(words)
for i in 1..n:
    for L in 1..maxWordLen:
        j = i - L
        if j >= 0 and dp[j] and s[j:i] in dict:
            dp[i] = true; break

# grouping / matching by signature (Word Pattern, Expressive, Anagram-dict)
buckets = map()
for w in words:
    buckets[canonical_key(w)].append(w)
answer = compare query.signature against buckets / bijection maps

graph.tldr: Model the dictionary as an implicit graph where words are nodes and one-letter edits are edges, then BFS for the shortest transformation chain.
insight: The unifying idea is **implicit graph construction**: a set of words becomes a graph where each word is a **node** and an **undirected edge** connects two words differing by exactly one character. "Word/Dict" problems that ask for the *minimum number of transformations* between words are secretly **shortest-path-on-unweighted-graph** problems, and the structural condition is that every legal move (a single-letter mutation that must land on a valid dictionary word) is reversible and costs 1 — exactly the regime where **BFS** gives optimal answers.

The realization an interviewer probes is *not building the graph explicitly* (that costs `O(N^2 * L)` adjacency comparisons), but generating neighbors on the fly via the **wildcard/pattern trick**: for a word of length `L`, mutate each position to all 26 letters and check membership in a hash set. BFS then explores layer by layer, and the layer index *is* the answer. The depth of the BFS frontier equals the transformation-sequence length — that one-to-one mapping between graph distance and the problem's objective is the whole insight.
tricks: Use a **hash set** for the dictionary so neighbor membership tests are `O(1)`; never scan the whole list per word.

Generate neighbors by the `*` **pattern trick**: for each position `i`, try all 26 letters (or precompute buckets keyed by `word with position i replaced by '*'`). Bucketing makes adjacency `O(N*L)` instead of `O(N*L*26)`.
**Remove a word from the set once visited** (or keep a `visited` set) — this is the de-duplication that prevents revisiting nodes and is the BFS analogue of marking visited.
Return `level + 1` at the moment you dequeue/match `endWord`; count *nodes in the sequence* (including both endpoints), not edges — `#127` wants the length of the chain.
If `endWord` is not in the dictionary, return 0 immediately — it can never be a graph node.

**Bidirectional BFS** (expand from both `beginWord` and `endWord`, always growing the smaller frontier) cuts the search from `O(b^d)` toward `O(b^{d/2})` and is the expected optimization for large word lists.
graph.pseudo:
BFS_word_ladder(begin, end, words):
  S = set(words)
  if end not in S: return 0
  queue = [(begin, 1)]            # node, sequence-length
  S.discard(begin)
  while queue:
    word, steps = queue.pop_front()
    if word == end: return steps
    for i in 0..len(word)-1:      # neighbor generation
      for c in 'a'..'z':
        cand = word[:i] + c + word[i+1:]
        if cand in S:             # valid graph edge
          S.discard(cand)         # mark visited
          queue.push_back((cand, steps+1))
  return 0

problems.title: Word Ladder
problems.note: Treat each word as a graph node with edges to all dictionary words one letter apart, then run BFS from `beginWord`; the first time you reach `endWord`, the BFS layer count is the shortest transformation sequence length. Generate neighbors by replacing each position with 'a'..'z' and testing the dictionary hash set, marking words visited by removing them; bidirectional BFS optimizes the large-input case.

array.tldr: Treat a sentence as a token **array** and let **index positions** encode word relationships — so word problems collapse into array scanning, reversal, and index-difference minimization.
insight: The unifying realization is that a sentence is just an **ordered array of word tokens**, and once you `split` it that way, every "word" question becomes an **index** question. Reversal of words is an in-place array reversal; "distance between words" is the **minimum absolute difference of indices** where two target words appear. The array's left-to-right order is the only structure you need — no graph, no tree, just positional bookkeeping.

Why Array fits Word/Dict here: word distance is defined positionally, so the array index *is* the answer's currency. The interviewer is probing whether you avoid the naive O(n*m) of collecting all positions of each word and pairing them, and instead do a **single linear sweep** tracking the last-seen index of each target. The structural condition is that you only care about the *closest* pair, so you never need to store all positions — only the most recent one, which a streaming scan exploits. #244 flips this: when queried repeatedly, you precompute per-word **sorted position arrays** once and merge them like two sorted lists per query.
tricks: **Single-pass min distance**: keep `i1 = i2 = -1` for last-seen indices of `word1`/`word2`; on each match update its index and, if both are seen, `ans = min(ans, abs(i1 - i2))`. O(n) time, O(1) space — never collect full position lists for a one-shot query.

**#245 same-word case**: when `word1 == word2`, you need consecutive occurrences of one word, so track a single `prev` index and compute `i - prev` each time you hit the word; branch on equality up front.
**#244 repeated queries**: build a hashmap `word -> sorted index array` once, then per query do a **two-pointer merge** of the two arrays advancing the smaller index — O(a+b) per query, not O(a*b).
**In-place word reversal (#151)**: reverse the entire char array, then reverse each individual word — two passes give correct word order with original intra-word spelling, all in O(1) extra space.
**Whitespace pitfall (#151)**: leading/trailing/multiple spaces must be collapsed; trim and split on runs of spaces, or compact during the in-place build.

Use `abs(i1 - i2)` not signed difference, and you can early-exit a sweep only if you track that the just-updated index always pairs with the other's last-seen — minimum can only improve at the moment of an update.

trie.tldr: A Trie turns a dictionary into a prefix tree so that `.`-wildcard searches become bounded DFS branching across all 26 children at the unknown position.
insight: **Word / Dict** problems share a structural condition: you store a *set of words* and repeatedly query them by **shared prefix** or **partial pattern**. A hash set gives O(1) exact lookup but throws away the prefix structure — and the moment a query contains a wildcard, a hash set degrades to scanning every key. A **Trie** (prefix tree) keeps that structure explicit: each node is a prefix, each edge is a character, and an `isEnd` flag marks where a real word terminates. This is exactly why Trie *fits* dictionaries — the cost of a lookup becomes proportional to word length, not dictionary size, and prefixes are physically shared.

The realization an interviewer probes in **#211** is that a `.` wildcard doesn't break the Trie model — it converts a linear walk into a **DFS that branches over all children** at the wildcard index. Concrete characters still advance deterministically down a single edge; only `.` forks. So the design pivot is: `addWord` is a plain insert, and `search` is a recursive descent parameterized by `(node, index)` that special-cases `.` versus a literal. Recognizing that the wildcard's branching factor is bounded by the alphabet (≤26) and the depth by word length is the key to arguing the complexity.
tricks: Store children as a fixed `child[26]` array (or a hashmap) plus a boolean `isEnd`; the **word terminates only where `isEnd` is true**, never at "any node we reached" — a prefix of a stored word must not match.
`search` must be **recursive** (or use an explicit stack) because a `.` forces branching; an iterative single-pointer walk cannot handle wildcards.
On a `.` at position `i`, iterate over **all 26 existing children** and recurse with `index+1`; return `true` on the first child whose subtree matches — short-circuit, don't continue.
On a literal char, if that specific child is `null`, return `false` immediately — no branching, no fallback.
Base case: when `index == len(word)`, return `node.isEnd`, **not** `node != null`. Forgetting this matches prefixes as if they were words.

Complexity: `addWord` is O(L); `search` is O(L) with no wildcards but worst-case O(26^k · L) when k positions are `.` — a pure-wildcard query like `"..."` can explode, so this is the pitfall to flag aloud.
trie.pseudo:
class Node: child[26] = null; isEnd = false
root = new Node()

addWord(w):
  cur = root
  for c in w:
    if cur.child[c] == null: cur.child[c] = new Node()
    cur = cur.child[c]
  cur.isEnd = true

search(w): return dfs(root, 0, w)

dfs(node, i, w):
  if node == null: return false
  if i == len(w): return node.isEnd
  c = w[i]
  if c == '.':
    for nxt in node.child:        # branch over all 26
      if dfs(nxt, i+1, w): return true
    return false
  return dfs(node.child[c], i+1, w)

problems.title: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
problems.note: Insert every word into a Trie with an `isEnd` flag; `search` runs a DFS that walks one edge per literal character but branches over all 26 children whenever it hits a `.` wildcard, returning true only if some leaf path ends on a node where `isEnd` is set.

backtrack.tldr: Backtracking turns Word/Dict problems into DFS over a constrained search tree — grid paths, string cuts, or pattern bindings — where each step extends a partial word and dictionary/Trie membership prunes dead branches before they explode.
insight: Word/Dict problems share a hidden structure: you build a string (or a mapping) one decision at a time, and the **dictionary** is the oracle that says whether a partial commitment can still succeed. Backtracking fits because the solution is a *sequence of reversible choices* — pick the next grid cell, the next cut position, the next character a token maps to — and each choice must be **undone** on failure (unmark visited cell, pop the prefix, erase the binding). The art is not the DFS itself but the **pruning**: a `Trie` lets you abandon a path the instant the accumulated prefix matches no word, a feasibility check (`canBreak`) kills cut-points whose suffix is undecomposable, and an injectivity invariant rejects pattern maps that collide.

The interviewer is probing whether you see that *naive enumeration is exponential and the dictionary is what makes it tractable*. The key realization: fold the dictionary INTO the traversal rather than testing membership at the leaves. A Trie shared across all words (#212) converts "search 1 word" into "search all words simultaneously," memoizing on the suffix (#140) collapses overlapping subproblems, and for pattern/abbreviation problems the constraint itself (bijection, bitmask coverage) is the pruner. Recognize the **partial-candidate + constraint-check + undo** triad and every problem here reduces to the same skeleton.
tricks: **Mark-then-unmark** is the universal invariant: set `visited[r][c]` (or temporarily overwrite the grid char with `#`) before recursing and restore it after — forgetting the restore corrupts sibling branches.

**Prune with the dictionary structure, not at the leaf**: walk a shared `Trie` alongside the DFS so a prefix matching no word fails immediately; for #212 also *delete* leaf nodes once a word is found to shrink the Trie and dedupe.

**Memoize on the suffix** for word-break style problems (#140): cache `index -> list of sentences` so the same tail is decomposed once; guard with a fast `wordBreak` (boolean DP) feasibility precheck so you never recurse into a suffix that can't be split.

**Maintain a bijection** in pattern matching (#291): use two maps `char->word` and `word->char`; before binding check neither side conflicts, and `backtrack` by erasing BOTH entries — a one-way map silently accepts non-injective matches.

**Order/bound the search smartly**: in #411 try abbreviation bitmasks by increasing length (fewer kept letters = shorter abbr) and reject any mask that fails to distinguish the target from a same-length dictionary word; in #843 pick the guess that *minimizes the worst-case remaining candidate set* (minimax) and filter by returned match-count.
**Watch the grid restart cost**: #79/#212 launch a DFS from every cell, so total work is `O(R*C*4^L)` worst case — early Trie/prefix pruning is what keeps it alive on large boards.
backtrack.pseudo:
function dfs(node, r, c, path):        # Word Search II via Trie
    ch = grid[r][c]
    if ch == '#' or ch not in node.children: return
    nxt = node.children[ch]
    path += ch
    if nxt.word: results.add(nxt.word); nxt.word = null   # dedupe
    grid[r][c] = '#'                    # mark visited
    for (dr,dc) in 4-directions:
        nr, nc = r+dr, c+dc
        if in_bounds(nr,nc): dfs(nxt, nr, nc, path)
    grid[r][c] = ch                     # UNDO (backtrack)
    if nxt is leaf: prune(nxt)          # shrink Trie

for each cell (r,c): dfs(root, r, c, "")

dfs.tldr: DFS-with-backtracking walks the board cell-by-cell, matching one character of the target word per recursion level and undoing the visited mark on the way back up.
insight: A **Word/Dict** problem on a 2-D grid becomes a **DFS** the moment the *answer is a path*: the word is an ordered sequence of characters, and each character must sit on a grid cell adjacent to the previous one. The recursion state is exactly `(row, col, index_into_word)` — DFS fits because at every step you have ≤4 choices (up/down/left/right) and a single linear constraint (`board[r][c] == word[index]`), so the search tree is naturally a depth-first exploration of partial prefixes that either extends to a full match or dead-ends and prunes.

The realization an interviewer is probing is that this is **backtracking, not plain traversal**: a cell may be reused by a *different* word path, so the 'visited' mark must be **temporary** — set on entry, cleared on exit. Forgetting to unmark turns the search into a global visited set (wrong answers); a permanent mark only works for connected-component style problems, not for path-finding where the same cell is fair game on an alternate route from a different starting cell.
tricks: **Prune at the call boundary**: check bounds, `board[r][c] != word[index]`, and the visited mark *before* recursing — return early so dead branches never spawn 4 children.

**Mark-then-restore in place**: overwrite `board[r][c]` with a sentinel like `'#'` on entry and write the original char back before returning — avoids a separate `visited` matrix and keeps O(1) per-cell extra memory.
**Base case is `index == len(word)`**: once you have matched the last character you have already consumed it, so success is reaching length, not matching the final cell again.
**Try every cell as a start**: the outer loop launches a DFS from each `(r,c)`; short-circuit (`return true`) on the first full match.
**Cheap frequency pre-check**: if any char in `word` appears more often than on the board, fail instantly; reversing `word` to start the search from its rarer end prunes huge subtrees.
**Pitfall — sharing one global visited set across start cells**: visited state must be local to the current path; only the temporary in-place mark (restored on backtrack) is correct.
dfs.pseudo:
function exist(board, word):
  for r, c in all cells:
    if dfs(board, word, r, c, 0): return true
  return false

function dfs(board, word, r, c, i):
  if i == len(word): return true
  if out_of_bounds(r,c) or board[r][c] != word[i]: return false
  saved = board[r][c]; board[r][c] = '#'        // mark visited
  found = dfs(r+1,c,i+1) or dfs(r-1,c,i+1)
        or dfs(r,c+1,i+1) or dfs(r,c-1,i+1)
  board[r][c] = saved                            // backtrack / restore
  return found

Mark the current cell with a sentinel before recursing and restore it on return so the same cell can be reused by other candidate paths — return true the instant `i` reaches the word's length.

trie-topic.tldr: A **Trie** turns a dictionary of words into a single prefix-indexed graph so you can prune DFS the instant a path stops being a valid prefix, or match a shortest prefix in one walk.
insight: The unifying realization is that when a problem checks **many words against many positions/strings**, repeatedly scanning each word independently is wasteful because the words share prefixes. A **Trie** collapses the whole dictionary into one structure keyed by character, so common prefixes are merged into shared paths. This converts "is this string a word / does any word start with this prefix?" from an O(W) per-word question into an O(1) edge-follow during traversal. The structural condition that makes Trie fit Word/Dict is precisely **shared prefixes plus prefix-incremental queries**: you build a candidate character-by-character and want to know, at each step, whether continuing is still viable.

For grid/search problems the key insight an interviewer probes is **flipping the loop**: instead of running a separate search per dictionary word (#212 done naively as #79 in a loop), you walk the grid ONCE while walking the Trie in lockstep — the Trie node carries the set of all still-possible words, and a dead-end Trie edge prunes that DFS branch immediately. For replacement problems (#648) the Trie gives you the **shortest matching root** in a single forward scan that stops at the first terminal node.
tricks: **Walk grid and Trie in lockstep** (#212): the DFS argument is the current Trie `node`, not a target word. Recurse to `node.children[grid[r][c]]` only if that child exists — a missing edge prunes the entire branch, which is the whole point versus looping #79.
**Store the full word at terminal nodes** (`node.word = word`) instead of a boolean `isEnd`. When you hit a node with non-null `word`, push it to results — no need to reconstruct the path string.
**De-dupe and prune the Trie as you find words**: set `node.word = null` after collecting to avoid duplicate results, and you may prune leaf nodes to shrink later searches.
**Mark cells visited in-place** (e.g. set `grid[r][c] = '#'`) before recursing and restore after — standard backtracking; never reuse a cell within one word path.

**Shortest root wins** (#648): insert all roots, then for each query word walk the Trie following the word's chars and stop at the FIRST terminal node — that is the shortest prefix root; if you fall off the Trie, keep the original word.

Pitfall: building one Trie of dictionary roots/words is O(total chars); don't rebuild per query. Pitfall in #79's single word, a Trie is overkill — plain backtracking suffices; Trie pays off only with many words (#212) or many lookups (#648).
trie-topic.pseudo:
build Trie: for word in dict: node=root; for c in word: node=node.child[c]; node.word=word

# Word Search II (grid x Trie lockstep)
function dfs(r, c, node):
    ch = grid[r][c]
    if ch=='#' or ch not in node.child: return
    nxt = node.child[ch]
    if nxt.word: result.add(nxt.word); nxt.word=null   # de-dupe
    grid[r][c]='#'
    for (nr,nc) in neighbors(r,c): dfs(nr, nc, nxt)
    grid[r][c]=ch                                       # backtrack

for each cell (r,c): dfs(r, c, root)

# Replace Words: walk one word, stop at first terminal
function shortestRoot(w): node=root; pre=""
    for c in w: if c not in node.child: return w
        pre+=c; node=node.child[c]; if node.word: return pre
    return w

problems.title: Word Search
problems.note: Single target word, so a Trie is unnecessary overkill — plain backtracking DFS suffices. It is the BASE CASE: #212 generalizes it by replacing the one-word match with a Trie of many words walked in lockstep with the grid.

problems.title: Word Search II
problems.note: Build a Trie of all dictionary words, then DFS the grid ONCE passing the current Trie node; only step to existing child edges so dead prefixes prune the branch, and emit `node.word` at terminal nodes (nulling it to avoid duplicates) instead of running #79 per word.

problems.title: Replace Words
problems.note: Insert all dictionary roots into a Trie, then for each word in the sentence walk the Trie char-by-char and replace it with the prefix at the FIRST terminal node reached (shortest matching root); if the walk falls off the Trie, keep the original word.

bfs.tldr: Word transformation problems become shortest-path graphs where words are nodes and one-letter edits are edges, so BFS finds the minimum transformation sequence by level.
insight: The unifying realization is that a **word ladder is an implicit unweighted graph**: each word is a node and an edge connects two words differing by exactly one letter. Because every edge has unit cost, the **shortest transformation sequence** is exactly a shortest path, which **BFS** computes optimally by expanding level-by-level. The structural condition that makes BFS apply is uniform edge weight (one edit = one step); the moment edits had varying costs you would reach for Dijkstra instead.

The key trick an interviewer probes is **how you generate neighbors without an O(n^2) all-pairs comparison**: for each position, replace the character with every letter `a-z` and test membership in a `dict` set, giving `O(L * 26 * L)` per word instead of comparing against all words. The second realization is the distinction between the two problems: #127 only needs the **distance** (BFS level count), while #126 needs **all** shortest paths, which requires recording the BFS **parent/predecessor DAG** during the level-by-level expansion and then backtracking it via DFS.
tricks: Build neighbors by the **`a-z` substitution pattern**, not pairwise comparison: for each index `i` of the word, swap in all 26 letters and check the `wordList` set — `O(L*26)` lookups beat `O(N*L)` cross-checks when the dictionary is large.
Use a **`set`/`HashSet` for the dictionary** so membership and the visited check are `O(1)`; mark a word visited the instant you enqueue it to avoid re-enqueueing duplicates within the same frontier.
Return level count `+1` (number of words in the path, not edges) for #127; the canonical answer counts nodes including start and end, so `0` if `endWord` is absent from the dictionary.

For #126, do NOT mark visited globally per-word during a level — defer removal until the level finishes, otherwise you drop valid alternate shortest paths that arrive at the same word in the same level (multiple parents).
Build a **parent/predecessor map** during BFS for #126, then **DFS-backtrack** from `endWord` to `beginWord` to reconstruct every shortest path; stop BFS at the first level that reaches `endWord`.
**Bidirectional BFS** (expand the smaller frontier from both ends, swapping sets) roughly halves the explored branching factor `26^d` to `2*26^(d/2)` and is the optimal-grade answer for #127.
bfs.pseudo:
BFS_wordladder(begin, end, dict):
  if end not in dict: return 0
  q = queue([begin]); dict.remove(begin); steps = 1
  while q not empty:
    for _ in range(len(q)):          # process one level
      w = q.pop()
      if w == end: return steps
      for i in range(len(w)):        # neighbor generation
        for c in 'a'..'z':
          nw = w[:i] + c + w[i+1:]
          if nw in dict:
            dict.remove(nw); q.push(nw)   # mark visited on enqueue
    steps += 1
  return 0
# Word Ladder II: keep parents[level] per word, don't remove until
# level ends, then DFS-backtrack parents from end -> begin.

problems.title: Word Ladder
problems.note: Model words as nodes with one-letter-edit edges and run BFS from `beginWord`; the first level at which `endWord` is dequeued gives the shortest transformation length (number of words in the path). Generate neighbors via the `a-z` substitution-and-set-lookup trick and mark visited on enqueue; bidirectional BFS is the optimal speedup.

problems.title: Word Ladder II
problems.note: Run the same level-by-level BFS but record a predecessor map (all parents that first reach each word at its minimal level), deferring the visited removal until each level completes so multiple shortest paths to the same word are preserved. Once `endWord` is reached, DFS-backtrack the parent map from `endWord` to `beginWord` to emit every shortest transformation sequence.

shortest-path.tldr: Treat each word as a graph node with edges between words differing by one letter, then **BFS** gives the shortest transformation sequence — an unweighted-shortest-path problem in disguise.
insight: Word-ladder problems hide a graph: every word in the dictionary is a **vertex**, and an undirected **edge** connects two words that differ in exactly one character. Because every transformation costs exactly 1, all edges have unit weight, so the shortest transformation sequence is precisely the **shortest path in an unweighted graph** — the canonical job of **BFS**. The realization the interviewer probes is that you should *never* build the full adjacency matrix by comparing all O(N^2) word pairs; instead you generate neighbors on the fly via the **wildcard / pattern-bucket** trick (`h*t`, `*ot`, `ho*`).

The structural condition that makes BFS apply is uniform edge cost plus the question asking for a *minimum count* of steps (length of the ladder), not all paths or a weighted optimum. BFS explores level by level, so the first time you pop `endWord` the current level number is the answer. The whole art is making neighbor enumeration cheap: for a word of length `L` over alphabet of size 26, generating neighbors by substituting each position is O(26L), independent of dictionary size, which dominates the design.
tricks: Build a **pattern map**: for each word, for each position, key `word` with that char replaced by `*` (e.g. `*ot`, `h*t`, `ho*`). Words sharing a pattern are neighbors — this replaces O(N^2 * L) pairwise comparison with O(N * L) bucketing.
Return **level + 1** counting nodes (Word Ladder counts words in the sequence, not edges); start BFS at distance 1 for `beginWord` so popping `endWord` yields the sequence length directly.

Use a **visited set** (or remove words from the dict on visit) to avoid revisiting and infinite loops; mark a node visited when you *enqueue* it, not when you dequeue, to prevent duplicate enqueues at the same level.
If `endWord` is not in `wordList`, immediately return 0 — no valid path can exist since the target must be a real dictionary node.

Optimize with **bidirectional BFS**: expand simultaneously from `beginWord` and `endWord`, always growing the smaller frontier; meet-in-the-middle cuts the branching-factor exponent roughly in half (`b^(d/2)` vs `b^d`).
Each wildcard bucket can be cleared (or its words removed) once consumed so the same intermediate pattern is not reprocessed across levels.

problems.title: Word Ladder
problems.note: Model each word as a node with unit-weight edges between words differing by one letter, then run **BFS** from `beginWord`; the first level at which `endWord` is dequeued gives the shortest transformation length. Neighbors are found via the **`*`-wildcard pattern map** to avoid O(N^2) pairwise comparison, and bidirectional BFS further reduces the explored frontier.

dp.tldr: DP over a word/dictionary turns "can I form/score this string from dictionary pieces?" into reusing answers to smaller prefixes or subsets, eliminating the exponential blowup of trying every split or word combination.
insight: Word/Dict problems ask whether a target can be **assembled** from dictionary entries and, if so, **how well** (segmentable / maximum score). The exponential trap is the **combinatorial choice of pieces**: every prefix can be cut in many places, every word can be taken or skipped. DP applies because these choices have **overlapping subproblems** and **optimal substructure** — the answer for a prefix `s[0..i)` (or for a remaining letter-budget / set of usable words) depends only on answers for *smaller* states, not on the path taken to reach them.

The structural condition is that the state can be compressed to something **small and reusable**: a prefix index `i` in #139, or a subset/index over a *small* word list in #1255. The interviewer is probing whether you recognize that naive recursion recomputes the same sub-answer many times, and that you can memoize on (a) a **string position** when pieces are consumed left-to-right, or (b) a **resource vector** (available letters) plus a **choice index** when each dictionary word is an all-or-nothing item — i.e. that #1255 is really a 0/1-knapsack-style pick/skip DP, not a string DP.
tricks: **Choose the right state.** #139: 1-D over prefix length, `dp[i]` = is `s[0..i)` segmentable. #1255: state is the *word index* plus the *remaining letter multiset* — never the target string, because words are picked as whole items, not concatenated to match a string.
**Dictionary as a hash set** for #139 so each candidate suffix `s[j..i)` is checked in O(len). Bound the inner cut by `maxWordLen` to cut the constant factor.
**Transition direction.** Prefix DP: `dp[i] = OR over j<i of (dp[j] AND s[j..i) in dict)`; base `dp[0]=true` (empty prefix always formable).

**#1255 is 0/1 knapsack, not unbounded** — each word usable at most once and each board letter has a finite count, so you must *subtract a letter histogram* on pick and *restore* it on backtrack (or carry it in the memo key).

**Letters are the real budget.** In #1255, score the word's letters minus the available `letters[]` counts; a word is takeable only if every required letter count is still available. Skipping is always allowed.
**Pitfall: don't greedily take high-score words** in #1255 — letter contention means a locally optimal word can block two better ones; you must compare `max(skip, take+recurse)`.
dp.pseudo:
// #139 Word Break — prefix DP
dp[0] = true
for i in 1..n:
  for j in 0..i-1:
    if dp[j] and s[j..i) in dictSet: dp[i] = true; break
return dp[n]

// #1255 Max Score — pick/skip DP over word index with letter budget
def solve(idx, avail):           // avail = remaining letter counts
  if idx == words.length: return 0
  best = solve(idx+1, avail)                 // skip word
  if canForm(words[idx], avail):             // every letter count ok
    gain = score(words[idx])
    best = max(best, gain + solve(idx+1, avail - histogram(words[idx])))
  return best                                 // take vs skip

problems.title: Word Break
problems.note: Classic prefix DP: `dp[i]` is true iff `s[0..i)` splits into dictionary words, computed as an OR over all earlier cut points `j` where `dp[j]` holds and the suffix `s[j..i)` is in the dictionary set; answer is `dp[n]`.

problems.title: Maximum Score Words Formed by Letters
problems.note: 0/1-knapsack-style DP over the word list: at each word index recurse on take-vs-skip, where taking is allowed only if the shared `letters[]` budget covers the word's letter histogram, accumulating the word's score and subtracting its letters; return the max over all subsets.

two-pointers.tldr: In Word/Dict problems, two pointers march over parallel positions — two indices into one array of word occurrences, or one index per string in a parse/scan — collapsing nested comparison into a single linear sweep.
insight: The unifying idea is that **Word/Dict** problems here reduce to scanning **two monotonically-advancing positions** that never backtrack. Two flavors appear: (1) *two indices into the same sorted list* — the occurrence positions of two target words — where the classic 'minimum gap between two sorted lists' merge applies; and (2) *two indices into two different strings* — one cursor per string (word vs. abbreviation, word vs. stretched word) — advanced in lockstep while a local invariant (character match, run length) is validated. In both cases the structural condition that licenses two pointers is **monotonicity**: occurrence indices are increasing, and string scans only move forward, so each pointer makes at most n moves for an O(n) sweep.

The realization an interviewer probes is recognizing that nested loops (compare every occurrence of word1 against every occurrence of word2, or backtrack on a mismatch) are unnecessary because the comparison space is *ordered*. For distance problems, advance whichever pointer points to the *smaller* index, because moving the larger one can only widen the gap. For parse/scan problems (abbreviation, expressive words), the trick is to treat each string with its own cursor and reason about **runs** — consecutive equal characters or a numeric block — so a digit group or a stretched group is consumed in one step rather than character-by-character with rewind.
tricks: **Distance merge invariant**: keep one index into word1's positions and one into word2's; at each step compute `|i-j|`, then advance the pointer with the *smaller* value — advancing the larger can never shrink the distance.

**Single-pass distance (no precompute)**: for a one-shot query, scan the array once keeping `last1` and `last2` (most recent index of each word); on every hit, update the answer with `|last1 - last2|` — this is two 'trailing pointers' over one array.

**word1 == word2 edge case** (#245): when the two words are identical, track a single `prev` index and answer with the gap between *consecutive* occurrences, not two separate lists — a common off-by-pattern trap.

**Abbreviation scan** (#408): one pointer per string; on a digit, parse the full number (reject a leading `0`) and jump the word pointer forward by that count; on a letter, require an exact match and advance both; accept only if both pointers reach the end together.

**Run-length two pointers** (#809): walk word and query with paired cursors; the characters must match, then compare the lengths of the maximal equal-char runs — a stretchy group is valid iff `wordRun == queryRun`, or `wordRun > queryRun and wordRun >= 3`.

**Pitfall — backtracking**: never reset a pointer on mismatch in these problems; the monotonic structure guarantees the answer is reachable in a single forward pass, and any rewind signals a wrong model.

problems.title: Shortest Word Distance
problems.note: Single forward scan keeping trailing indices `last1` and `last2` of the two words; on each occurrence update `best = min(best, |last1 - last2|)`. Two pointers as two 'most-recent-seen' cursors over one array, O(n) one shot.

problems.title: Shortest Word Distance II
problems.note: Precompute a map word to sorted occurrence-index list once; per query, run the two-pointer merge over the two lists, always advancing the index with the smaller value to converge on the minimum gap in O(|P1|+|P2|).

problems.title: Shortest Word Distance III
problems.note: Same trailing-pointer scan as #243, but handle `word1 == word2` specially: track a single `prev` index and take the gap between consecutive occurrences, since the two cursors collapse onto the same word's positions.

problems.title: Valid Word Abbreviation
problems.note: One cursor per string; when the abbreviation shows a digit, parse the whole numeric run (reject leading zero) and jump the word cursor forward by that amount, else require an exact character match — valid iff both cursors finish together with no backtracking.

problems.title: Expressive Words
problems.note: Run-length two pointers: walk the query and word in lockstep, characters must match, then a query group of length `q` stretches to a word group of length `w` iff `w == q`, or `w > q and w >= 3`; each maximal run is consumed in one step.

hash.tldr: Hash maps turn word problems into membership-and-correspondence checks: a `set` for "is this word special?" and a `dict` for "does this token still map to the same word?"
insight: Word/Dict problems reduce to questions about **identity** and **lookup**: "have I seen this token before, and what did it map to?" A hash table answers both in `O(1)`. The two canonical roles are a **set** (membership: is a word in a banned/special collection) and a **dictionary** (association: bind a key to a previously-seen value and verify consistency on every reuse). The interviewer is probing whether you recognize that the constraint is really a *function* — each distinct input must map to exactly one output, and vice versa.

The structural condition that makes hashing fit is **token-level discreteness**: the input is naturally chunked into words (split on spaces/punctuation), and the answer depends only on *equality* of those chunks, not their order or internal structure. That equality test is exactly what a hash table's keys provide. The deeper realization for #290 is that a one-to-one mapping (**bijection**) requires checking *both directions* — a single forward `dict` is insufficient because two distinct keys could collide onto the same value.
tricks: **Normalize first**: lowercase and strip punctuation before tokenizing. In #819, replace every non-letter with a space, then `split`, so `"ball,"` and `"ball"` hash identically.

**Bijection needs two maps (or one map + one set)**: in #290 maintain `char->word` AND track used words; if `char` is unseen but its candidate `word` is already claimed, return `false`. A lone forward map wrongly accepts `"ab" / "dog dog"`.
**Length guard before iterating**: #290 must compare `len(pattern)` against `len(words)`; `zip` silently truncates and can falsely report a match (`"aaa" / "dog dog"`).
**Set for exclusion, dict-counter for ranking**: #819 puts banned words in a `set` for `O(1)` filtering and a `Counter`/frequency `dict` for the most-common word.

**The first-index-of-equality idiom**: an alternative bijection check is `map(c) for c in pattern` equals `map(w) for w in words` where `map` returns first-seen index — encodes the structural pattern without explicit two-way checks.
**Pitfall — case sensitivity of the answer**: #819 banned list and paragraph must be compared case-insensitively, but the returned word is lowercase regardless of input casing.

problems.title: Word Pattern
problems.note: Treat the pattern-to-word correspondence as a bijection: maintain two hash maps (`char->word` and `word->char`) and reject any token whose mapping conflicts with a prior binding; also guard `len(pattern) == len(words)` since `zip` truncation can mask a mismatch.

problems.title: Most Common Word
problems.note: Normalize the paragraph (lowercase, punctuation->space) and tokenize, store the banned list in a `set` for `O(1)` exclusion, then tally survivors in a frequency `dict` and return the key with the maximum count.

simulation.tldr: Valid Word Square is pure index-mapping simulation: walk the grid and verify the transpose-equality invariant `word[r][c] == word[c][r]` without ever materializing the transpose.
insight: A **word square** is a list of strings that reads identically across rows and down columns: the k-th row equals the k-th column. Under the **Word / Dict × Simulation** lens, the problem is not about dictionaries or string algorithms at all — it is about *faithfully reproducing the definition* by walking the structure exactly as stated. The unifying idea is that the validity condition is a symmetry invariant, `words[r][c] == words[c][r]` for every coordinate, and simulation means checking that invariant character-by-character rather than reasoning about it cleverly.

Simulation fits because the data is a **ragged (jagged) 2D grid** — rows have different lengths — so the real difficulty is bookkeeping, not logic. The interviewer is probing whether you handle the asymmetric bounds correctly: position `(r, c)` is valid only if `r < len(words)` AND `c < len(words[r])`, and the symmetric cell `(c, r)` has its own independent bounds. A character existing on one side but being out of range on the other is exactly the failure mode that breaks naive solutions.
tricks: The core invariant: for every `(r, c)`, the character `words[r][c]` must exist iff `words[c][r]` exists, and when both exist they must be equal. Both *existence mismatch* and *value mismatch* are failures.

Guard ragged bounds before indexing: when scanning row `r` at column `c`, you must check `c >= len(words)` (no such row `c` to act as the column) OR `r >= len(words[c])` (row `c` too short to supply the symmetric char) and return `false`.
Iterate only the upper triangle (`c` from `r` to `len(words[r])`) to halve work and avoid double-checking symmetric pairs — but you still need the bounds guard on the mirrored cell.

Pitfall: assuming the matrix is square. A valid word square need not be square overall, but each row's used length is constrained by the number of rows; e.g. row `r` cannot be longer than the count of rows that reach column index `r`.
Pitfall: off-by-one on the mirror — comparing `words[r][c]` against `words[c][r]` requires `words[c]` to exist (so `c < len(words)`) and to be long enough (`r < len(words[c])`).
No extra data structures needed: O(1) space, O(total characters) time — pure in-place index simulation.
simulation.pseudo:
function validWordSquare(words):
  for r in 0 .. len(words)-1:
    for c in 0 .. len(words[r])-1:
      # need symmetric cell (c, r) to exist and match
      if c >= len(words):            # no row c to serve as column
        return false
      if r >= len(words[c]):         # row c too short for char at r
        return false
      if words[r][c] != words[c][r]: # value mismatch
        return false
  return true

problems.title: Valid Word Square
problems.note: Simulate the word-square definition directly: scan each cell `(r, c)` and verify the transpose invariant `words[r][c] == words[c][r]`, guarding the ragged bounds by returning false whenever the mirrored row `words[c]` is missing (`c >= len(words)`) or too short (`r >= len(words[c])`). It is an O(total chars), O(1)-space index walk with no auxiliary structures.

heap.tldr: For Word/Dict problems, a heap turns "rank words by frequency then break ties lexicographically" into an `O(n log k)` top-k selection over `(count, word)` pairs.
insight: The Word/Dict subject matter contributes the **dictionary build** — a hash map from word to frequency count — while Heap contributes the **selection mechanism**. The unifying idea is that once you have a `Map<word, count>` you rarely need to fully sort all distinct words; you only need the **top `k`**, and a bounded **min-heap of size `k`** extracts those in `O(n log k)` instead of `O(n log n)`. This is the canonical heap-for-top-k pattern, but with a word-specific twist that makes it the actual interview probe.

The twist is the **composite ordering**: ties in frequency must be broken **lexicographically (alphabetically ascending)**. Because the two sort keys point in opposite directions (higher count is 'better', but smaller string is 'better'), the heap comparator cannot be a naive single-key compare. The realization the interviewer wants is that for a **min-heap of size k** you must invert BOTH keys relative to the final desired order so the 'worst' element (lowest count, or on tie the lexicographically largest word) sits at the root and gets evicted — then a final reverse yields the correct output.
tricks: Build the frequency map first (`O(n)`); the heap operates only over **distinct words**, so its size is the vocabulary, not the token count.

For a **size-`k` min-heap**, the comparator must rank the *least desirable* item at the top: order by `count` ascending, and on equal count by word **descending** (lexicographically larger word is 'smaller' for the heap) so it gets evicted first.
After collecting `k` elements, **pop and reverse** — the heap yields worst-to-best, so the answer list must be reversed to get most-frequent-first with alphabetical tie-breaking.
Pitfall: using a max-heap of ALL distinct words and popping `k` is `O(n log n)` build but simpler to reason about — valid, but the size-`k` min-heap is the `O(n log k)` optimum the question targets.

Pitfall: getting tie-break direction backwards. In a min-heap the lexicographic comparison must be **reversed** relative to the final output; double-check with a same-count example like `['i','love']`.
Bucket sort is the `O(n)` alternative (index buckets by count), but each bucket still needs lexicographic sorting — the heap is cleaner when only `k` results are wanted.

problems.title: Top K Frequent Words
problems.note: Build a `word -> count` hash map, then maintain a **size-`k` min-heap** of `(count, word)` whose comparator ranks by count ascending and breaks ties by word lexicographically descending, so the least-frequent (or alphabetically-last on ties) word sits at the root and is evicted. Pop the remaining `k` entries and reverse to emit them most-frequent-first with ascending alphabetical tie-breaking in `O(n log k)`.

sorting.tldr: Sorting turns a word-frequency map into a deterministic ranking by composing a numeric key (count, descending) with a lexicographic tiebreak (word, ascending) in a single comparator.
insight: The core of every **Word / Dict** ranking problem is a `HashMap<word, count>`: the dictionary collapses duplicate strings into frequency counts. **Sorting** then imposes the *output order* the problem demands. What makes this intersection distinctive is the **compound comparator**: the primary key is `count` in *descending* order, but ties must break on the *word itself* in *ascending lexicographic* order. Strings are first-class sort keys here, so the same comparator mixes a reverse-numeric field with a forward-string field — a classic source of bugs when someone naively negates the whole comparison.
tricks: Build the **frequency map first** (`O(n)`), then sort only the *distinct* words — sort cost is `O(d log d)` over `d` unique keys, not `n`.

The comparator is **two-tiered and asymmetric**: `count` descending, `word` ascending. Do NOT negate the string comparison — only the count is reversed: `b.count - a.count`, else `a.word.compareTo(b.word)`.

For `Top K` specifically, prefer a **size-`k` heap** with the *inverted* comparator (least-frequent / lexicographically-largest at the top) so you can pop the loser; this gives `O(d log k)` instead of `O(d log d)`.
Heap pitfall: because the heap holds the *worst* element at its root, its internal order is the reverse of the final answer — you must **reverse the popped sequence** before returning.
Lexicographic order means natural `String` comparison (`compareTo`), not length; "apple" < "app" is false — "app" < "apple" because it is a prefix.
Edge: words with **equal counts** must come out alphabetically; verify your tiebreak with a case where every count is 1 (pure lexicographic sort).
sorting.pseudo:
freq = {}
for w in words:
    freq[w] += 1

# Comparator: count DESC, then word ASC
distinct = keys(freq)
sort distinct by (a, b):
    if freq[a] != freq[b]: return freq[b] - freq[a]   # higher count first
    else: return compare(a, b)                         # lexicographic

return distinct[0 .. k-1]

# Heap variant (size k): use INVERTED comparator,
#   keep k best, pop excess, then reverse the drained list.

problems.title: Top K Frequent Words
problems.note: Count words into a `HashMap`, then sort the distinct keys with a compound comparator (`count` descending, word lexicographically ascending) and take the first `k`; alternatively maintain a size-`k` min-heap using the inverted comparator and reverse the drained output to respect the tie-break ordering.

greedy.tldr: Mark which characters belong to any dictionary word, then greedily merge maximal contiguous runs of marked indices into the fewest, longest bold spans.
insight: The unifying idea is a two-phase greedy: a **coverage pass** that paints every character index touched by some dictionary word with a boolean `mark[]`, followed by a **merge pass** that walks the marks left-to-right and emits a tag at each boundary where coverage starts or stops. The greed lives in the merge: you never close a bold region while the next character is still covered, so you always produce the *minimum number* of `...` tags and equivalently the *maximal-length* runs. This is the key realization an interviewer probes — overlapping or adjacent dictionary matches must coalesce into one span rather than emitting nested or back-to-back tags.

Greedy fits Word/Dict here because the marking step decouples *which* words match from *how* to wrap them: once every covered index is known, the optimal wrapping is forced — there is no choice to backtrack on. A covered index is bold iff any word matches at some start position that spans it, an OR-accumulation that is order-independent, so a single left-to-right sweep with the invariant "open a tag at the first marked index after an unmarked one, close it at the first unmarked index after a marked one" is provably optimal.
tricks: Use a boolean `bold[]` (or `set`) of length `len(s)`; for each word, find every occurrence (sliding/`indexOf` loop) and set `bold[i..i+len(word)-1] = true`. OR-ing is what fuses overlapping matches automatically.
Find ALL occurrences of each word, not just the first — restart the search at `pos+1`, not `pos+len(word)`, so overlapping self-matches (e.g. `aaa` in `aaaa`) are all captured.
Emit `` exactly when `bold[i] && (i==0 || !bold[i-1])` and `` when `bold[i] && (i==len-1 || !bold[i+1])`; this single-pass boundary test guarantees adjacent bold regions never produce ``.
Pitfall: closing a tag per-word-match yields nested/redundant tags — the merge MUST be driven by the combined `bold[]` array, not by individual matches.
Aho-Corasick or a Trie speeds the marking pass to near-linear when the dictionary is large; the greedy merge phase is unchanged and still O(n).
This is identical to LeetCode 616 'Add Bold Tag in String' and generalizes to 'merge overlapping intervals' — the marks are just intervals collapsed onto a bitmap.
greedy.pseudo: bold = array(len(s), false) for word in dict: start = 0 while (i = s.indexOf(word, start)) != -1: for k in i .. i+len(word)-1: bold[k] = true start = i + 1 # allow overlapping matches result = "" for i in 0 .. len(s)-1: if bold[i] and (i==0 or not bold[i-1]): result += "" result += s[i] if bold[i] and (i==len(s)-1 or not bold[i+1]): result += "" return result

problems.title: Bold Words in String
problems.note: Paint a boolean `bold[]` over `s` by OR-ing in every occurrence of every dictionary word (searching all overlapping positions), then greedily sweep once to open `` at the start of each maximal covered run and close `` at its end, guaranteeing the fewest, longest tags.

bits.tldr: Encode each word's multiset of letters and each candidate word-subset as **bitmasks/counts**, then brute-force all `2^n` word subsets so set membership and letter-budget checks become cheap bit/array operations.
insight: Word/Dict problems with a small word list (`n <= ~15`) reduce to **subset enumeration**: which words do I pick? A **bitmask over the words** (`0..2^n-1`) enumerates every subset, and the bit `i` tells you whether `word[i]` is included. **Bit manipulation** is the natural index over the power set, turning 'try every combination' into a single integer loop with `mask & (1<<i)` membership tests.
