The structural condition is that each word is consumed *atomically* (you either use all its letters or none) and the only coupling between words is a shared letter budget. That lets you precompute each word's letter-count vector and incrementally test feasibility against the available `letters` multiset. The realization an interviewer probes: with `n` tiny, exponential subset enumeration over words is fine, and bitmasks make the bookkeeping O(1)-ish per word; the letter constraint is just a 26-bucket budget, not a per-character search.
tricks: Precompute `cnt[i][26]` for each word and `score(word)` once; never recount letters inside the `2^n` loop.
Use a single integer `mask` from `0` to `(1<<n)-1`; word `i` is in the subset iff `mask & (1 << i)` is nonzero.
Validate a subset by accumulating letter counts into a temp `need[26]` and comparing against the available `avail[26]`; bail early once any letter exceeds its budget.

**Pitfall**: letters are a *multiset* (counts), not a set — you cannot OR 26-bit presence masks, because two words may both need two `e`s. Use counts, or pack small per-letter counts into wider bit fields.

An equivalent cleaner formulation is **backtracking/DFS** that include-or-excludes each word and restores the letter budget on return — same `2^n` shape, often less constant overhead than scanning all masks.
Score only counts if the *entire* subset fits; a partially-affordable word contributes nothing, so check feasibility of the whole mask before adding its score.

problems.title: Maximum Score Words Formed by Letters
problems.note: Enumerate all `2^n` subsets of the word list via a bitmask (bit `i` = include `words[i]`); for each subset, sum the per-word letter-count vectors and verify none exceeds the available `letters` multiset, tracking the max total score. The bitmask is the index over the power set of words, while the 26-entry letter counts enforce the shared budget.

string.tldr: Anagram problems reduce to a **canonical fingerprint** of a string — a sorted key or a 26-slot count vector — so that "same letters, different order" becomes a simple equality or hash-key match.
insight: The unifying idea is that an anagram class is an **equivalence relation** over strings: two strings are equivalent iff they share an identical multiset of characters. To compute on that relation you need a **canonical form** — a representative that is identical for every member of the class and different across classes. Strings give you two natural canonicalizers: `sorted(s)` (`O(n log n)`, lexicographic representative) and a fixed-width **frequency vector** (`O(n)`, typically `int[26]` for lowercase ASCII). The whole family collapses to: build the canonical form, then test equality, group by it, or slide it across a window.

The structural condition that makes String the right dimension is that the alphabet is small and fixed, so a count array is `O(1)` space and comparison is `O(1)` per step — this is exactly what an interviewer probes: do you recognize that *order is irrelevant but multiplicity is not*, and do you pick the count-vector canonicalization (and reuse it incrementally in a sliding window) rather than re-sorting or recomparing from scratch?
tricks: Prefer a **`int[26]` count vector** over `sorted(s)`: it is `O(n)` vs `O(n log n)`, and the array itself doubles as the equality test (compare arrays) AND as a hashable group key.
For Unicode or unknown alphabets, fall back to `sorted(s)` as the canonical key or use a hashmap-based counter instead of a fixed `[26]` array.
Length mismatch is an instant **early-exit** for equality/anagram checks (`#242`): different lengths can never be anagrams.

When the canonical form must be a **map key** (`#49` grouping), serialize the count vector into a string (e.g. comma-joined counts or a `tuple`) since raw arrays don't hash by value in most languages.

For substring-anagram search (`#438`), do NOT rebuild the count for each window — maintain a **single sliding-window frequency array**, incrementing the entering char and decrementing the leaving char in `O(1)`.
Track a **`matches` counter of satisfied character buckets** (0..25) instead of comparing the full 26-array every step, turning each window check from `O(26)` into `O(1)` amortized.

problems.title: Group Anagrams
problems.note: Compute a canonical key for each word (sorted string or a serialized `int[26]` count vector) and bucket words into a hashmap keyed by that fingerprint; each bucket is one anagram group. Count-vector keys give `O(N*K)` over sorted keys' `O(N*K log K)`.

problems.title: Valid Anagram
problems.note: Reject immediately if lengths differ, then compare canonical forms: build one `int[26]` by incrementing for `s` and decrementing for `t`, and the strings are anagrams iff the array is all zeros (or equivalently `sorted(s) == sorted(t)`).

problems.title: Find All Anagrams in a String
problems.note: Slide a fixed window of length `len(p)` across `s`, maintaining one frequency array updated in `O(1)` per step (add entering char, remove leaving char); record each start index where the window's counts equal `p`'s counts, ideally via a `matches` bucket counter for `O(1)` checks.

array.tldr: Find Anagram Mappings is "anagram" in name only — the array is a permutation, and the real move is to invert it via a value→index hash map for O(1) lookups.
insight: The **Anagram** label here is structural, not lexical: an array `B` that is an *anagram* of array `A` is simply a **permutation** of the same multiset of values. There are no strings or character frequencies — the "anagram" condition guarantees every element of `A` appears somewhere in `B`, so a total mapping `A[i] -> some j with B[j] == A[i]` always exists. The dimension **Array** supplies both the input form (two parallel index-addressable arrays) and the output form (an index array `P` where `P[i]` is the source index of `A[i]` inside `B`).

The realization an interviewer probes is the **inversion**: instead of scanning `B` for each `A[i]` (O(n^2)), build a single hash map from `value -> index in B`, then map each `A[i]` in O(1). Because the problem guarantees values are *distinct*, the value→index relation is a clean function with no collision-handling needed; the array's positional identity is exactly what's being recovered.
tricks: Build the lookup **over `B`** (`val -> j`), then iterate `A` — not the reverse — so each answer slot `P[i]` is filled in one pass.
The guarantee of **distinct values** means one index per value; if duplicates were allowed you'd store a list/stack of indices and pop to avoid reusing a position.
**Anagram = permutation** is the only property you need: equal length and equal multisets ensure every `A[i]` has a home in `B`, so no missing-key checks are required.
Total cost is **O(n) time, O(n) space**; the naive `indexOf` per element is the O(n^2) pitfall the map eliminates.
The output is itself an **array of indices into `B`**, so `B[P[i]] == A[i]` is the post-condition invariant to assert.

problems.title: Find Anagram Mappings
problems.note: Treat `B` as a permutation of `A`; hash `value -> index` over `B`, then for each `A[i]` look up its index in `B` to fill the result array `P` in O(n). Distinct values make the inverse map a clean function, turning the naive O(n^2) per-element search into O(n).

hash.tldr: Anagrams are equal as multisets of letters, so a **canonical signature** (sorted string or 26-count vector) used as a **hash key** turns "is/group anagram" into O(1) dictionary lookups.
insight: The unifying realization is that anagrams form an **equivalence class**: two strings are anagrams iff their character multisets are identical. A hash table is the natural fit because it lets you collapse each equivalence class to a single **canonical key** — either the **sorted string** `sorted(s)` or, better, a **frequency fingerprint** (a length-26 count array, or a `Counter`). Strings sharing a key are anagrams; the map's buckets *are* the groups.

What an interviewer is probing is whether you see that comparison can be reduced to a **key derivation** rather than pairwise checks. The structural condition is that order is irrelevant and only letter counts matter, which is exactly the invariant a hash key should encode. The choice of canonical form trades time for clarity: sorting is `O(k log k)` per string but trivial to write; a count-vector key is `O(k)` and the classic optimization. Problem #760 widens the lens — here the hash table isn't grouping by content but **inverting** a value→index relationship, the same dictionary-as-lookup primitive.
tricks: **Canonical key choice**: `sorted(s)` is simplest; a `tuple` of 26 counts is faster (`O(k)` vs `O(k log k)`) and is the editorial-preferred key for #49.
For #242, **early-exit on length mismatch** (`len(s) != len(t)`) before counting; then increment for `s`, decrement for `t`, and assert every bucket is zero — equivalently `Counter(s) == Counter(t)`.
When building the count-vector key, use a **hashable** type: `tuple(counts)` or a fixed string like `'#'.join(...)`, since a raw list/array can't be a dict key.
For Unicode or arbitrary alphabets, **don't hardcode size 26** — use a `Counter`/`defaultdict(int)` so the key space adapts.

Pitfall: when mapping values to indices (#760), build the lookup over the **target** array and iterate the source; assumes a guaranteed match (and ties broken arbitrarily) so no collision handling is needed.
`defaultdict(list)` cleanly accumulates groups in #49 — append the original (unsorted) string under its canonical key.

problems.title: Group Anagrams
problems.note: Derive a canonical key per word — either `sorted(s)` or a length-26 `tuple` of letter counts — and append the original word into a `defaultdict(list)` keyed by that signature; the dict's value lists are the anagram groups.

problems.title: Valid Anagram
problems.note: Short-circuit if lengths differ, then compare frequency maps: build `Counter(s)` and `Counter(t)` (or increment for `s` / decrement for `t` in one 26-slot array and check all zeros). Equal multisets mean valid anagram.

problems.title: Find Anagram Mappings
problems.note: Not a multiset problem but the same hash-table-as-lookup move: build a `value -> index` dict over `B`, then map each element of `A` to its position via `O(1)` lookups, yielding the index mapping in `O(n)`.

sliding-window.tldr: Slide a fixed-width window equal to the pattern length and flag every position where the window's character multiset equals the pattern's.
insight: An **anagram** is defined purely by its **character frequency multiset**, ignoring order. So "does substring `s[i..i+len(p))` anagram `p`?" reduces to "do their frequency counts match?" Because every candidate substring has the **exact same length** as `p`, the natural tool is a **fixed-size sliding window**: as the window advances one step, exactly one character enters on the right and one leaves on the left, so the frequency table can be updated in `O(1)` rather than recomputed in `O(len(p))`. This collapses a naive `O(n·m)` scan into `O(n)`.

The realization an interviewer probes is twofold: (1) anagram-equality is a **stateless function of counts**, so you never sort or compare strings; and (2) since the window width is constant, you don't need two moving pointers chasing a condition — you need an **incremental count + a match check**. The elegant version avoids comparing two arrays every step by maintaining a single `matches` counter that tracks how many of the 26 letters currently have the correct count, updating it in constant time per character event.
tricks: Window width is **fixed** at `len(p)` — this is *not* the expand/shrink variable-window template; add the entering char and remove the char `len(p)` positions back every step.

Avoid recomparing the whole count array each step. Keep a `need` map and a single `matchCount` of satisfied letters; when an update makes a letter's count hit exactly its target, `matchCount++`, when it moves off the target, `matchCount--`. Record a hit when `matchCount == 26` (or `== distinct letters in p`).
Use a **fixed `int[26]` array** keyed by `c - 'a'` rather than a hash map for speed and to make the equality/comparison `O(26)` constant.
Off-by-one on window start: only begin removing the left char once the window has reached full size, i.e. when `i >= len(p)`; the first valid check happens at index `i == len(p) - 1`.
Record the **start index** `i - len(p) + 1` when a match is found, not the current right pointer.
Edge cases: `len(s) < len(p)` yields no answers; an empty `p` is degenerate — guard before entering the loop.
sliding-window.pseudo:
if len(s) < len(p): return []
need = freq(p); window = empty count[26]; res = []
for i in 0..len(s)-1:
    window[s[i]] += 1                      # char enters on right
    if i >= len(p):                        # window too big
        window[s[i - len(p)]] -= 1         # char leaves on left
    if i >= len(p) - 1:                    # window now exactly len(p)
        if window == need:                 # multisets equal -> anagram
            res.append(i - len(p) + 1)     # record START index
return res

problems.title: Find All Anagrams in a String
problems.note: Slide a window of width `len(p)` across `s`, maintaining a 26-letter frequency count that is incrementally updated (add right char, drop left char) each step; whenever the window's counts equal `p`'s counts, append the window's start index `i - len(p) + 1`. The fixed window plus incremental counts gives an `O(len(s))` solution.

string.tldr: Subsequence problems on strings are matching/counting questions answered by two-pointer scans for existence and DP grids over `(i,j)` index pairs for counting and longest/common variants.
insight: The unifying object is **order-preserving, non-contiguous matching**: a subsequence keeps relative order but allows gaps, which is exactly what string indices encode. Every problem here reduces to advancing one or two pointers/indices through strings `s` and `t` and asking either *does it fit* (greedy two-pointer), *how many ways* (counting DP), or *how long/where* (length/window DP). String is the natural carrier because its 1-D index space makes the subsequence relation a clean `i<j` ordering, and equality of characters `s[i]==t[j]` is the only transition condition.

The structural condition an interviewer probes is recognizing when **greedy** suffices versus when you need **DP**. Pure existence (`Is Subsequence`) is greedy/two-pointer in `O(n)`; but the moment you must *count* matches or optimize over *all* alignments, overlapping subproblems force a `dp[i][j]` table indexed by prefixes of the two strings. The second realization is **preprocessing for batch queries**: when many patterns are tested against one fixed text, you flip from per-query scanning to indexing the text (next-position tables or bucketing patterns by their next-needed char).
tricks: **Two-pointer existence**: walk `i` over the pattern, `j` over the text; advance `i` only on match, always advance `j`; subsequence exists iff `i` reaches `len(pattern)`. This is the `O(n)` skeleton behind #392.

**Prefix-DP grid for counting/LCS**: `dp[i][j]` over prefixes `s[:i]`, `t[:j]`. On `s[i-1]==t[j-1]` you *take* the diagonal; otherwise you carry from neighbors. Distinct-Subsequences *adds* (count paths), LCS takes `max` — same grid, different combinator.

**Batch matching beats re-scanning**: for one text vs. K patterns, don't run K independent scans. Bucket patterns by their *next required character* (waiting lists, #792) or build a `next[i][c]` table so each pattern advance is `O(1)`.

**Minimum-window subsequence is two-phase**: scan forward to find an end that completes `t` as a subsequence, then scan *backward* from that end to tighten the start to the smallest window — greedy two-pointer, not sliding window, because order matters with gaps.

**Pitfall — contiguity confusion**: subsequence ≠ substring; never use Rabin-Karp/KMP/sliding-window-of-fixed-content reasoning here. Gaps are allowed, so transitions skip non-matching text chars freely.

**Disjoint/independent subsequences via bitmask** (#2002): enumerate character subsets, check each is a valid palindromic subsequence, and combine only *disjoint* index sets — bitmask over the small alphabet replaces a string DP.

problems.title: Distinct Subsequences
problems.note: Count how many subsequences of `s` equal `t` via `dp[i][j]` over prefixes: on `s[i-1]==t[j-1]` sum the take (`dp[i-1][j-1]`) and skip (`dp[i-1][j]`) branches, else carry the skip. The grid counts distinct index alignments of `t` inside `s`.

problems.title: Is Subsequence
problems.note: Canonical greedy two-pointer: advance the `t`-pointer through `s`, incrementing only on character match; `t` is a subsequence iff the pointer consumes all of `t`. For many `t` against one `s`, precompute `next[i][c]` to answer each in `O(|t| log)`.

problems.title: Minimum Window Subsequence
problems.note: Find the shortest substring of `s` that contains `t` as a subsequence. Forward-scan to match all of `t` (record the end), then backward-scan from that end to shrink the start to the minimal window; repeat across the string keeping the smallest.

problems.title: Number of Matching Subsequences
problems.note: One text `s` versus many words: bucket each word by its next-needed character, then sweep `s` once — each character `c` releases the waiting bucket, advancing those words to their next char (or counting them done). Avoids K independent two-pointer scans.

problems.title: Longest Common Subsequence
problems.note: Classic prefix DP `dp[i][j]`: on `a[i-1]==b[j-1]` take `dp[i-1][j-1]+1`, else `max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])`. Same grid shape as Distinct Subsequences but with `max` (optimize length) instead of `+` (count paths).

problems.title: Maximum Product of the Length of Two Palindromic Subsequences
problems.note: With a short string, bitmask-enumerate subsets of indices, keep those forming a palindromic subsequence, and maximize the length product over pairs of subsets whose index masks are *disjoint*. The string drives a subset-DP rather than a two-string grid.

array.tldr: Subsequence-on-Array problems trade exponential 2^n enumeration for a 1D DP table indexed by array position, where each `dp[i]` summarizes the best subsequence *ending at* element `i` and earlier indices feed it.
insight: The unifying move is to **anchor the subsequence by its ending index** in the array and let `dp[i]` mean "answer for the best valid subsequence terminating at `a[i]`." Because a subsequence preserves order but drops elements, the array index becomes both the time axis and the only legal direction of dependency: `dp[i]` may only consult `dp[j]` for `j < i`. This converts the combinatorial "pick any subset in order" into a clean prefix recurrence, and the array's random access lets you scan all earlier candidates (the `O(n^2)` family) or maintain a compact structure over already-seen values (the `O(n log n)` family).

Why Array fits so naturally: the data already arrives in the order subsequences must respect, so no sorting or reindexing is needed — position *is* the constraint. The interviewer is probing whether you recognize that **"ending here" is the right state**, that transitions only look backward, and that the value-relationship (increasing, +d, sign-flip) is checked as a *guard on the transition*, not baked into the state. Master that and the same skeleton retiles across LIS, counting, wiggle, and arithmetic variants; the only differences are the transition predicate and what you store (length, count, two-state, or a hash map keyed by value).
tricks: **State = subsequence ending at `i`.** Always include the current element; `dp[i]` is built from `max/sum over j<i with predicate(a[j],a[i])`, then the global answer is `max over all i` (not just `dp[n-1]`).

**`O(n log n)` LIS trick:** maintain a `tails` array where `tails[k]` = smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length `k+1`; binary-search the insertion point (`lower_bound` for strict-increasing, `upper_bound` for non-decreasing). The array's length is the answer, but its contents are NOT a real subsequence.
**Hash-map indexing for arithmetic/diff constraints:** when the predicate is `a[i]-a[j]==d` (#1218), drop the inner loop — use `dp[value] = dp[value-d] + 1`, turning `O(n^2)` into `O(n)`.
**Two-state DP for sign-alternating wiggle:** track `up[i]` and `down[i]` (or two running scalars) so the transition guard depends on the *direction* of the last step, not just magnitude.

**Counting requires a tie-break rule:** for #673 carry `cnt[i]`; when extending, if a longer chain is found reset `cnt`, if an equal-length chain is found *add* to it — order of these two checks is the classic bug.
**Pitfall — distinct subsequences need dedup:** in #491 you enumerate (not optimize), so use a per-level visited set or skip duplicate values to avoid emitting the same subsequence twice.

problems.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
problems.note: The archetype: `dp[i]` = longest increasing subsequence ending at `a[i]`, transition `dp[i]=max(dp[j]+1)` over `j<i` with `a[j]<a[i]` for `O(n^2)`, or the `tails` patience-sorting array with binary search for `O(n log n)`.

problems.title: Increasing Triplet Subsequence
problems.note: Degenerate LIS of length 3: scan the array keeping two running mins `first` and `second`; if an element exceeds both, a triplet exists — an `O(n)`, `O(1)` collapse of the tails idea.

problems.title: Wiggle Subsequence
problems.note: Two-state DP over the array: `up[i]` and `down[i]` track the longest alternating subsequence ending with a rising vs falling step, each extending the opposite state; collapses to two scalars in one pass.

problems.title: Non-decreasing Subsequences
problems.note: Enumeration rather than optimization — backtrack over array indices building non-decreasing picks, using a per-recursion-level visited set on values to dedup, since the array may contain repeats.

problems.title: Number of Longest Increasing Subsequence
problems.note: Augment LIS with a parallel count array: `dp[i]` length plus `cnt[i]`; when `dp[j]+1>dp[i]` reset `cnt[i]=cnt[j]`, when equal add `cnt[i]+=cnt[j]`, then sum counts of all maximum-length endings.

problems.title: Longest Arithmetic Subsequence of Given Difference
problems.note: Fixed difference `d` makes the predecessor unique, so replace the inner loop with a hash map `dp[a[i]] = dp[a[i]-d] + 1` keyed by value — an `O(n)` index-by-value variant of the ending-at-i DP.

problems.title: Maximum Subsequence Score
problems.note: Pair each index's two arrays, sort by the multiplier (`nums2`) descending so it becomes the running minimum, then sweep maintaining a min-heap of the top-`k` `nums1` values; `score = (sum of heap) * current_multiplier`, a greedy over an ordered array rather than a length DP.

problems.title: Check if each recipe is a contiguous subsequence
problems.note: A contiguity check, not an optimization: walk the array with a two-pointer/index match, advancing through the pattern only when consecutive array positions align, confirming the recipe appears as an unbroken run.

dp.tldr: Subsequence problems are DP's home turf: a subsequence is built by a sequence of independent keep/skip decisions over indices, so you tabulate over prefixes (and pairs of prefixes) and let optimal substructure assemble the answer.
insight: A subsequence is exactly a sequence of **keep-or-skip** decisions scanned left-to-right, which gives the **optimal substructure** DP requires: the best answer ending at (or using a prefix up to) index `i` depends only on answers at earlier indices. That is why the canonical states are **`dp[i]` = best subsequence ending at `i`** (single sequence, as in LIS) or **`dp[i][j]` = relation between prefixes `A[..i]` and `B[..j]`** (two sequences, as in LCS / edit-style). The transition is always "extend a smaller valid subsequence by one element if a local condition holds."

The interviewer is probing whether you recognize the **state dimension**: one axis per sequence whose prefix matters, plus extra axes for any carried constraint (last-direction in Wiggle, a count alongside the length in #673). Because keep/skip is binary and order-preserving (not contiguous, unlike substrings), transitions reach back to *all* smaller indices (`O(n^2)` LIS) or to a single diagonal/up/left neighbor (`O(nm)` LCS). The key realization: **'ending at i' states compose**, whereas 'within i' states for substrings do not — that distinction picks the right recurrence.
tricks: Pick state by sequence count: **one sequence → `dp[i]` ending at `i`** (LIS, Wiggle); **two sequences → `dp[i][j]` over prefix pairs** (LCS, Distinct Subsequences, Min Window Subsequence).

**'Ending at i' vs 'over prefix [0..i]'** are different invariants: LIS uses ending-at (answer is `max` over all `i`), while count/match DPs use prefix-inclusive (answer is `dp[n][m]`). Don't mix them.
Counting variants (#115, #673) **add not max**: combine sub-results by summation, and for #673 carry a parallel `count[]` array updated when a new max ties or beats the old.
For two-string match DP, the diagonal `dp[i-1][j-1]` advance happens **only when chars match**; the `dp[i-1][j]`/`dp[i][j-1]` fallbacks encode "skip a character of A or B."
Watch base cases: empty target is achievable in exactly **one** way (#115 `dp[i][0]=1`), and direction/parity DPs (#376) need both an `up` and a `down` state seeded to 1.
LIS-family can drop to **`O(n log n)`** via patience sorting (`tails[]` + binary search) when you only need the length, not the per-index table.

problems.title: Distinct Subsequences
problems.note: Count how many ways `t` appears as a subsequence of `s` with `dp[i][j]` = ways to form `t[0..j)` from `s[0..i)`; when `s[i-1]==t[j-1]` you may either use it (`dp[i-1][j-1]`) or skip it (`dp[i-1][j]`), so transitions **add**, with base case `dp[i][0]=1` (empty target).

problems.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
problems.note: Canonical single-sequence DP: `dp[i]` = longest increasing subsequence ending at `i`, extended from any earlier `j` with `nums[j] < nums[i]`; `O(n^2)`, or `O(n log n)` by maintaining a `tails[]` array of smallest tails via binary search.

problems.title: Wiggle Subsequence
problems.note: Carry the **last move direction** as an extra state: track `up[i]` (ends rising) and `down[i]` (ends falling); on `nums[i] > nums[i-1]` update `up = down+1`, on `<` update `down = up+1`, a two-state LIS variant solvable in `O(n)`.

problems.title: Non-decreasing Subsequences
problems.note: An enumeration-not-optimization variant: DP/recursion over the index builds all non-decreasing subsequences of length >= 2, with a per-level **used-value set** to dedupe choices when the same value could be kept or skipped at the same position.

problems.title: Number of Longest Increasing Subsequence
problems.note: Augment LIS with a parallel `count[i]`: while computing `dp[i]` from each valid `j`, if `dp[j]+1 > dp[i]` reset `count[i]=count[j]`, if it ties add `count[j]`; the answer sums `count[i]` over all `i` achieving the global max length.

problems.title: Minimum Window Subsequence
problems.note: Two-sequence prefix DP where `dp[i][j]` stores the **start index** in `S` of the shortest window of `S[0..i)` containing `T[0..j)` as a subsequence; on match inherit from `dp[i-1][j-1]`, else from `dp[i-1][j]`, then scan row `j=|T|` for the minimum-length window.

problems.title: Longest Common Subsequence
problems.note: The archetypal two-sequence DP: `dp[i][j]` = LCS length of prefixes `A[0..i)` and `B[0..j)`; on `A[i-1]==B[j-1]` take `dp[i-1][j-1]+1`, otherwise `max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])` to skip one character from either string.

greedy.tldr: For subsequence-existence problems you greedily keep the *smallest possible* tail value at each chain length, so a longer chain becomes feasible as early and as cheaply as possible.
insight: A subsequence problem asks whether a relatively-ordered selection (here, an increasing chain) exists, and the **greedy exchange argument** is what licenses a single linear scan: among all ways to realize a length-`k` increasing prefix, keeping the **minimal achievable tail** dominates every alternative. A smaller tail can be extended by anything a larger tail can, and possibly more, so there is never a reason to retain the larger one. This is the same monotone-tail intuition that underlies patience sorting / LIS-in-`O(n log n)`, collapsed to the tiny case of length 3.

The realization an interviewer probes is that you do **not** need to track positions or do `O(n^2)` DP to detect a length-3 increasing subsequence: maintain two thresholds `first < second`, each lowered greedily as smaller candidates appear. The subtle correctness point is that `second` may end up holding a value whose actual predecessor occurs *later* in the array than that predecessor's recorded slot — yet the answer is still valid, because the existence of any value greater than `second` proves some earlier `first < second` pair really existed in order.
tricks: Maintain two running minima `first = +inf`, `second = +inf`; on each `x`: if `x <= first` set `first = x`, else if `x <= second` set `second = x`, else **return true** (you found a third strictly larger than a valid pair).
Use `<=` (not `<`) when updating, so duplicates don't fake a strict increase — `[2,2,2]` must return false.
The `else if x <= second` branch greedily *lowers* `second` rather than rejecting `x`; this is the exchange step that keeps future feasibility maximal.

Don't be alarmed that `second` can be set even when its current `first` came *after* it temporally — a stale-looking `first` from earlier history guarantees correctness, so no positional bookkeeping is needed.
Generalizes to a 'longest increasing subsequence of length k' by holding an array of `k-1` tails kept sorted/minimal; triplet is just `k = 3` with two scalars.
Pitfall: returning early on `>= second` instead of `> second`, or initializing thresholds to the first element instead of `+inf`, both corrupt the duplicate/edge handling.

problems.title: Increasing Triplet Subsequence
problems.note: Greedily track the smallest length-1 tail (`first`) and smallest length-2 tail (`second`) in one pass; the first element strictly exceeding `second` certifies a strictly increasing triple, giving `O(n)` time and `O(1)` space. Using `<=` on the update branches keeps the minimal tails and correctly rejects non-strict cases like all-equal arrays.

two-pointers.tldr: Subsequence checking reduces to a one-directional scan: advance a pointer over the source `t` for every character of the target `s`, matching greedily — never backtracking.
insight: The interesting tension appears when you must match **many** targets against **one** source (#792). The naive answer is to rerun the two-pointer scan per target, costing `O(numTargets * |t|)`. The professor-level realization is to invert control: scan `t` once and let each in-progress subsequence advance its own pointer via a bucketing/waiting-list structure keyed on the next-needed character. Two Pointers is still the per-target engine; you just multiplex many pointers over a single pass of `t`. The third problem twists the definition to *contiguous*, turning the loose forward scan into a tight merge-walk where a mismatch resets the run.
tricks: Match direction matters: pointer `i` over the (usually shorter) target `s` is the loop guard; you succeed iff `i` reaches `len(s)`, and the source pointer `j` is the one you may run off the end.
Greedy-first-match is provably optimal for *plain* subsequence — never store or branch on alternative match positions; a forward-only scan suffices.

For #792, do NOT loop per word: bucket words by their **next required character**. On reading `t[j]=c`, drain bucket `c`, advance each word's pointer, and re-bucket on its new next char (or count it done).
Preprocessing alternative for repeated `392` queries: build `pos[char] -> sorted indices` in `t`, then binary-search the next index `> j`; this beats re-scanning when `s` streams in.

Pitfall: 'subsequence' (order-preserving, gaps allowed) vs 'substring/contiguous' (no gaps). #10021 is contiguous, so on mismatch you cannot just keep `j` advancing — the matched run breaks and must restart.
Edge cases: empty `s` is always a subsequence; equal characters and full consumption of `t` before `s` finishes means failure.

problems.title: Is Subsequence
problems.note: The canonical case: two pointers `i` over `s` and `j` over `t`, advancing `j` every step and `i` only on a match; return `i == len(s)`. The follow-up (many `s` against one `t`) motivates precomputing `char -> indices` in `t` and binary-searching the next position.

problems.title: Number of Matching Subsequences
problems.note: Run the two-pointer match for many words simultaneously by streaming `t` once and keeping each word's pointer in a bucket keyed on its next-needed character; when `t[j]` arrives, advance every word waiting on it and re-bucket, counting words whose pointer reaches the end.

problems.title: Check if each recipe is a contiguous subsequence
problems.note: A `tp-merge-walk` variant where the recipe must appear as a *contiguous* run inside the master sequence, so two pointers walk in lockstep but a mismatch breaks/restarts the current run rather than merely skipping — closer to substring matching than gap-tolerant subsequence.

backtrack.tldr: Backtracking enumerates subsequences by a take/skip decision per index, with a same-level dedup rule to emit each distinct (non-decreasing) subsequence exactly once.
insight: A **subsequence** is defined by *choosing or not choosing* each element while preserving order, so the natural search tree is binary at every index — this is exactly what **backtracking** models. You walk the array left-to-right; at each position you either append `nums[i]` to the current path or skip it, recurse, then undo. Order is automatically preserved because you never revisit earlier indices, which is what distinguishes subsequence backtracking from permutation/subset-with-reorder problems.

The narrowed intersection here is **constrained subsequence enumeration with duplicate suppression**. The key realization an interviewer probes: you cannot sort (sorting destroys the original order that defines a subsequence), so the usual `i > start && nums[i] == nums[i-1]` skip trick is illegal. Instead you dedup *per recursion level* using a `seen` set scoped to the current call — ensuring that among all branches starting at the same `start`, each distinct value is used as the next element only once. The non-decreasing constraint is enforced by only appending `nums[i]` when `nums[i] >= path.last`.
tricks: **Never sort** — the input order *is* the subsequence semantics; sorting would change which subsequences exist. Dedup must work on the unsorted array.
Use a **per-level `seen` set** (local to each recursive frame) to skip a value already chosen as the next element at this `start`; this kills duplicate subsequences without sorting.
Enforce the monotonic rule inline: only recurse with `nums[i]` if `path` is empty or `nums[i] >= path.back()` — combine this guard with the `seen` check in the same loop.
**Emit on length ≥ 2**, not at the leaves only: record `path` whenever its size reaches 2, since valid answers are interior nodes of the tree, not just full-length paths.

Loop form `for i in [start..n)` with `seen` beats the explicit take/skip recursion here because dedup is cleaner — the skip is implicit (values not chosen) and `seen` blocks re-choosing an equal value at the same depth.
Pitfall: putting `seen` outside the loop/at the wrong scope — a global or parent-shared set wrongly suppresses legitimate subsequences that reuse a value at a *deeper* level.
backtrack.pseudo:
function backtrack(nums, start, path, result):
    if len(path) >= 2:
        result.add(copy(path))
    seen = empty_set            # per-level dedup, NO sorting
    for i in range(start, len(nums)):
        if nums[i] in seen:           # already tried this value at this depth
            continue
        if path is empty or nums[i] >= path.last:   # non-decreasing guard
            seen.add(nums[i])
            path.push(nums[i])
            backtrack(nums, i + 1, path, result)
            path.pop()            # undo choice
    return

backtrack(nums, 0, [], result)

problems.title: Non-decreasing Subsequences
problems.note: DFS over indices with a take/skip choice per element; append `nums[i]` only when it is `>=` the last chosen value to keep the path non-decreasing, and record any path of length `>= 2`. Because the array cannot be sorted, use a `seen` set local to each recursive call to ensure each distinct value is selected at most once per level, eliminating duplicate subsequences.

hash.tldr: A hash map keyed by the subsequence's last value turns longest-arithmetic-subsequence into one O(n) DP pass, since a fixed difference makes each element's predecessor uniquely determined.
insight: The defining structural condition is that the **arithmetic difference `d` is fixed and given**. For any element `x`, the only value that can precede it in a valid subsequence is `x - d` — a single, deterministic predecessor. This collapses the usual O(n^2) subsequence DP (which scans all earlier indices) into an O(1) lookup, and a **hash table keyed by value** is the natural store: `dp[x] = dp[x - d] + 1`.

The realization an interviewer is probing is that you don't need indices at all — order matters only in that you must process left to right, but the *transition* depends purely on value identity, not position. The hash table doubles as both the DP table and the membership test for the predecessor, so a later occurrence of `x` simply overwrites the earlier `dp[x]`, which is correct because a later index can extend any chain an earlier one could plus chains formed in between.
tricks: Key the map by **value**, not index: `dp[x]` = length of the longest valid subsequence ending at value `x`. The fixed `d` is what makes value-keying sound.
The transition is `dp[x] = dp.get(x - d, 0) + 1`. A missing predecessor defaults to `0`, so `x` starts a fresh subsequence of length `1`.
Process strictly **left to right** and **overwrite** `dp[x]` on each occurrence — you never want a future predecessor lookup to use a stale shorter chain; the latest write dominates.
Track the running max during the pass rather than scanning the map at the end; the answer is at least `1`.
Pitfall: `d` can be negative or zero. The formula still holds — for `d == 0` the chain counts repeats of the same value, which is intended.
Do NOT pre-build the map then iterate; building and reading in the same forward pass is what guarantees the predecessor's value reflects only earlier indices.
hash.pseudo:
function longestSubseq(arr, d):
    dp = empty hash map        # value -> best length ending at that value
    best = 0
    for x in arr:              # left to right preserves index order
        prev = dp.get(x - d, 0)   # unique predecessor value
        dp[x] = prev + 1          # extend chain, overwrite any older entry
        best = max(best, dp[x])
    return best

problems.title: Longest Arithmetic Subsequence of Given Difference
problems.note: Because the common difference `d` is given, each value `x`'s only possible predecessor is `x - d`, so a single forward pass with `dp[x] = dp.get(x - d, 0) + 1` over a value-keyed hash map yields O(n) time and space. The answer is the maximum `dp[x]` seen, replacing the naive O(n^2) index-scanning subsequence DP.

bits.tldr: When the alphabet is tiny (lowercase letters), encode each subsequence's character set as a 26-bit mask so two subsequences are checkable for disjointness in O(1) via `mask1 & mask2 == 0`.
insight: The bridge between **subsequences** and **bit manipulation** is that a string over a small alphabet has only 26 possible characters, so any subset of characters fits in a single `int` as a **26-bit bitmask**. A palindromic subsequence depends only on *which* indices it uses; if we enumerate subsets of indices via a bitmask over positions, each subset both (a) selects a candidate subsequence and (b) can be tested for the palindrome property by walking the chosen indices.

The key realization an interviewer probes is the **two-dimensional bitmask trick**: index masks let you brute-force all 2^n subsequences when `n` is small (n ≤ 12 here), while a character/position mask lets you enforce **disjointness** between two chosen subsequences in O(1). Because the two palindromic subsequences must use *disjoint indices*, you only need to check that their two index masks share no set bit (`m1 & m2 == 0`), turning an otherwise quadratic-partition problem into a clean ANDed pair-scan over precomputed palindrome masks.
tricks: Enumerate all `1<<n` subsets of **indices** (not characters) since the partition into two groups is over positions; the disjointness constraint is exactly `m1 & m2 == 0`.
Precompute, for every mask, whether the subsequence it selects is a palindrome and its popcount (`__builtin_popcount`), so the final pairing loop is pure bit-AND filtering.
Use a complement/submask enumeration trick: for a fixed palindromic `m1`, only consider `m2` drawn from the complement `((1<<n)-1) ^ m1` to guarantee disjointness automatically.
Palindrome check on a mask: extract set-bit positions left-to-right, then two-pointer compare those selected characters — n ≤ 12 keeps this cheap.
Answer is `max(popcount(m1) * popcount(m2))` over all disjoint palindromic mask pairs; initialize to 0 since a single-char subsequence is a valid palindrome.
Pitfall: don't confuse character masks (for set-equality / distinctness) with position masks (needed here for disjoint partitioning) — this problem requires position masks.

problems.title: Maximum Product of the Length of Two Palindromic Subsequences
problems.note: With n ≤ 12, enumerate all 2^n index bitmasks, keep those whose selected characters form a palindrome along with their popcount, then maximize the length product over every pair of masks satisfying `m1 & m2 == 0` (disjoint positions). Bit manipulation makes both the subsequence enumeration and the disjointness test O(1) per pair.

heap.tldr: Sort by the gated factor, sweep candidates, and keep a min-heap of the top-`k` summable values so every prefix yields the best subsequence score for its current minimum.
insight: A **subsequence** problem asks you to pick `k` elements respecting some constraint; here each chosen index contributes both an additive term (`nums1[i]`) and a multiplicative gate (`nums2[i]`), and the score is `(sum of nums1 over the k picks) * (min of nums2 over the k picks)`. The structural trick is that the score is governed by **two coupled axes**: a quantity you want to maximize by *summing* and a quantity you want to maximize by taking a *minimum*. You cannot greedily optimize both at once, so you fix one axis to make the other tractable.

The realization the interviewer probes: **sort the pairs by `nums2` descending**, then iterate. When you process element `i`, every element seen so far has `nums2 >= nums2[i]`, so if `i` is the *weakest* (the gating minimum) of your chosen set, all other picks must come from the prefix before/at `i`. Thus the answer for `nums2[i]` as the minimum is `nums2[i] * (largest sum of k-1 nums1 values among elements with nums2 >= nums2[i], plus nums1[i])`. A **min-heap of size `k`** maintains exactly that running 'top-k largest `nums1`' set in `O(log k)` per step — Heap fits because we need a fast, sliding 'keep the k biggest, evict the smallest' under a moving boundary.
tricks: **Sort descending by the `min`-axis** (`nums2`): this turns the global `min` over a subset into 'the current element is the min', so a simple prefix scan covers all candidate minimums.
Use a **min-heap keyed on `nums1`** holding at most `k` elements; maintain a running `sum` of what's in the heap so the score is `sum * nums2[i]` in `O(1)` — never recompute the sum.
Only evaluate the score **once the heap reaches size `k`** (you need exactly `k` picks). Evict the smallest `nums1` (`sum -= heap.pop()`) before/after pushing to keep size `k`.

**Push the current element first, then check/pop** if size exceeds `k`, and update the answer when `size == k` — order matters so element `i` (the current min) is always included in its own evaluation.
Pitfall: don't sort by `nums1` or by the product — sorting must be on the gating `min` factor `nums2`, otherwise the 'current element is the minimum' invariant breaks.
Use a **64-bit accumulator**; `sum` of up to 10^5 values times a large `nums2` overflows 32-bit.
heap.pseudo:
pairs = sort(zip(nums1, nums2)) by nums2 descending
minHeap = []        // keeps k largest nums1 values
sum = 0
ans = 0
for (n1, n2) in pairs:
    heap.push(n1); sum += n1
    if heap.size > k:
        sum -= heap.popMin()      // drop smallest nums1
    if heap.size == k:
        ans = max(ans, sum * n2)  // n2 is the running minimum
return ans

problems.title: Maximum Subsequence Score
problems.note: Pair `(nums1[i], nums2[i])`, sort descending by `nums2`, and sweep while keeping a size-`k` min-heap of the largest `nums1` values with a running `sum`; at each step the current `nums2` is the subsequence's minimum, so the best score for that minimum is `sum * nums2[i]`. Take the max over all steps where the heap holds exactly `k` elements.

array.tldr: The stock series is a 1-D price array scanned once while you carry forward the best cash/holding states — a DP over the array index where transactions are encoded as state transitions, not nested loops.
insight: Every problem here is a `prices[]` array indexed by **time**, and the only operations are buy (pay `prices[i]`) and sell (gain `prices[i]`). The unifying idea is that you walk the array **left-to-right exactly once** maintaining a small set of running states — typically the best achievable cash while *holding* a share vs. *not holding* one — and update them with the rule `new = max(keep, transition)`. The array's left-to-right order *is* the causality constraint: you cannot sell before you buy, so the `hold` state can only ever pull from earlier indices, which is precisely what a forward scan guarantees for free.

The interviewer is probing whether you see that 'maximize profit over an array' is not a search over O(2^n) buy/sell subsets but an O(n) (or O(n*k)) **state machine**. The structural condition is that gain depends only on the *difference* `prices[j]-prices[i]` with `i<j`, so any optimal multi-transaction plan decomposes into independent rises — and a constraint like a transaction cap `k`, a cooldown, or a fee just adds one more dimension or one more state to the same array sweep. Recognizing 'track the minimum-so-far' (#121) and 'sum every positive delta' (#122) as the degenerate `k=1` and `k=infinity` ends of the same DP is the key realization.
tricks: **Two-state core:** keep `cash` (max money, no share) and `hold` (max money, holding a share, starts at `-infinity` or `-prices[0]`); each step `cash = max(cash, hold + prices[i])`, `hold = max(hold, cash - prices[i])`. All six problems are variations on these two lines.

**Degenerate ends:** #121 = single transaction = track running `min` price and best `price - min`; #122 = unlimited = `sum of max(0, prices[i] - prices[i-1])` (grab every uphill segment). No DP table needed for these two.

**Cap k via 2k states:** for at-most-`k` transactions keep arrays `buy[1..k]`, `sell[1..k]`; iterate `buy[j]=max(buy[j], sell[j-1]-p)`, `sell[j]=max(sell[j], buy[j]+p)`. Pitfall: when `k >= n/2` the cap is non-binding, so fall back to the unlimited #122 formula to avoid O(n*k) blowup/overflow.
**Cooldown adds a third state** (#309): after a sell you must skip one index, so `hold` must transition from `cash` *as of two steps ago* (`prev_cash`), not the current `cash`.
**Fee folds into one transition** (#714): subtract the fee once per round trip — either `cash = max(cash, hold + p - fee)` on sell or `hold = max(hold, cash - p - fee)` on buy, never both.

**Initialization & overflow:** seed `hold = -prices[0]` (or `-infinity`), `cash = 0`; with negative `-infinity` sentinels guard against `+prices[i]` overflow, and process exactly one share at a time (no fractional/multiple holdings).

problems.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
problems.note: Single transaction: scan the array tracking the minimum price seen so far and the best `prices[i] - minSoFar`. The degenerate `k=1` case — two-state DP collapses to one min-tracking pass.

problems.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II
problems.note: Unlimited transactions: sum every positive consecutive delta `max(0, prices[i] - prices[i-1])`, capturing each uphill run of the array. The `k=infinity` end of the spectrum, greedy over adjacent pairs.

problems.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock III
problems.note: At most two transactions: run the 2k-state DP with `k=2`, maintaining `buy1, sell1, buy2, sell2` updated in one array sweep. `sell2` is the answer.

problems.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock IV
problems.note: At most `k` transactions: the general 2k-state DP over the array, `buy[j]/sell[j]` for `j=1..k`. Short-circuit to the #122 formula when `k >= n/2` to keep it O(n*k) and avoid waste.

problems.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown
problems.note: Unlimited transactions but one rest day after each sell: add a cooldown state so reopening `hold` pulls from `cash` two indices back (`prev_cash`), enforcing the one-step gap during the single array pass.

problems.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Transaction Fee
problems.note: Unlimited transactions with a per-trade fee: same two-state sweep but subtract `fee` exactly once per round trip (on the sell transition `cash = max(cash, hold + prices[i] - fee)`).

dp.tldr: Track the maximum profit as a small **state machine over (day, transactions-used, holding-or-not)** and let each day's decision—buy, sell, or rest—be a `max` recurrence over the previous day's states.
insight: Every stock problem is the SAME DP: at each day you are in one of two **holding states**—`hold` (own a share) or `cash` (own nothing)—and the only moves are stay, buy (`cash→hold`), or sell (`hold→cash`). The recurrence is `hold[i] = max(hold[i-1], cash[i-1] - price[i])` and `cash[i] = max(cash[i-1], hold[i-1] + price[i])`. This works because the problem has **optimal substructure** (best profit by day `i` depends only on best profit by `i-1`) and **no aftereffect** (future decisions depend on the past only through your current holding state, not the path taken). The answer is always `cash[n-1]`, since ending while holding a share is never optimal.

The interviewer is probing whether you see that all six variants are ONE template with extra state dimensions bolted on: a **transaction-count axis** `k` (for #123/#188), a **cooldown lag** (#309, which forces buying from `cash[i-2]`), and a **fee** subtracted at sell or buy (#714). Recognizing that the unbounded case (#122) is just the greedy collapse of this DP, and that `k ≥ n/2` makes any `k`-limited problem degenerate into the unbounded one, separates a memorized solution from genuine understanding.
tricks: Carry only **two rolling scalars** `hold` and `cash` (or arrays `hold[k]`, `cash[k]`) instead of a full 2D/3D table—every recurrence reads only day `i-1`, so space drops to `O(1)` or `O(k)`.
Initialize `hold = -infinity` (or `-prices[0]`) and `cash = 0`; the `-infinity` start forbids selling before you have ever bought, preventing phantom profit.

When updating in place, the **order matters**: compute `cash` from the OLD `hold`, or compute `hold` first then `cash`—either is fine, but using a freshly-updated `hold` to compute same-day `cash` would allow an illegal same-day buy-then-sell that double-counts.
If `k ≥ n/2` you can make **as many transactions as you want**, so short-circuit to the #122 greedy (`sum of all positive day-to-day deltas`)—this avoids a huge useless `k` loop in #188.
Apply the **fee once per transaction**: subtract it either at buy (`hold = max(hold, cash - price - fee)`) or at sell, never both—#714.
For **cooldown** (#309), the buy must come from two days back: `hold[i] = max(hold[i-1], cash[i-2] - price[i])`, so keep a `prevCash` lagged variable.

problems.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
problems.note: Single transaction (`k=1`): the DP collapses to tracking `minPrice` so far and `maxProfit = max(maxProfit, price - minPrice)`, which is exactly `cash = max(cash, hold + price)` with `hold = max(hold, -price)`.

problems.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II
problems.note: Unlimited transactions: the two-state DP `hold/cash` with no `k` cap, which provably equals the greedy of summing every positive `prices[i] - prices[i-1]` delta.

problems.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock III
problems.note: At most two transactions: run the `k`-indexed DP with `k=2`, tracking four states `buy1, sell1, buy2, sell2` and updating each per day as `max(keep, transition from previous state)`.

problems.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock IV
problems.note: The general `k`-transaction case solved by the `hold[j]/cash[j]` arrays in `O(nk)`; when `k ≥ n/2` short-circuit to the #122 unlimited greedy to avoid a wasteful large `k` loop.

problems.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown
problems.note: Unlimited transactions with a one-day rest after selling: add the cooldown lag so a buy draws from `cash` two days earlier, `hold[i] = max(hold[i-1], cash[i-2] - price)`, via a lagged `prevCash` variable.

problems.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Transaction Fee
problems.note: Unlimited transactions where each round-trip costs a fee: subtract `fee` exactly once per transaction at buy time, `hold = max(hold, cash - price - fee)`, leaving `cash` as the standard sell update.

greedy.tldr: Greedy works for these stock problems because the optimal profit decomposes into locally optimal decisions: track the running minimum (one transaction) or sum every positive day-over-day gain (unlimited transactions).
insight: Both problems ask for maximum profit over a price array, and the **greedy** key is recognizing that profit is a function of price *differences*, not absolute prices. For a single transaction (#121), the best sell at day `i` is constrained only by the **minimum price seen so far**, so a single left-to-right sweep maintaining `minSoFar` and `maxProfit` captures the global optimum — the locally optimal buy point never needs revisiting. For unlimited transactions (#122), the realization is that any multi-day rise from a valley to a peak equals the **sum of consecutive positive deltas** along the way (`telescoping`), so you greedily harvest every `price[i] > price[i-1]` increase.

The structural condition enabling greedy here is the **absence of cross-day coupling beyond the immediate predecessor**: in #121 the only state is the cheapest prior buy; in #122 each adjacent upslope is independently bankable because buying and selling on the same day is free (you can re-buy immediately). The interviewer is probing whether you see that #122's 'unlimited transactions' collapses to 'capture every positive slope' rather than needing a DP over peaks and valleys — and that #121 needs exactly one pass with O(1) memory, not an O(n^2) all-pairs scan.
tricks: #121 invariant: `maxProfit = max(maxProfit, price - minSoFar)` and update `minSoFar = min(minSoFar, price)` AFTER (order matters — same-day buy/sell yields 0, never negative).
#122 reduction: total profit `= sum of max(0, price[i] - price[i-1])`; peak/valley detection gives the identical answer but the delta-sum is shorter and bug-resistant.
Telescoping intuition: a rise `a→d` equals `(b-a)+(c-b)+(d-c)`; summing only positive steps is provably ≥ any partition, so greedy is optimal.
Pitfall: don't try to 'wait for the global max' in #122 — locking in small gains and re-buying is never worse since there's no transaction cost or holding constraint.
Both are O(n) time, O(1) space single-pass — initialize `minSoFar = price[0]` (or +infinity) to avoid off-by-one on the first day.
Distinguish the two at a glance: #121 = best single delta (constrained min), #122 = sum of all positive deltas (unconstrained).

problems.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
problems.note: Greedily track the minimum price seen so far and, at each day, take the best profit if selling today; one O(n) pass with O(1) state captures the single best buy-low/sell-high pair without comparing all pairs.

problems.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II
problems.note: With unlimited free transactions, greedily bank every positive consecutive delta: sum `prices[i] - prices[i-1]` whenever it is positive, which telescopes to the optimal multi-segment profit.

array.tldr: RPN evaluation is the canonical stack-as-array problem: scan the token array left-to-right, push operands, and collapse each operator against the array's top two slots.
insight: **Reverse Polish (postfix) notation** is precisely the linearization of an expression tree in **post-order**: every operator appears immediately after its two operands are fully resolved. That structural guarantee is what lets an **array used as a stack** replace explicit tree construction — when you reach an operator, its operands are guaranteed to be the two most recently produced values, i.e. the top two array slots. The array IS the implicit recursion stack of evaluating the tree, flattened.

The interviewer is probing whether you recognize that postfix needs **no operator precedence, no parentheses, and no parsing lookahead** — order alone encodes structure. The key realization: an operand pushes, an operator pops two and pushes one result, so the stack size strictly decreases by one per operator. A valid expression ends with **exactly one value** on the stack — that final element is the answer and doubles as a validity invariant.
tricks: **Pop order matters for non-commutative ops**: the *second* pop is the left operand. Compute `a = pop(); b = pop(); result = b OP a` for `-` and `/`, or you'll silently invert `5 - 3`.
Use a real array/dynamic array as the stack — `push`/`pop`/`top` are all O(1) at the tail, giving O(n) time and O(n) worst-case space (all operands before any operator).

**Integer division truncates toward zero**, not floor: `6 / -132 == 0`, not `-1`. Many languages' `//` floors, so guard division explicitly (e.g. truncate after a float divide or use C-style `int` division).
Distinguish operator from operand by membership test against the four-symbol set `{+,-,*,/}`, NOT by `isdigit`, since negative operands like `-11` also start non-digit.
Invariant check: before every operator the stack must hold ≥ 2 elements, and after the full scan exactly 1 element remains — use these to assert well-formed input.
No precedence/parenthesis handling is ever needed; if you find yourself writing a shunting-yard pass, you've over-engineered postfix evaluation.

problems.title: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
problems.note: Scan the token array once, treating a backing array as a stack: push parsed integer operands, and on each operator pop the top two (top = right operand, next = left operand), apply the op with truncate-toward-zero division, and push the result. The single remaining stack element after the scan is the evaluated expression.

string.tldr: Expression problems are string-parsing problems in disguise: you walk the raw character stream once, building numbers digit-by-digit and dispatching on operators/brackets via a stack or recursion that mirrors the grammar.
insight: The unifying idea is that an **expression is a serialized parse tree** — the String IS the only data you get, so every solution begins by re-deriving structure (precedence, nesting, scope) from a flat sequence of `chars`. String fits Expression because the two universal hazards both live at the character level: **multi-digit number accumulation** (`num = num*10 + (c-'0')`) and **nesting via brackets** (`()`, `[]`, ternary `?:`, or s-expr parens). The structural condition is that the grammar is **recursive**: a sub-expression can appear wherever a value can, which is exactly what a **stack** (iterative) or **recursion + parse index** (mutable pointer `i`) handles uniformly.

The realization an interviewer probes is **operator precedence and associativity without a full parser**: the canonical trick is to defer addition by pushing signed terms and resolving `*`/`/` immediately against the stack top, evaluating only when you hit a lower-precedence boundary or a closing bracket. Recognizing that `(`/recursion just resets this same machine on a substring — and that the *previous* operator (not the current one) decides what to do with the number you just finished reading — is the whole game.
tricks: **Accumulate multi-digit numbers** with `num = num*10 + (c - '0')` and only act on `num` when the next non-digit char (the delimiter) arrives — never on each digit.

**`prevOp` drives the stack, not `curOp`**: when you finish a number, look at the operator *before* it. `+`/`-` push `±num`; `*`/`/` pop, combine, push back. The answer is `sum(stack)` at the end — this elegantly bakes in `*`/`/` over `+`/`-` precedence (#227, #772).

**Parentheses = recursion or sign-stack**: #224 (no `*`/`/`) pushes the running `result` and `sign` on `(`; #772/#227 recurse on the inner substring or push the whole evaluator state. Either way `(` starts a fresh sub-machine and `)` collapses it.

**Carry a mutable parse index** (`self.i` / pass-by-ref) so recursive sub-parses advance the shared cursor — critical for nested decode (#394), ternary (#439), boolean (#1106), and Lisp (#736) where you don't know substring boundaries up front.

**Don't forget the trailing token**: most bugs are dropping the last number/term because evaluation is triggered by a delimiter — process the final pending `num` after the loop, or append a sentinel like `+`.

**Scope and variables** turn parsing into evaluation-with-environment: #736 and #10018 need a **scoped symbol table** (dict stack / copy-on-recurse) so inner `let` bindings shadow outer ones and are popped on exit.

problems.title: Basic Calculator
problems.note: Only `+`/`-` and parentheses; scan chars accumulating `num`, and on `(` push the current `result` and `sign` onto a stack, restoring them on `)`. No precedence stack needed since there is no `*`/`/`.

problems.title: Basic Calculator II
problems.note: No parentheses but `*`/`/` precedence: keep a stack, and when you hit an operator (or string end) apply the *previous* op — push `±num` for `+`/`-`, but pop-and-combine for `*`/`/` — then `sum(stack)`.

problems.title: Different Ways to Add Parentheses
problems.note: Treat each operator char as a split point: recurse on the left and right substrings, then combine every pair of results under that operator. The string indexing of operators defines the divide-and-conquer recursion (memoize on substring).

problems.title: Expression Add Operators
problems.note: DFS over positions in the digit string, choosing to insert `+`, `-`, `*`, or nothing between digits; carry running `value` and a `prev` term so `*` can retroactively fix precedence (`value - prev + prev*cur`). Watch leading-zero substrings.

problems.title: Decode String
problems.note: Bracketed repetition `k[...]`: scan chars, push the current string and count `k` on `(`/`[`; on `]` pop and repeat the built segment. Multi-digit `k` needs the same `num*10` accumulation as calculators.

problems.title: Ternary Expression Parser
problems.note: Right-associative `?:` — easiest scanned right-to-left with a stack, or recursively with a parse index where on `?` you evaluate the condition char and recurse into the chosen branch, skipping the other via bracket-style `?`/`:` depth counting.

problems.title: Number of Atoms
problems.note: Parse element names (uppercase + optional lowercase), trailing multiplicity counts, and `()` groups multiplied by a following number; use a stack of count-maps that get merged and scaled on `)`. Final output sorted with formula-style counts.

problems.title: Parse Lisp Expression
problems.note: S-expression recursion with a **scoped environment**: tokenize within parens, and for `let` bind variables into a copied/stacked dict before evaluating the body, so inner scopes shadow and are discarded on return. Parse index advances through the nested string.

problems.title: Basic Calculator III
problems.note: Full combination of #224+#227: precedence stack for `*`/`/` plus parentheses handled by recursing on the inner substring (or pushing evaluator state), then `sum(stack)`. The canonical char-scan + `prevOp` template.

problems.title: Parsing A Boolean Expression
problems.note: Recursive grammar `!(...)`, `&(...)`, `|(...)`, `t`, `f`: scan chars onto a stack, and on `)` pop operands until the matching `(`, apply the operator just below it, and push the resulting `t`/`f`. Index-driven recursion is the clean alternative.

problems.title: Evaluate arithmetic expression with variables
problems.note: Arithmetic-with-environment: parse the expression string while resolving identifiers against a **symbol table**, combining the precedence/parenthesis machinery of #772 with variable lookup like #736 so leaves are either numeric literals or bound variable values.

stack-topic.tldr: Expression problems are solved with a stack because operator precedence, parentheses, and nesting are inherently LIFO — you push pending context and pop it the moment a higher-priority or closing token forces evaluation.
insight: Every expression is a tree, but you almost never build the tree explicitly. The stack **is** the tree's spine: it holds the partially-evaluated context you must resume after finishing a deeper sub-expression. The structural trigger is **nesting plus precedence** — a `(`, a string multiplier `[`, a function call, or a higher-priority operator all mean "suspend what I'm doing, descend, and come back." That suspend/resume is exactly a stack push/pop, so the moment you see balanced delimiters or mixed `+ - * /`, the answer is a stack (often two: one for operands, one for operators/signs/context).

The key realization an interviewer probes is that you do NOT need a separate tokenizer + parser + evaluator pass. You can fold lexing and evaluation into a single left-to-right scan: accumulate multi-digit numbers, and resolve each operator **as late as legally possible** — `* /` resolve immediately against the operand stack, `+ -` defer by pushing a signed term, and `( )` recurse by snapshotting state on the stack. Whether you carry an explicit sign, a `(prev_result, prev_op)` frame, or recurse on the index, the invariant is the same: the stack reconstructs the evaluation order that precedence and parentheses imply.
tricks: **Two-stack vs. sign-deferral**: for `+ - * /` keep a `nums` stack and apply `* /` instantly while pushing `+a` / `-a` for additive terms, then sum at the end — this auto-handles precedence without an operator stack. Basic Calculator (only `+ - ( )`) collapses to a single `sign` + result stack.

**Parentheses = push the whole context**: on `(` push `(result_so_far, sign_or_op)` and reset; on `)` pop and combine. Equivalently, recurse and let the call stack BE the stack — cleaner for Lisp/nested-`[` problems.

**Postfix (RPN) is the trivial case**: no precedence logic at all — push operands, on an operator pop two (mind operand ORDER: `b` popped first is the right operand, so compute `a OP b`), push result.
**Always finish the last token**: numbers and the final pending operator are flushed after the loop ends — a classic off-by-one bug is forgetting to apply the trailing `+ num` or last operand.
**Reset the accumulator after consuming it**: set `num = 0` and clear the pending sign/op right after pushing, or digits bleed across operators.

**Nesting needs paired stacks**: Decode String and Number of Atoms push a count/multiplier on one stack and the partial string/atom-map on another at each `[` / `(`, multiplying on the matching close.

problems.title: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
problems.note: Pure postfix evaluation: push every operand; on an operator pop the top two (second-popped is the left operand), apply, and push the result back — the stack top at the end is the answer.

problems.title: Basic Calculator
problems.note: Only `+ - ( )`, no precedence among operators, so carry a running `result` and current `sign`; on `(` push `(result, sign)` and reset, on `)` pop and fold the inner result back with the saved sign.

problems.title: Basic Calculator II
problems.note: No parentheses but `* /` outrank `+ -`: scan with a `nums` stack, push `+num`/`-num` for additive terms and immediately apply `* /` against `nums.pop()`, then return the sum of the stack.

problems.title: Decode String
problems.note: Nested `k[...]` decoding uses two stacks — a count stack and a string stack; on `[` push the current count and built string and reset, on `]` pop and append `prev_string + count * current_string`.

problems.title: Ternary Expression Parser
problems.note: Right-associative `a?b:c`: scan right-to-left pushing characters; when you hit `?`, the top is the true-branch and next the false-branch — pop both, select by the boolean before `?`, and push the chosen token so nesting resolves outward.

problems.title: Number of Atoms
problems.note: Parentheses with multipliers over count-maps: push a fresh atom→count map on `(`; on `)` read the trailing multiplier, scale the popped map, and merge it into the map now on top of the stack.

problems.title: Parse Lisp Expression
problems.note: `let/add/mult` with lexical scope: recurse so the call stack holds nested expressions while a scope stack (or chained maps) holds variable bindings, popping/restoring the `let` scope as each parenthesized form returns.

problems.title: Basic Calculator III
problems.note: Combines precedence and parentheses: use the two-stack `* /`-immediate / `+ -`-deferred scheme, and on `(` recurse (or push full context) so the inner expression evaluates as one operand before applying the outer operator.

problems.title: Parsing A Boolean Expression
problems.note: Nested `!`, `&`, `|` over `t/f`: push tokens until `)`, then pop operands back to the matching `(`, apply the operator sitting just before `(`, and push the single boolean result back onto the stack.

problems.title: Evaluate arithmetic expression with variables
problems.note: Same operand/operator two-stack evaluation as Basic Calculator III, except identifier tokens are resolved through a variable→value lookup before being pushed as operands, with `( )` recursion handling nesting.

backtrack.tldr: Both problems recursively split an expression string into pieces and combine sub-results — backtracking over operator placement (or split points), where the operator choice IS the decision tree.
insight: The unifying idea is that an arithmetic expression is a **recursive structure**: any full evaluation is determined by *where you split the digit string and which operator binds at each split*. Backtracking fits because the set of legal splits/operator placements forms a decision tree — at each position you branch over the available choices (`+`, `-`, `*`, or a parenthesis boundary), recurse on the remainder, then undo. The structural condition that makes this apply is that the input is a *flat string with no fixed structure*: you must enumerate all ways to impose structure, which is exactly what backtracking enumerates.

The key realization an interviewer probes is the difference between **enumerate-all-groupings** (#241, divide-and-conquer recursion over split indices returning *sets of values*) and **enumerate-all-operator-strings** (#282, classic incremental backtracking that builds one expression character-by-character and evaluates on the fly). Both are backtracking over expression structure, but #282 adds the crucial twist that `*` violates left-to-right evaluation, forcing you to carry the *last appended operand* so multiplication can be applied with correct precedence without a parser.
tricks: **Multiplication precedence trick (#282):** maintain `prev` = the value of the last term added. For `+`, recurse with `cur = val + d` and pass `prev = d`; for `-`, pass `prev = -d`; for `*`, undo the last term and reapply: `cur = val - prev + prev*d`, passing `prev = prev*d`.

**Leading-zero pitfall (#282):** an operand may not have a leading zero unless it is exactly `0` — break the loop after consuming a `0`-started multi-digit operand, i.e. `if s[start]=='0' and i>start: break`.

**No operator before first operand (#282):** the first operand is fixed (no leading `+`/`-`/`*`); only positions *after* the first digit chunk branch over the three operators or 'no operator' (extend the current number).
**Overflow:** use 64-bit/long for the running value and parsed operands; expression substrings up to length 10 still produce values that overflow 32-bit when multiplied.

**#241 returns value sets, not one value:** for each operator at index `i`, recursively compute `left = solve(s[:i])` and `right = solve(s[i+1:])`, then combine every pair — the recursion branches on *every* operator position, not characters.

**Memoization on substrings (#241):** identical substrings recur; cache `solve(substring) -> list of results` (or split on index ranges) to cut exponential blowup, turning Catalan-number recomputation into polynomial reuse.

problems.title: Different Ways to Add Parentheses
problems.note: Backtrack/divide over every operator index `i`: recursively evaluate the left substring `s[:i]` and right substring `s[i+1:]` into all possible value lists, then combine each `(l op r)` pair — every distinct split corresponds to a distinct parenthesization, with memoization on substrings to avoid recomputing shared sub-expressions.

problems.title: Expression Add Operators
problems.note: Classic incremental backtracking: at each boundary after the first operand, branch into inserting `+`, `-`, `*`, or extending the current number, carrying the running value `cur` and the last term `prev` so multiplication is reapplied with correct precedence (`cur - prev + prev*d`); emit paths where `cur == target`, pruning leading-zero operands.

graph.tldr: Model scheduling constraints as a directed graph and let cycle-detection, topological order, and reachability closure decide feasibility, ordering, and dependency queries.
insight: Scheduling problems are almost always **precedence problems in disguise**: "do A before B," "B requires A," "each person sits next to their favorite." Each constraint is a directed edge `u -> v`, turning the schedule into a **directed graph**. The structural realization an interviewer probes for is that a valid schedule exists **iff the graph is a DAG** (no directed cycle), and any valid schedule is exactly a **topological order**. So feasibility = cycle detection, an explicit ordering = topo sort (Kahn's BFS on in-degrees, or DFS post-order reversed).

The four problems span the full spectrum of what a precedence graph answers: pure feasibility (#207), an explicit order (#210), all-pairs *reachability* / transitive closure for dependency queries (#1462), and the harder #2127 where the *favorite* relation gives each node out-degree exactly 1 (a **functional graph**), forcing you to reason about its **cycles plus the trees hanging off them** rather than topo order. The unifying lens: define the edge direction precisely, then pick the graph primitive — cycle check, topo sort, closure, or functional-graph decomposition — that the question is really asking for.
tricks: Fix **edge direction** first and write it on paper: "prereq `a` then course `b`" → edge `a -> b`, so a topo order lists prereqs first. Reversing direction silently flips your answer.

**Kahn's algorithm** doubles as the cycle detector: if the number of nodes popped (in-degree hitting 0) is less than `n`, a cycle remains and the schedule is **infeasible** — no separate check needed.

For #1462's many queries, precompute **transitive closure** once: either `O(V*(V+E))` BFS/DFS from every node, or process nodes in topo order propagating ancestor bitsets (`reach[v] |= reach[u]`), then answer each query in `O(1)`.

#2127 is NOT a topo/DAG problem: out-degree is exactly 1, so it is a **functional graph**. The seating is a circle, so detect cycles via `in-degree`-style peeling or visited-timestamps; **2-cycles (mutual favorites)** are special — chains can attach to both nodes.

Answer for #2127 = `max(largest pure cycle length, sum over all mutual pairs of (2 + longest chain into each of the two nodes))`. Compute longest incoming chains with a **reverse-graph BFS / topo peeling** of the non-cycle nodes.

Prefer **iterative DFS or BFS** for large prerequisite graphs to avoid recursion-stack overflow, and use an adjacency list plus an `in-degree` array rather than an adjacency matrix when `V` is large and sparse.

problems.title: Course Schedule
problems.note: Build the prerequisite digraph (`prereq -> course`) and ask only whether a valid order exists; run Kahn's topo sort and return true iff all `n` nodes get processed (no cycle), which is pure DAG feasibility detection.

problems.title: Course Schedule II
problems.note: Same prerequisite digraph as #207 but now emit the order: the sequence in which nodes reach in-degree 0 during Kahn's algorithm is a valid topological schedule, or return an empty array if a cycle blocks completion.

problems.title: Course Schedule IV
problems.note: Answer many `isPrerequisite(u, v)` queries by precomputing the **transitive closure** of the prerequisite DAG — propagate ancestor sets in topological order (`reach[v] |= reach[u]`) — then each query is an `O(1)` membership test for `u` in `v`'s ancestor set.

problems.title: Maximum Employees to Be Invited to a Meeting
problems.note: Each employee points to one favorite, giving a **functional graph** (out-degree 1) seated around a table; the answer is the larger of the longest single cycle, or the sum over all mutual pairs (2-cycles) of two plus the longest chains feeding into each member, found via reverse-graph BFS.

array.tldr: In Scheduling problems the array is first **sorted by a chosen key** (start, end, or cost), turning ordering chaos into a single sweep where greedy choices or interval DP become provably correct.
insight: Scheduling is fundamentally about resolving conflicts among **intervals or tasks laid out on a 1-D timeline**, and an array is the natural container for that timeline. The recurring move is to **sort the array by the key that linearizes the decision**: sort by `start` to detect/process overlaps in time order, sort by `end` to make a greedy 'finish earliest' choice safe, or sort by `cost`/`profit` to drive an exchange argument. Once sorted, a single left-to-right sweep — often paired with a heap, a difference array, or a `prev_end` scalar — answers the question without re-examining pairs.

The interviewer is probing whether you recognize that **the right sort key is the whole problem**: overlap counting needs the events split and ordered; minimum-rooms needs start/end timelines merged; profit maximization needs sort-by-end plus binary search into the DP array (the **weighted interval scheduling** template). When tasks have no inherent timeline (Task Scheduler, partitioning a sequence into days), the array instead encodes either frequencies to be greedily spread out or a contiguous sequence sliced by interval DP — the array's *index adjacency* becomes the scheduling constraint.
