tricks: **Pick the sort key deliberately**: by `end` for 'max non-overlapping / earliest finish' greedy, by `start` for sweep-line overlap detection, by `cost`/profit for exchange-argument greedy.

**Sweep-line via two sorted arrays or events**: separate starts and ends (or emit `(+1)` at start, `(-1)` at end), sort, and track a running counter — its peak is the max concurrent intervals (rooms needed).
**Sort-by-end + min-heap of end times** is the room-allocation idiom: reuse a room when the earliest-freeing end `<=` current start, else allocate; heap size = answer.
**Weighted interval scheduling**: sort by `end`, build `dp[i] = max(skip, take + dp[p(i)])` where `p(i)` is found by **binary search** for the latest job ending `<= start_i` in the sorted-end array.
**Half-open intervals** `[start, end)`: treat touching endpoints as non-overlapping; order ties so `end` events process before `start` events to avoid off-by-one room over-counting.
**Frequency/cooldown scheduling** uses the array of counts, not a timeline: place the most frequent task first (max-heap) and compute idle slots from `(maxFreq-1)*(n+1) + countOfMax`.
array.pseudo:
// Canonical: sweep + heap (room/overlap class)
sort(intervals, key = start)
heap = minHeap()          // stores end times
maxRooms = 0
for [s, e] in intervals:
    while heap and heap.top() <= s:   // half-open: a room freed
        heap.pop()
    heap.push(e)
    maxRooms = max(maxRooms, heap.size())
return maxRooms

// Canonical: weighted interval scheduling (profit class)
sort(jobs, key = end)
dp[0] = 0
for i in 1..n:
    j = binarySearch latest job with end <= start_i
    dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], profit_i + dp[j])
return dp[n]

problems.title: Meeting Rooms
problems.note: Sort the interval array by `start`, then sweep once checking `intervals[i].start < intervals[i-1].end`; any overlap means a meeting can't be attended. Pure ordering + adjacent comparison.

problems.title: Meeting Rooms II
problems.note: Sort by `start` and keep a min-heap of end times (or split into sorted start/end arrays as a sweep): the peak count of simultaneously-open intervals is the minimum rooms.

problems.title: Task Scheduler
problems.note: Build a frequency array over tasks (not a timeline); the answer is `max(len, (maxFreq-1)*(n+1) + countOfMaxFreq)` — schedule the most frequent task first and fill cooldown gaps with others.

problems.title: Two City Scheduling
problems.note: Sort the cost array by `costA - costB` (the savings of sending to A over B); send the first half to A and the rest to B — an exchange-argument greedy over a single sorted key.

problems.title: Meeting Scheduler
problems.note: Sort both availability arrays by `start` and two-pointer sweep, taking the overlap `[max(s1,s2), min(e1,e2)]`; report the first window whose length `>= duration`, advancing the pointer with the smaller end.

problems.title: Maximum Profit in Job Scheduling
problems.note: The textbook **weighted interval scheduling**: sort jobs by `end`, and `dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], profit_i + dp[p(i)])` where `p(i)` is binary-searched as the latest job ending `<= start_i`.

problems.title: Minimum Difficulty of a Job Schedule
problems.note: Jobs form a contiguous ordered array that must be partitioned into `d` days; interval DP `dp[i][k]` minimizes sum of per-day maxima over slices, using array adjacency (not time) as the scheduling constraint.

problems.title: Task Scheduler II
problems.note: Iterate the task array in order while keeping a map of each task's next-available day; advance the day to `max(day+1, nextAvail[task])` then set `nextAvail[task] = day + space + 1`. Sequence position, not sorting, drives the schedule.

problems.title: Meeting Rooms III
problems.note: Sort meetings by `start`; use a min-heap of free room ids plus a min-heap of `(freeTime, roomId)` for busy rooms. If none free, pop the earliest-freeing room and delay the meeting; tally a per-room count array and return the busiest room.

greedy.tldr: In Scheduling, Greedy means sort by the right key (start, end, or cost-delta) and make an irreversible locally-optimal choice per interval — the sorted order *is* the proof of correctness.
insight: Scheduling problems live on a timeline of intervals, and Greedy works because of an **exchange argument**: once you sort by the correct key, the first choice in sorted order can always replace any choice in an optimal solution without making it worse. The entire skill is identifying that key — sort by **end time** when you want to fit the most non-overlapping intervals or test feasibility, sort by **start time** when you want to detect overlap or track concurrency, and sort by a **cost difference** (`costA - costB`) when you must split items between two options under a constraint.

The interviewer is probing whether you recognize that local optimality propagates globally here. The tell is the **structural condition**: greedy is exact only when the objective lacks the kind of weight that breaks the exchange (e.g. unweighted interval scheduling). The moment intervals carry **profit** (#1235), pure greedy collapses and you must fall back to **DP over sorted intervals with binary search** — sorting still sets up the problem, but the decision becomes 'take vs skip' computed bottom-up, not a one-shot greedy pick.
tricks: Pick the sort key by goal: **earliest end** = max non-overlapping count / feasibility; **earliest start** = concurrency / room counting; **cost-delta** = two-bucket partition under a count constraint.
Overlap test invariant: after sorting by start, two meetings conflict iff `prev.end > curr.start` (touching endpoints `==` do NOT overlap — Meeting Rooms uses strict `>`).

Meeting Rooms II: a **min-heap of end times** sized to the max concurrency is the room count; pop every room whose `end <= curr.start` before pushing. Equivalently, sweep separated start/end arrays with a two-pointer counter.

Two City Scheduling: sort by `costA - costB`; the `n` most negative deltas (cheapest-to-send-to-A) go to city A, the rest to B — this beats any per-person greedy because you greedily minimize the *regret* of forcing the constraint.

Weighted intervals (#1235) break greedy: sort by end, then `dp[i] = max(skip, profit[i] + dp[ p(i) ])` where `p(i)` is the last non-conflicting job found by **binary search** — never just pick highest profit or earliest end.
Pitfall: forgetting that the sort dominates complexity at `O(n log n)`, and confusing 'max meetings attended' (greedy by end) with 'min rooms' (heap by start) — they use opposite intuitions.

problems.title: Meeting Rooms
problems.note: Sort meetings by start time, then sweep once checking `prev.end > curr.start`; any strict overlap means a person cannot attend all meetings, so return false. Pure feasibility greedy in `O(n log n)`.

problems.title: Meeting Rooms II
problems.note: Sort by start, maintain a **min-heap of end times**: before booking each meeting, pop any room whose end `<= curr.start`, then push the new end; the heap's maximum size is the minimum number of rooms. Equivalently a two-pointer sweep over sorted start and end arrays tracking peak concurrency.

problems.title: Two City Scheduling
problems.note: Sort the `2n` people by the delta `costA - costB`; send the first `n` (most negative delta, i.e. relatively cheaper for city A) to A and the rest to B. The exchange argument on cost-difference guarantees minimal total cost under the equal-split constraint.

problems.title: Maximum Profit in Job Scheduling
problems.note: The profit weight breaks pure greedy, so sort jobs by **end time** and run DP: `dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], profit_i + dp[p(i)])` where `p(i)` is found by **binary search** for the latest job ending at or before job `i`'s start. Greedy sorting sets up an `O(n log n)` weighted-interval-scheduling DP.

interval.tldr: Scheduling feasibility reduces to detecting whether any two time intervals overlap, which you find in `O(n log n)` by sorting on start time and checking adjacent pairs.
insight: A meeting is literally an **interval** `[start, end)` on the timeline, so the scheduling question "can one resource serve all meetings?" is exactly the question "are these intervals pairwise non-overlapping?". The key structural realization is that you don't need all O(n^2) pairs: if you **sort by start time**, the only candidate for a conflict with meeting `i` is its immediate predecessor `i-1`. Once sorted, overlap becomes a purely local check between neighbors.

The invariant an interviewer is probing for is the **half-open interval** convention: a meeting ending at `t` and another starting at `t` do NOT conflict, so the conflict test must be `interval[i].start < interval[i-1].end` (strict `<`), not `<=`. Recognizing that sorting collapses a quadratic pairwise problem into a single linear sweep — and getting the boundary semantics right — is the entire point.
tricks: **Sort by start time first**, then only compare each interval to the previous one — sorted order guarantees no earlier-starting meeting can be the hidden conflict.
Use a **strict `<` for overlap**: `cur.start < prev.end` means conflict. Touching endpoints (`[0,30]` then `[30,45]`) are allowed because end is exclusive — using `<=` is the classic off-by-one bug.

After sorting by start, track `prev_end` as a running max only if intervals can be nested; for plain Meeting Rooms, comparing `cur.start` to the immediately previous `end` suffices since sorted starts make the previous end the relevant boundary.
Return `false` on the first detected overlap (early exit) — no need to scan the rest.
Edge cases: 0 or 1 meetings are trivially feasible (`true`); never index `i-1` without the sort and the `i >= 1` guard.
Sorting dominates at `O(n log n)` time, `O(1)` or `O(n)` extra space depending on whether the sort is in place.

problems.title: Meeting Rooms
problems.note: Treat each meeting as an interval `[start, end)`; sort by start time, then scan adjacent pairs and return `false` the moment `intervals[i].start < intervals[i-1].end` (strict comparison so back-to-back meetings don't count as overlapping). If no adjacent pair overlaps, one room suffices and the answer is `true`.

heap.tldr: A min-heap is the engine that always surfaces the next event to process — the room that frees earliest or the task whose cooldown expires soonest — turning scheduling into a greedy "pop-soonest, push-when-done" simulation.
insight: Scheduling problems share a structural core: you have resources (CPU slots, meeting rooms) and a stream of jobs competing for them under timing constraints, and at every decision point you must know **which resource frees up next** or **which job is most urgent right now**. A **min-heap keyed on availability/finish time** answers that `O(log n)` query repeatedly, which is exactly the primitive greedy scheduling needs. The unifying realization an interviewer probes for is that the *next* relevant moment in a schedule is never arbitrary — it's the minimum over a small frontier of pending end-times or counts — so a priority queue lets you jump event-to-event instead of ticking through every time unit.

The two canonical shapes differ in what the heap holds. In **resource-allocation** scheduling (Meeting Rooms III) you keep two heaps — `free` rooms (keyed by index) and `busy` rooms (keyed by end time) — and lazily roll the clock forward by popping freed rooms; this is the classic two-heap 'event simulation'. In **bounded-cooldown** scheduling (Task Scheduler) the heap is keyed by remaining frequency: you greedily fire the most-frequent available task each tick and hold cooling tasks in a side queue until their cooldown lapses, balancing load so idle slots are minimized.
tricks: Use **two heaps** for room/resource allocation: `available` (min-heap by smallest index, so ties pick the lowest-numbered room) and `occupied` (min-heap by `end_time`, tie-broken by index). Before assigning, drain everything in `occupied` whose `end_time <= now` back into `available`.

**Lazy time advance**: when no room is free at a meeting's `start`, do NOT scan — pop the earliest-finishing busy room, set the new start to its end time, and keep its duration (delayed meetings preserve their original length).

Tie-breaking is load-bearing: in #2402 a freed room must be re-keyed by **index** not end time, and you must process meetings **sorted by start**; sorting wrong or breaking ties wrong silently fails edge cases.
In #621, key the heap by **remaining count** (max-heap) and always discharge the most frequent task first; this is what guarantees the minimal number of forced idle slots.

After firing a task in #621, push it into a **cooldown queue with a ready-time** `(count, t + n + 1)`; only return it to the heap once `time` reaches that ready-time — the side queue, not the heap, models the cooldown window.

Pitfall: don't literally loop one time-unit at a time for large `n` in #621 — either simulate tick-by-tick (`O(total_tasks)`, fine since ≤ a few thousand) or use the closed-form `max(len, (maxFreq-1)*(n+1) + countOfMax)`; the heap version is the recall-friendly one.
heap.pseudo:
// Resource-allocation scheduling (Meeting Rooms III shape)
sort meetings by start
free  = min-heap of room indices [0..rooms-1]
busy  = min-heap of (end_time, room_index)
for (start, end) in meetings:
    while busy not empty and busy.top.end <= start:
        free.push(pop(busy).room)
    if free not empty:
        r = free.pop();  busy.push((end, r))
    else:                      // all rooms occupied -> delay
        (e, r) = busy.pop()
        busy.push((e + (end - start), r))   // keep duration
    count[r] += 1
return argmax(count)           // lowest index on ties

problems.title: Task Scheduler
problems.note: Push task frequencies into a **max-heap**; each tick pop the most-frequent available task, decrement it, and stash it in a cooldown queue tagged with ready-time `time + n`. When the heap is empty but the cooldown queue is not, the gap counts as idle time — the heap's greedy 'most-frequent-first' choice minimizes those idles.

problems.title: Meeting Rooms III
problems.note: Run a **two-heap** event simulation over meetings sorted by start: a min-heap of free rooms by index and a min-heap of busy rooms by end time. Free up rooms whose end `<= start`, assign the lowest-index free room, or if none, pop the earliest-finishing room and **delay** the meeting (preserving its duration); tally per-room usage and return the most-used (lowest index on ties).

two-pointers.tldr: Sort both availability lists, then sweep two pointers in lockstep to find the earliest overlapping window long enough to hold the meeting.
insight: Scheduling problems reduce to **interval intersection**: given two people's free slots, find a common open window. The structural enabler is that each person's slots are (or can be) **sorted by start time** and are **non-overlapping**, so the two timelines are monotone. That monotonicity is exactly the precondition for a **two-pointer merge sweep** — you never need to revisit an earlier slot, because once a slot ends before the other timeline's current slot starts, it can never overlap anything later either.

The key realization an interviewer probes for: the overlap of `[s1,e1]` and `[s2,e2]` is `[max(s1,s2), min(e1,e2)]`, which is valid iff `start < end`, and you require `end - start >= duration`. Then you **advance the pointer of whichever slot finishes first** (smaller `end`), because that slot is exhausted relative to the other timeline. This is an `O(m+n)` sweep after the `O(m log m + n log n)` sort — strictly better than the `O(m*n)` brute-force pairing.
tricks: **Sort first, then sweep**: if slots aren't guaranteed sorted by start, sort both lists; the lockstep advance is only correct on monotone timelines.
**Overlap formula**: `start = max(a[i].start, b[j].start)`, `end = min(a[i].end, b[j].end)`; a usable window exists iff `start + duration <= end` (equivalently `end - start >= duration`).
**Advance rule**: move the pointer whose slot has the smaller `end` (`a[i].end < b[j].end ? i++ : j++`); advancing the earlier-ending slot is what guarantees no overlap is skipped.
**Earliest answer is automatic**: because both lists are sorted and you scan left-to-right, the first valid window found is the earliest-starting one — return immediately.
**Pitfall — strict vs inclusive ends**: meetings are typically half-open, so a zero-length touch (`start == end`) is not a real overlap; guard with `+ duration` rather than `start < end` alone.
**Tie-break on equal ends**: when `a[i].end == b[j].end`, advancing either pointer is fine, but be consistent to avoid an infinite loop — always strictly advance one.

problems.title: Meeting Scheduler
problems.note: Sort both `slots1` and `slots2` by start, then run two pointers `i,j`; at each step compute the intersection `[max(start), min(end)]` and return `[start, start+duration]` the moment its length is `>= duration`. Advance the pointer of the slot with the smaller `end` since it can't overlap any later slot, yielding the earliest valid window in `O(m+n)` after sorting.

dp.tldr: Scheduling DP partitions an *ordered* job sequence into d contiguous days, with `dp[i][k]` = min cost to schedule jobs i.. into k remaining days, choosing each day's cut point.
insight: Scheduling problems become DP when the schedule is an **ordered, contiguous partition**: jobs must be done in sequence (a job depends on its predecessors), and you must split that sequence into a fixed number of groups (days). The decision at each step — *where does today's batch end?* — has **optimal substructure**: the best way to schedule jobs `i..n` in `k` days is the best first-day cut plus the optimal schedule of the remainder. Because each prefix-to-day assignment only cares about the boundary index and the days left, the state collapses to `(start_index, days_remaining)`, giving a polynomial table instead of exponential enumeration of all partitions.

The key realization an interviewer probes: the day's cost is the **max difficulty within the contiguous block** (not the sum), and total cost is the sum of those per-day maxes. So as you extend today's block by one more job, you incrementally update a running max and pay it once for the whole block. The hard constraint — you need at least one job per remaining day — is what makes the loop bounds non-trivial and is the classic off-by-one trap.
tricks: State is `dp[i][d]` = min total difficulty to schedule jobs `i..n-1` using exactly `d` days; answer is `dp[0][D]`, with `-1` (infeasible) if `n < D`.

Feasibility pruning: at state `(i, d)` you must leave `>= d-1` jobs for the remaining days, so today's block can extend only while `n - j >= d - 1`; equivalently `j` (last index of today) ranges so that enough jobs remain.
The cost of a day is the **running max** over its block, not a prefix sum — maintain `curMax = max(curMax, jobDifficulty[j])` as you grow the block, and add `curMax` once per candidate split.
Base case: when `d == 1`, the only choice is to take *all* remaining jobs in one day, so the cost is the max over the entire suffix — handle this explicitly or as the natural last layer.
Complexity is `O(n^2 * D)` (for each (i,d) you scan the day's end), `O(n*D)` space; this beats the `C(n-1, D-1)` brute-force partition count.
Watch the bridge from 1-indexed math to 0-indexed arrays and ensure `D <= n` up front, otherwise no valid assignment exists.
dp.pseudo:
function minDifficulty(jobs, D):
    n = len(jobs)
    if n < D: return -1
    # dp[i][d] = min cost to schedule jobs[i:] in d days
    dp = table[n+1][D+1] filled with INF
    for i in 0..n: dp[i][0] = (i == n) ? 0 : INF
    for d in 1..D:
        for i in 0..n-d:                 # need >= d jobs left
            curMax = 0
            # today's block = jobs[i..j], rest in d-1 days
            for j in i..n-d:             # leave >= d-1 jobs after j
                curMax = max(curMax, jobs[j])
                dp[i][d] = min(dp[i][d], curMax + dp[j+1][d-1])
    return dp[0][D]

problems.title: Minimum Difficulty of a Job Schedule
problems.note: Jobs are done in order and split into exactly `d` contiguous days; `dp[i][k]` = min sum-of-daily-maxes to finish jobs `i..n-1` in `k` days, where each transition picks how far today's block extends and pays its running max. Answer is `dp[0][d]`, returning `-1` when `n < d` since each day needs at least one job.

hash.tldr: A hash table maps each task type to the earliest day it may run again, turning "respect a cooldown gap" scheduling into O(1) lookups and updates.
insight: Scheduling problems with **cooldown** or **spacing** constraints share one structural condition: each distinct task type carries its own independent timing rule, and you must repeatedly answer "when is this type next allowed?" A **hash table** keyed by task type is the natural fit because task labels are arbitrary (strings, ints, anything hashable) and sparse — you never need a dense array, just O(1) access to the per-type state that the scheduling rule depends on.

The key realization an interviewer probes is that you don't simulate every idle/wait day — you *jump time forward* by computing the day directly from stored state. The map holds the **next-allowed day** (or equivalently the last-done day) per type; for each task you advance the clock to `max(current+1, nextAllowed)` and then write back the new cooldown horizon. Hash Table converts a potentially O(days) simulation into O(n) over the task sequence.
tricks: Store **next-allowed day** (`lastDone + space + 1`), not last-done day — it removes an addition from the hot path and makes the guard a single comparison.
Always advance the clock as `day = max(day + 1, nextAllowed[type])`: the `+1` accounts for the task itself consuming a day, the `max` enforces the cooldown without looping over idle days.
Use `getOrDefault(type, 0)` (or `0` for absent keys) so a first-seen task runs immediately with no special-casing — day 0/1 initialization falls out naturally.
Update the map *after* picking the day: write `nextAllowed[type] = day + space + 1` so the same type's next occurrence is correctly gated.
Pitfall: the cooldown is per-type, not global — do not keep a single shared timer; the whole point of the hash map is independent horizons keyed by task identity.
Off-by-one: distinguish 'days between' (gap of `space`) from 'next allowed index'; verify with a 2-task adjacent-duplicate example before committing.

problems.title: Task Scheduler II
problems.note: Maintain a hash map from each task type to the earliest day it may be repeated (`completedDay + space + 1`); iterate the task list advancing `day = max(day + 1, nextAllowed[type])`, which skips idle days in O(1) instead of simulating them, then refresh the map entry. The map's sparse per-type keying handles arbitrary task ids and gives the total days as the final clock value.
